🧩 Algorithms, Data Structures & ADTs — the vocabulary

TermDefinitionExample
AlgorithmA finite, precise set of steps that solves a problembinary search
Data structureA way of ORGANIZING data in memory so it can be used efficientlyarray, linked list, tree
ADT (Abstract Data Type)A model defined by WHAT operations it supports — not how they're implementedStack ADT: push, pop, peek
THE KEY DISTINCTION
An ADT is a contract ("what"): a Stack promises push/pop/peek with LIFO order. The underlying data structure is the "how": that Stack could be built on an array OR a linked list — callers never need to know which.
WORKED EXAMPLE — same ADT, two implementations
ADTImplementation AImplementation BCaller sees
StackArray with a top-indexLinked list with head insertOnly push()/pop()/peek() — identical either way
ListArray (contiguous)Linked list (nodes+pointers)Only add()/get()/remove()
⚠️ ADT ≠ DATA STRUCTURE
"Stack" is an ADT (a set of rules); "array" is a data structure (a memory layout). Don't call an array an ADT, and don't call the Stack ADT a "data structure" on the OA.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
An ADT is best defined as:
  1. A specification of operations and behavior, independent of implementation
  2. A specific block of memory
  3. A sorting algorithm
  4. A programming language feature
Show answer + steps
A. ADT = the WHAT (contract). The underlying array/linked-list/tree is the HOW (implementation), and can change without affecting callers.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before diving into specific data structures, you need crisp definitions of three terms the OA constantly mixes: algorithm, data structure, and abstract data type (ADT). Confusing them is the most common foundational mistake. Get these straight and the rest of the course slots into a clean mental framework.

Algorithm

An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. It must be:

FIVE PROPERTIES OF AN ALGORITHM
1. Finite — terminates after a bounded number of steps
2. Well-defined — each step is unambiguous
3. Input — accepts zero or more values
4. Output — produces at least one result
5. Effective — each step is doable with basic operations
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Finding the maximum in a list
def find_max(numbers):
 largest = numbers[0]
 for n in numbers[1:]:
 if n > largest:
 largest = n
 return largest
✓
Finite: stops after n iterations.
✓
Well-defined: each comparison is unambiguous.
✓
Input: a list. Output: the maximum value.
✓
Effective: comparison and assignment are basic.

Data structure

A data structure is a SPECIFIC way of organizing and storing data in memory. It's an IMPLEMENTATION choice — how the bytes are laid out and how you access them.

EXAMPLES OF DATA STRUCTURES
Array: contiguous memory cells indexed by integer
Linked list: nodes scattered in memory connected by pointers
Hash table: array of buckets accessed via hash function
Binary tree: nodes with left/right pointers
Heap: complete binary tree (often stored in an array)

Abstract Data Type (ADT)

An ADT is a SPECIFICATION — what operations the data type supports and what they should do, WITHOUT saying HOW. It's the interface, not the implementation.

EXAMPLES OF ADTs
List: ordered sequence with insert/remove/get-by-index
Stack: LIFO with push/pop/peek
Queue: FIFO with enqueue/dequeue/peek
Deque: both ends with addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast
Map: key-value with put/get/remove/contains
Set: unique elements with add/remove/contains
Priority Queue: insert/extract-min (or max)

ADT vs data structure — the critical distinction

ADTPossible implementations
ListArray, linked list, dynamic array
StackArray (top at end), linked list (head as top)
QueueLinked list (head + tail), circular array
MapHash table, balanced BST (TreeMap)
SetHash set, tree set, bit set
Priority QueueBinary heap, Fibonacci heap, sorted array

Key insight: the SAME ADT can have many DIFFERENT implementations. Each gives different performance trade-offs but same external behavior.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Stack ADT, two implementations
# Implementation 1: linked list
class Stack1:
 def __init__(self):
 self.head = None
 def push(self, x):
 node = Node(x)
 node.next = self.head
 self.head = node
 def pop(self):
 x = self.head.value
 self.head = self.head.next
 return x

# Implementation 2: array
class Stack2:
 def __init__(self):
 self.items = []
 def push(self, x):
 self.items.append(x)
 def pop(self):
 return self.items.pop()
1
Both expose the SAME interface (push, pop) — the Stack ADT.
2
Both behave identically from the outside (LIFO).
3
Internal implementations are completely different (pointers vs contiguous array).

Algorithm correctness and efficiency

TWO QUALITY DIMENSIONS
Correctness: produces the right output for every valid input.
Efficiency: uses minimal time and space.

Both matter. A correct but slow algorithm may be useless. A fast but wrong algorithm is worse than nothing.

Why use ADTs at all?

BENEFITS OF ABSTRACTION
Modularity: callers don't need to know the implementation
Substitutability: swap implementations without changing client code
Reasoning: design with high-level concepts, optimize details later
Testing: test the interface independently from implementation

The big picture

LayerWhat it answersExample
ProblemWhat needs solving?"Sort a list of names"
AlgorithmWhat's the procedure?"Use merge sort"
ADTWhat operations needed?"List with random access"
Data structureHow do we store it?"Dynamic array"
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing ADT with data structure. Stack is an ADT; the linked list backing it is a data structure.

Calling a "list" both ADT and data structure ambiguously. Be specific: "List ADT" vs "linked list" vs "array list (dynamic array)."

Forgetting that the SAME ADT can have multiple implementations with very different performance.

Skipping algorithm correctness because the code "seems to work." Test edge cases.

Ignoring efficiency because "the algorithm produces correct output." For large inputs, slowness can be a correctness problem too (timeout = wrong answer).

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What is an ADT?" → an abstract specification of operations (interface), not a concrete implementation.

"What is a data structure?" → a concrete way of organizing data in memory.

"Examples of ADTs?" → list, stack, queue, map, set, priority queue.

"Examples of data structures?" → array, linked list, hash table, binary tree, heap.

"Implementations of the Stack ADT?" → linked list (head as top) or array (end as top).

"Required properties of an algorithm?" → finite, well-defined, input, output, effective.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Algorithm: well-defined procedure that takes input → produces output
  • Data structure: concrete way of organizing data in memory
  • ADT (Abstract Data Type): specification of operations — interface, not implementation
  • Same ADT can have many implementations (Stack ADT → linked list OR array)
  • Common ADTs: list, stack, queue, deque, map, set, priority queue
  • Two quality dimensions: correctness and efficiency
  • Abstraction enables modularity, substitutability, testing

Matching ADTs to problems: hierarchical data — file systems, org charts — is a TREE (one parent per node, no cycles). Undo in a text editor is a STACK: the most recent action is the first reversed — pure LIFO. When a question says “most appropriate ADT,” match the data’s SHAPE to the structure’s guarantee.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Know the split: an ADT (abstract data type) is the interface — WHAT operations exist (e.g., a List supports get/insert/remove) — while a data structure is the implementation (array, linked list). The OA tests matching an ADT to a valid implementation and knowing operations are defined independent of storage.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
List ADT operations:  get(i), insert(i,x), remove(i), size()
Implementations:       dynamic array  OR  linked list

Result: same ADT, two different data structures

The ADT names the behavior; the data structure supplies it. Two structures can satisfy the same ADT with different performance — that trade-off is the exam's point.

📜 What Makes Something an Algorithm

PropertyDefinition
FinitenessMust terminate after a finite number of steps — no infinite loops allowed
DefinitenessEvery step is precisely, unambiguously defined
InputZero or more well-defined inputs
OutputOne or more well-defined outputs
EffectivenessEach step must be doable — basic and executable
PSEUDOCODE
A structured, language-independent way to describe an algorithm's steps — precise enough to implement, without real syntax to get bogged down in.
WORKED EXAMPLE — pseudocode: find the max of an array
StepPseudocode
1max ← array[0]
2for i ← 1 to length−1:
3  if array[i] > max: max ← array[i]
4return max
Trace on [3, 7, 2, 9, 4]: max starts at 3 → 7 → (2 skipped) → 9 → (4 skipped) → returns 9 ✓
⚠️ CORRECTNESS BEFORE EFFICIENCY
An algorithm that's fast but WRONG is worthless. Always verify correctness first (does it work on edge cases: empty array, one element, duplicates?), then worry about speed.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which property means an algorithm must eventually stop?
  1. Finiteness
  2. Definiteness
  3. Effectiveness
  4. Input
Show answer + steps
A. Finiteness guarantees termination — an algorithm that runs forever fails this property (it would just be a process).
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tracing algorithms by hand is one of the most-tested OA skills. Given pseudocode and an input, you must walk through step by step and report the output, intermediate state, or final result. Pseudocode itself is the language used in CS textbooks and most interview discussions. Master both and you'll never be stumped by an "trace this" question.

What is pseudocode?

Pseudocode is a language-neutral way of describing algorithms. It looks like code but uses everyday English for clarity, ignoring strict syntax rules.

PSEUDOCODE CONVENTIONS (zyBooks-style)
Procedure header: FUNCTION name(params):
Assignment: x = 5 or x ← 5
Conditional: IF condition: ... ELSE: ...
Loop: FOR i FROM 0 TO n-1: ... or WHILE condition: ...
Array access: arr[i]
Return: RETURN value
Comments: // or #

Tracing an algorithm — the technique

HOW TO TRACE
1. Write down all variables and their initial values
2. Step through one line at a time
3. After each line that changes a variable, update your tracking
4. For loops, repeat the body for each iteration
5. At the end, the trace tells you the output and final state
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Trace this algorithm with arr = [3, 7, 2, 8, 5]
FUNCTION find_max(arr):
 largest = arr[0]
 FOR i FROM 1 TO length(arr) - 1:
 IF arr[i] > largest:
 largest = arr[i]
 RETURN largest
1
largest = arr[0] = 3.
2
i=1: arr[1]=7. 7 > 3 → largest = 7.
3
i=2: arr[2]=2. 2 > 7 → no change.
4
i=3: arr[3]=8. 8 > 7 → largest = 8.
5
i=4: arr[4]=5. 5 > 8 → no change.
✓
Loop ends. RETURN 8.

Three parts of every algorithm

INPUT · PROCESSING · OUTPUT
Input: what data the algorithm needs (arrays, numbers, strings, etc.)
Processing: the step-by-step transformation
Output: the result(s) returned or printed
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Identify input/processing/output
FUNCTION sum_evens(arr):
 total = 0
 FOR each x IN arr:
 IF x mod 2 == 0:
 total = total + x
 RETURN total
Input
arr — a list of integers.
Processing
iterate through, accumulate total of even values.
Output
total — sum of even elements.

Correctness vs efficiency revisited

Two algorithms can be both correct, but one is much more efficient. Both find the maximum:

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two correct algorithms, different efficiency
# Algorithm 1: O(n) — single pass
def find_max_1(arr):
 largest = arr[0]
 for x in arr[1:]:
 if x > largest:
 largest = x
 return largest

# Algorithm 2: O(n log n) — sort then return last
def find_max_2(arr):
 sorted_arr = sorted(arr) # n log n
 return sorted_arr[-1]
1
Both produce the correct max.
2
Algorithm 1 is O(n) — one pass. Algorithm 2 is O(n log n) — sorts unnecessarily.
⚠
For 1 million elements: Algorithm 1 ≈ 1M ops; Algorithm 2 ≈ 20M ops. Same answer, 20x slower.

Designing an algorithm — the workflow

DESIGN STEPS
1. Understand the problem: what's the input? what's the desired output? are there edge cases?
2. Devise a plan: pick an approach (iteration, recursion, divide-and-conquer)
3. Write pseudocode: the steps in plain English-like form
4. Verify correctness: trace examples, including edge cases
5. Analyze efficiency: time and space complexity
6. Implement and test: code it up, run on real inputs

Why pseudocode (instead of real code)?

Pseudocode advantage
Language-independent — anyone can read it regardless of preferred language
Focuses on logic, not syntax
Faster to write and revise during design
Easier to teach and discuss

Common loop patterns to recognize

PatternExample
Accumulatortotal += arr[i] (sum)
Counterif condition: count += 1
Best so farif x > largest: largest = x
Search/findif x == target: return i
Filter/buildif condition: result.append(x)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Trying to memorize pseudocode rather than tracing it. The OA gives unfamiliar pseudocode and asks for outputs — you MUST be able to walk through.

Off-by-one errors when tracing. FOR i FROM 0 TO n-1 includes both 0 and n-1.

Forgetting to update the tracking after every variable change.

Reading code instead of executing it. Tracing means simulating execution mentally.

Confusing assignment (=) with comparison (==) when reading. x = 5 sets x; x == 5 tests x.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Trace this algorithm with input X" — practice tracking each variable.

"What is the output?" — walk to the RETURN statement, report the value.

"What's the input/output of this function?" — read the parameters and RETURN value.

"Identify the loop pattern" — accumulator, counter, search, etc.

"Two algorithms produce the same output. What's different?" → likely efficiency (O notation).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Pseudocode: language-neutral algorithm description
  • Algorithm has three parts: input, processing, output
  • Tracing means simulating execution one line at a time
  • Multiple correct algorithms can have very different efficiency
  • Common loop patterns: accumulator, counter, best-so-far, search, filter
  • Pseudocode is the standard medium for algorithm discussion in CS

Two algorithm properties students conflate: definiteness — each step is precisely, unambiguously specified; effectiveness — each step is basic enough to actually be carried out. A trace worth knowing: a loop guarded by a positive count, given non-positive input, prints nothing — the guard fails immediately. Engineering order: get a correct, clear development first, then optimize — efficient-but-wrong is worthless.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

An algorithm is a finite, well-defined sequence of steps solving a problem. OA asks you to compare algorithms by number of operations as input grows, not wall-clock time. 'Efficiency' = growth rate, independent of hardware.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
sum = 0
for x in list:     # n iterations
    sum += x       # 1 op each
# total work grows linearly with n

Result: work proportional to n → linear

Counting operations as a function of input size n is how every complexity question is framed; hardware speed never changes the growth class.

⚖️ Data Structures vs Algorithms — how the choice changes everything

THE RELATIONSHIP
An algorithm's efficiency often depends ENTIRELY on which data structure it operates over. The same task can be fast or slow purely based on that choice.
Data structureFast atSlow at
ArrayRandom access by index: O(1)Insert/remove in the middle: O(n) shifting
Linked listInsert/remove at a known node: O(1)Random access by index: O(n) traversal
Hash tableLookup by key: O(1) averageMaintaining sorted order: not supported directly
Balanced BSTSorted order + lookup: O(log n)Beats a hash table's O(1) average lookup
WORKED EXAMPLE — same task, two structures
Task: "Insert 1,000 items at the FRONT of a collection, one at a time."
StructureCost per insertTotal for 1,000
Array (insert at index 0)O(n) — must shift everything right~500,000 shifts
Linked list (insert at head)O(1) — just relink the head pointer1,000 operations
Same algorithm, same task — the DATA STRUCTURE choice is the entire difference.
⚠️ NO SINGLE "BEST" STRUCTURE
Every data structure trades one operation's speed for another's. Choosing one always means choosing what you're willing to make slower.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Repeatedly inserting at the FRONT of a large collection is fastest using:
  1. A linked list
  2. An array
  3. Either — no difference
  4. A sorted array
Show answer + steps
A. A linked list inserts at the head in O(1); an array must shift every existing element right, O(n) per insert.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The choice of data structure can change an algorithm's complexity by orders of magnitude. The same logical operation might be O(1), O(log n), or O(n) depending on what's underneath. The OA expects you to recognize when to swap one structure for another. Mastering the pairing — algorithm + data structure — is what distinguishes someone who knows definitions from someone who can build fast software.

The pairing principle

Algorithms and data structures are inseparable. The same algorithm becomes fast or slow depending on the data structure it operates on. The same data structure becomes useful or wasteful depending on the algorithm using it.

EXAMPLE: SAME ALGORITHM, DIFFERENT STRUCTURES
Operation: "find the smallest element"
Unsorted array: scan all → O(n)
Sorted array: arr[0] → O(1)
Min-heap: heap[0] → O(1)
Hash set: scan all → O(n) — hash sets aren't ordered
Balanced BST: leftmost node → O(log n)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Same problem, four implementations

Problem: "Was URL X visited?" Many checks, many additions.

1
Unsorted array: add O(1), check O(n). Bad for many checks.
2
Sorted array: add O(n) (shift to maintain order), check O(log n) via binary search. Better for read-heavy.
3
Balanced BST: both O(log n). Balanced for mixed read/write.
4
Hash set: both O(1) average. Best for this problem.
⚠
If we'd picked the wrong structure (unsorted array), millions of URLs = millions of seconds. Hash set keeps it under a second.

How structure changes algorithm complexity

OperationArrayLinked listHash tableBST (bal)
Access by indexO(1)O(n)N/AN/A
Search by valueO(n)O(n)O(1)O(log n)
Insert at endO(1)*O(1) w/tailO(1)O(log n)
Insert at startO(n)O(1)O(1)O(log n)
Remove by valueO(n)O(n)O(1)O(log n)
Min/maxO(n) unsortedO(n)O(n)O(log n)
Sorted iterationO(n) if sortedO(n) if sortedO(n log n)O(n)

* Dynamic array: amortized O(1).

Algorithm + structure = real performance

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Dijkstra with two queue choices

Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm needs a "give me the closest unvisited vertex" operation in its main loop.

1
Unsorted array: scan to find min — O(V) per pop. Total: O(V²).
2
Binary heap (min-heap): O(log V) per pop. Total: O((V + E) log V).
3
For sparse graphs (E ≈ V), the heap version is dramatically faster.
⚠
SAME algorithm. Different data structure. Different complexity class.

The ADT-to-data-structure mapping

ADTBest implementationWhy
List (sequential access)Dynamic arrayO(1) index access, cache-friendly
List (frequent inserts at front)Linked listO(1) prepend
StackDynamic arrayO(1) push/pop at end
QueueLinked list (head + tail) or circular arrayO(1) enqueue + dequeue
DequeDoubly linked list or circular arrayO(1) at both ends
Map (unordered)Hash tableO(1) avg lookup
Map (ordered)Balanced BST (red-black tree)O(log n) + sorted iteration
Set (unordered)Hash setO(1) avg add/contains
Priority QueueBinary heapO(log n) insert/extract

Decision framework — picking a data structure

QUESTIONS TO ASK
1. What are the dominant operations? Read-heavy? Write-heavy? Mixed?
2. Need ordered iteration? If yes → BST or sorted structure.
3. Random access by index? If yes → array.
4. Lookup by key? If yes → hash table.
5. Frequent inserts at the start? If yes → linked list (avoid arrays).
6. Worst-case guarantees needed? If yes → balanced BST (not hash table).
7. Memory constraints? If yes → arrays beat linked lists (no pointer overhead).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Pick the structure
A
"Implement undo for a text editor" → Stack (LIFO of edit operations).
B
"Track all unique IPs that visited the site today" → Hash set (membership + dedup).
C
"Process tasks by priority" → Priority queue (heap).
D
"Show employees sorted by salary as they're added" → Balanced BST (sorted iteration).
E
"Cache the last 100 page loads" → LRU cache (hash map + doubly linked list).
F
"Browser back button" → Stack.

How structure choice affects algorithm choice

EXAMPLE: SORTING
Quicksort needs random access → fast on arrays, slow on linked lists.
Merge sort works well on linked lists (no random access penalty, no extra space needed).
Heapsort needs an array (the heap is array-stored).

Same problem (sort), structure dictates which algorithm is best.

Memory layout matters too

Beyond complexity, MEMORY LAYOUT affects real-world speed because of CPU caches:

  • Arrays: contiguous memory → cache-friendly, sequential access is FAST in practice
  • Linked lists: scattered nodes → cache-unfriendly, random pointer chases are slow
  • Hash tables: depend on implementation (chaining = scattered; open addressing = contiguous)
  • Modern CPUs can fetch cache lines (64 bytes) in one go — arrays exploit this
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Picking a "fancy" structure when a simple one is enough. Linked lists rarely beat arrays in practice.

Using hash table when you need ordering. Hash tables are unordered.

Using balanced BST when O(1) hash lookup is enough. BST is O(log n).

Forgetting that the WRONG structure can change complexity by orders of magnitude (Dijkstra's example: V² vs V log V).

Confusing big-O with real-world speed. Cache locality often makes "slower" structures faster in practice for small n.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Best structure for [task]?" — match operations to structure strengths.

"Why use a hash table for X?" → O(1) average lookup.

"When does picking the wrong structure cost you?" → can change complexity (e.g., O(V²) vs O(V log V) Dijkstra).

"Implementation of Stack/Queue/Map?" → know the standard pairings.

"Linked list vs array for X?" → array for index access; linked list for frequent prepend.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data structure choice can change algorithm complexity by orders of magnitude
  • Same ADT can have multiple implementations with different trade-offs
  • Standard pairings: Stack→array, Queue→linked list/circular array, Map→hash table or BST, PQ→heap
  • Decision framework: ask about dominant operations, ordering needs, access patterns
  • Cache locality matters: arrays beat linked lists in real-world speed for small n
  • Hash tables = fastest for plain key lookup; BSTs = needed for ordered ops

Array insertion cost: inserting at the BEGINNING of an array of size n is O(n) — every existing element must shift right one slot. Insertion at the end (with capacity) is O(1). Position determines price.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Data structures store/organize data; algorithms process it. The OA rewards knowing that the choice of structure changes an algorithm's cost — e.g., search is O(n) on an unsorted array but O(log n) on a BST.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
unsorted array:  search = O(n)
sorted array:    search = O(log n)  (binary search)
hash table:      search = O(1) average

Result: structure choice drives algorithm cost

The same task (search) has different complexity depending on the structure — recognizing that link is a core OA skill.

🌍 Applications of ADTs — where each one actually shows up

ADTReal-world useWhy this ADT fits

WORKED EXAMPLE — matching a scenario to its ADT
"Undo the last 5 actions in an editor, most recent first." → Every undo removes the MOST RECENTLY added action → that's LIFO → Stack.
"Print jobs should come out in the order they were sent." → FIFO → Queue.
⚠️ THE OA TESTS SCENARIO-MATCHING
Expect questions phrased as a real scenario ("customers wait in line," "the most recent undo") — translate the ORDERING RULE (LIFO vs FIFO vs priority vs key-lookup) to find the right ADT.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A hospital triage system treats the most CRITICAL patient next, regardless of arrival order. Which ADT models this?
  1. Priority Queue
  2. Stack
  3. Queue
  4. List
Show answer + steps
A. Priority determines order, not arrival time or LIFO/FIFO — that's exactly a Priority Queue.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Knowing what ADTs ARE is half the battle; knowing WHEN to use each is the other half. The OA frequently asks "Which ADT models this real-world problem?" Recognizing the patterns — undo as Stack, print queue as Queue, cache as Map — is what lets you solve problems quickly. Master this and you'll see ADTs everywhere in production software.

Stack applications — LIFO problems

Use a Stack when the LAST item added needs to come out FIRST. The mental hook: "back tracking" or "most recent first."

STACK USE CASES
Undo / redo in editors and IDEs
Browser back button — pages visited
Function call stack — every language runtime
Expression evaluation — postfix calculators, infix-to-postfix conversion
Matching brackets — IDE syntax checkers
Backtracking algorithms — Sudoku solver, N-queens, maze pathfinding
DFS implementation — explicit stack instead of recursion
Reversing a sequence — push everything, then pop
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Undo as a Stack
undo_stack = []

# User types "Hello"
undo_stack.append({type: 'insert', text: 'H', pos: 0})
undo_stack.append({type: 'insert', text: 'e', pos: 1})
undo_stack.append({type: 'insert', text: 'l', pos: 2})

# User presses Cmd-Z
last_action = undo_stack.pop() # → {type: 'insert', text: 'l', pos: 2}
# Reverse the last action — delete char at pos 2
1
Each edit pushes onto the stack.
2
Undo pops the most recent edit and reverses it.
3
This works because undo conceptually goes backward in time — LIFO is the natural fit.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Bracket matching
def is_balanced(s):
 stack = []
 pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}
 for c in s:
 if c in '([{':
 stack.append(c)
 elif c in ')]}':
 if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[c]:
 return False
 return len(stack) == 0

is_balanced("({[]})") # True
is_balanced("({[})") # False — wrong closing order

Queue applications — FIFO problems

Use a Queue when the FIRST item in is the FIRST item out. The mental hook: "fairness" or "in the order they arrived."

QUEUE USE CASES
Print queue — jobs handled in submission order
Customer service ticket queue — first come, first served
BFS implementation — explore breadth-first
Buffering — keyboard buffer, network packet buffer, video frames
Task / job scheduling — without priorities, simple FIFO
Web server request handling — process in arrival order
Event handling — UI events processed in order generated
Producer-consumer patterns — one thread produces, another consumes
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Print queue
from collections import deque

print_queue = deque()
print_queue.append("doc1.pdf") # Alice submits
print_queue.append("doc2.pdf") # Bob submits
print_queue.append("doc3.pdf") # Carol submits

while print_queue:
 next_doc = print_queue.popleft()
 print_document(next_doc)
# Order: doc1, doc2, doc3 — fair
1
Each user appends to the back.
2
Printer pulls from the front (FIFO).

Use a Map when each piece of data has a unique identifier (key) and you frequently look it up by that key.

cache = {} # url → response

def fetch(url):

 return cache[url] # cache hit, O(1)
 response = http_get(url) # expensive: network call
 cache[url] = response
 return response

# First call to "/api/users" → network call, cached
# Second call to "/api/users" → cache hit, instant
1
Map's O(1) lookup is what makes caching effective — the cache check must be fast.
2
If the lookup were O(n), the cache would slow down as it grew — defeats the purpose.

from collections import Counter

text = "the cat sat on the mat the cat slept"
counts = Counter(text.split())
# Counter({'the': 3, 'cat': 2, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1, 'slept': 1})

most_common = counts.most_common(2)
# [('the', 3), ('cat', 2)]

SET USE CASES

Membership testing — is this URL visited? Is this user banned?
Permissions / capabilities — what can this user do?
Tag systems — tags on a blog post
Visited tracking in BFS/DFS — avoid revisiting
Common elements — friends in common (intersection)

PRIORITY QUEUE USE CASES

Operating system scheduler — run highest-priority ready process

Hospital triage — most critical patient first

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — LRU cache combines Map + Doubly Linked List

An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache evicts the item that was used longest ago. It needs:

1
Map: O(1) lookup by key
2
Doubly linked list: O(1) move-to-front (most recent) and O(1) remove-from-back (least recent)
3

Either ADT alone wouldn't work — Map alone has no notion of "recent"; list alone has O(n) lookup.

Using a Stack when order doesn't match LIFO (e.g., printing — you'd be unfair to early submitters).

Using a Queue for tasks when priority matters — use Priority Queue instead.

Using a List for membership testing — O(n) per check. Use a Set for O(1).

Using a Map for ordered iteration — hash maps are unordered. Use sorted keys or a TreeMap.

Not recognizing common patterns: undo IS always a stack; print queue IS always a queue.

"Which ADT for browser back button?" → Stack.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Linear search is the simplest search algorithm — and the only one that works on UNSORTED data without pre-processing. The OA tests its complexity, when to use it, and how it compares to binary search. Understanding linear search's best/average/worst cases is also your first concrete experience with case-based algorithm analysis, which sets up everything in chapter 2.

The algorithm

Linear search walks through a list one element at a time, comparing each to the target.

LINEAR SEARCH
FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1:
  IF arr[i] == target THEN RETURN i
RETURN -1   // not found 
def linear_search(arr, target):
 for i, x in enumerate(arr):
 if x == target:
 return i
 return -1
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Search for 7 in [3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 9]
1
i=0: arr[0]=3 ≠ 7. Continue.
2
i=1: arr[1]=5 ≠ 7. Continue.
3
i=2: arr[2]=2 ≠ 7. Continue.
4
i=3: arr[3]=7. Match! RETURN 3.
✓
4 comparisons made. Target was at index 3.

Best, average, worst cases

LINEAR SEARCH COMPLEXITY
Best case: target is the FIRST element → O(1) (1 comparison).
Average case: target found at expected position n/2 → O(n).
Worst case: target at LAST position OR not present → O(n) (n comparisons).
Space: O(1) — constant extra memory.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Three cases on [3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 9]
Best
Search for 3: 1 comparison (i=0). Best case.
Average
Search for 7: 4 comparisons (i=0..3). Roughly n/2.
Worst
Search for 9: 6 comparisons (i=0..5). Worst case.
⚠
Worst case is also when target is NOT in the list — must check every element to be sure.

When linear search is the right choice

USE LINEAR SEARCH WHEN
Data is UNSORTED (binary search needs sorted data)
Data is small (n < ~50, overhead of fancier algorithms beats linear's simplicity)
You're searching only ONCE (sorting first costs O(n log n))
Data structure doesn't allow random access (linked list)
You need to find ALL matches, not just the first
Memory is tight (no extra structures needed)
DON'T USE LINEAR SEARCH WHEN
Data IS sorted AND you'll search many times → use binary search (O(log n))
Data is large AND searches are frequent → use a hash table (O(1) average)
You need range queries (give me everything between 5 and 10) → balanced BST

Linear search vs binary search

PropertyLinear searchBinary search
TimeO(n)O(log n)
Requires sorted dataNoYes
Works on linked listYesNo (no random access)
Best caseO(1)O(1) (target = mid)
Code complexityTrivialEasy to get wrong

The cross-over point

For very small arrays, linear search BEATS binary search in practice — the simple loop runs faster than the more complex midpoint logic. The cross-over is typically around n=10-50 depending on hardware, which is why hybrid sorts (Timsort) use linear/insertion methods on small subarrays.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Find ALL occurrences with linear search
def find_all(arr, target):
 indices = []
 for i, x in enumerate(arr):
 if x == target:
 indices.append(i)
 return indices

find_all([3, 5, 2, 5, 7, 5], 5) # → [1, 3, 5]
⚠
Binary search returns ONE match. Linear search can collect ALL matches in one pass.

Sentinel linear search (a small optimization)

def sentinel_search(arr, target):
 arr.append(target) # add sentinel at end
 i = 0
 while arr[i] != target:
 i += 1
 arr.pop() # remove sentinel
 return i if i < len(arr) else -1

By placing the target at the end, the loop's bounds check is eliminated (we know we'll find it eventually). Slightly faster in tight loops, though modern compilers usually do this optimization automatically.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Calling linear search "fast" because it's simple. It's O(n) — fast for small n, slow for big.

Confusing best case (O(1)) with average/worst (O(n)). Don't quote best case as "the" complexity.

Returning the WRONG sentinel for "not found." Common conventions: -1 (Python), null/None, or false. Be consistent.

Forgetting to handle empty arrays. arr[0] on empty array throws.

Trying to use binary search on unsorted data. It silently fails (returns -1 even when target is present).

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What's the worst-case complexity of linear search?" → O(n).

"Best case?" → O(1) — target is first.

"When does worst case occur?" → target is last OR not in list.

"Linear vs binary search?" → linear works on unsorted, binary needs sorted but is O(log n).

"How many comparisons to search for X?" → trace through, count.

"What's the space complexity?" → O(1).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Linear search: walk through array, compare each element to target
  • Best: O(1) (first element). Average/Worst: O(n).
  • Space: O(1)
  • Works on unsorted data (binary search doesn't)
  • Works on linked lists (binary search needs random access)
  • Use linear search for: small arrays, unsorted data, single searches, finding all matches
  • For frequent searches on sorted data → binary search; for unsorted with frequent searches → hash table

✂️ Binary Search — cut the space in half every time

THE REQUIREMENT
The array MUST be SORTED first. Binary search compares against the MIDDLE element and eliminates half the remaining search space each step.
WORKED EXAMPLE — find 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 45, 56]
Steplowhighmidarray[mid]Action
10841623 > 16 → search RIGHT half
25863823 < 38 → search LEFT half
355523MATCH → return index 5
9 elements checked in just 3 steps, not 9 — that's the power of halving.
TIME COMPLEXITY
O(log n) — each comparison halves the remaining elements: 1,000,000 elements takes at most ~20 comparisons.
⚠️ UNSORTED DATA = BROKEN ALGORITHM
Run binary search on an unsorted array and it can miss the target entirely — the halving logic only works because sorted order guarantees which half to discard.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK

  1. Sorted
  2. An even length
  3. Unsorted

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Binary search is the canonical example of divide-and-conquer and one of the most-implemented algorithms in production code. It's also famously easy to get WRONG — even experienced programmers introduce off-by-one errors. The OA tests trace execution, complexity, and the critical sorted-data prerequisite. Mastering binary search also primes you for understanding O(log n) growth.

The idea

Binary search repeatedly halves the search range. Compare target to the middle element. Eliminate half the array on each step. Done in O(log n) time — but only on SORTED data.

BINARY SEARCH (ITERATIVE)
lo = 0, hi = n - 1
WHILE lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  IF arr[mid] == target: RETURN mid
  IF arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
  ELSE: hi = mid - 1
RETURN -1 
def binary_search(arr, target):
 lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
 while lo <= hi:
 mid = (lo + hi) // 2
 if arr[mid] == target:
 return mid
 elif arr[mid] < target:
 lo = mid + 1
 else:
 hi = mid - 1
 return -1
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Search for 23 in [1, 4, 7, 10, 14, 19, 23, 28, 35]
1
lo=0, hi=8. mid=(0+8)/2=4. arr[4]=14. 14<23 → lo=5.
2
lo=5, hi=8. mid=(5+8)/2=6. arr[6]=23. Match! RETURN 6.
✓
2 comparisons to find it. Linear search would have taken 7.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Search for 16 (not present) in same array
1
lo=0, hi=8. mid=4, arr[4]=14. 14<16 → lo=5.
2
lo=5, hi=8. mid=6, arr[6]=23. 23>16 → hi=5.
3
lo=5, hi=5. mid=5, arr[5]=19. 19>16 → hi=4.
4
lo=5 > hi=4. Loop exits. RETURN -1.
✓
3 comparisons confirm 16 isn't there. Linear would have walked all 9 elements.

Recursive version

def binary_search_rec(arr, target, lo, hi):
 if lo > hi:
 return -1
 mid = (lo + hi) // 2
 if arr[mid] == target:
 return mid
 elif arr[mid] < target:
 return binary_search_rec(arr, target, mid + 1, hi)
 else:
 return binary_search_rec(arr, target, lo, mid - 1)

Equally correct. Iterative is preferred in practice — O(1) space vs O(log n) call stack.

The sorted-data prerequisite

SORTED IS NON-NEGOTIABLE
Binary search ONLY works on sorted data.
Why: the algorithm assumes "if mid is too small, target is in the right half." That's only true if larger values are always to the right.

Run binary search on unsorted data → returns wrong answer (or -1) silently. No error thrown.

Complexity

BINARY SEARCH COMPLEXITY
Best case: target is at mid → O(1) (1 comparison)
Average / worst case: target is at an end or absent → O(log n)
Space: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive (call stack)

Why O(log n)?

DERIVING O(log n)
Each iteration halves the search range.
Starting size: n. After 1 step: n/2. After 2 steps: n/4. ... After k steps: n/2^k.
Loop ends when size = 1 → 2^k = n → k = log₂(n).

So worst-case iteration count is log₂(n).
For n = 1,000,000: log₂(n) ≈ 20 iterations.
For n = 1,000,000,000: log₂(n) ≈ 30 iterations.

Off-by-one traps

⚠ THE THREE COMMON BUGS

1. while lo < hi instead of lo <= hi: misses the case where lo == hi and target is at that position.

2. lo = mid or hi = mid instead of mid + 1 / mid - 1: causes infinite loop when target is absent.

3. (lo + hi) / 2 in languages with bounded integers: overflows for large arrays. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 in C/Java for safety.

Variants

BINARY SEARCH VARIANTS
Find leftmost occurrence: when arr[mid] == target, keep searching left.
Find rightmost occurrence: when arr[mid] == target, keep searching right.
Find smallest value ≥ target (lower bound): standard in C++ STL.
Find largest value ≤ target: useful for floor functions.
Search rotated sorted array: classic interview question — modified binary search.

Linear vs binary search comparison

nLinear (worst)Binary (worst)
1010~4
100100~7
1,0001,000~10
1,000,0001,000,000~20
1,000,000,0001,000,000,000~30

The point: at billion-element scale, binary search is 30 comparisons vs a billion. That's the power of O(log n).

When NOT to use binary search

DON'T USE BINARY SEARCH WHEN
Data is unsorted (and you won't search again — sorting first is O(n log n))
Data is in a linked list (no random access — mid lookup is O(n))
Data is small (n < ~10) — linear's simplicity beats binary's overhead
You need to find ALL matches (binary returns one)
You need O(1) average lookup — use a hash table
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting that data MUST be sorted. Binary search on unsorted = silently wrong.

Off-by-one in lo/hi/mid arithmetic. Test boundary cases: 0 elements, 1 element, target at start, target at end, target absent.

Saying binary search is O(log n) without specifying log BASE 2. (Big-O hides the base anyway, but conceptually it's log₂.)

Using binary search on linked list. Linked list lacks random access — getting to mid is O(n), defeating the purpose.

Calling (lo + hi) / 2 safe in all languages — overflow risk in fixed-width int languages.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Time complexity of binary search?" → O(log n).

"What's the prerequisite for binary search?" → sorted data.

"Trace binary search on this array" — practice; iteration count = ⌈log₂(n)⌉ in worst case.

"How many comparisons in worst case for n=1024?" → log₂(1024) = 10.

"Why doesn't binary search work on a linked list?" → no O(1) random access to mid.

"Iterative vs recursive?" → iterative O(1) space; recursive O(log n) call stack.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Binary search: divide-and-conquer on a SORTED array, halves search range each step
  • Time: O(log n); Space: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive
  • Sorted data is required — binary search on unsorted data fails silently
  • Off-by-one bugs are the #1 implementation pitfall (use lo <= hi, mid±1)
  • For n=1B: 30 comparisons vs 1B for linear — staggering difference
  • Don't use on: unsorted data (single search), linked lists, very small arrays
  • Variants: leftmost/rightmost match, lower/upper bound, rotated array
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Binary search REQUIRES a sorted array and runs in O(log n). Each step halves the range. OA loves 'how many comparisons?' — the answer is about ⌊log₂ n⌋+1, and 'why can't binary search be used here?' (answer: not sorted).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
search 7 in [1,3,5,7,9,11]  (mid = index 2 -> 5)
5 < 7  -> search right half [7,9,11]
mid -> 7  -> FOUND

Result: found in 2 steps (log₂6 ≈ 2.6)

Halving each step gives log n; ~1,000,000 items need only ~20 comparisons. The sorted precondition is the classic trap.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before you can use Big-O, you need an intuition for how different growth rates behave at scale. The OA tests this directly: "rank these functions from slowest to fastest growing" or "which is faster for large n: O(n²) or O(n log n)?" Building a mental table of growth rates is the foundation that makes every later complexity question easy.

Constant time — O(1)

Constant time operations take the same time regardless of how big the input is. The runtime is bounded above by some fixed value.

EXAMPLES OF O(1) OPERATIONS
Array element access by index: arr[i]
Hash table get/put (average): map[key]
Stack push/pop, queue enqueue/dequeue
Heap peek (top element)
Adding two numbers, comparing two values
Linked list head insertion (with head pointer)
Returning a result, assigning a value

O(1) does NOT mean "fast" — it means "doesn't grow with n." A constant operation could be 1 nanosecond or 1 hour, but the time stays the same as input grows.

The growth-rate hierarchy

SLOWEST → FASTEST GROWING (best → worst)
O(1) < O(log n) < O(√n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

Concrete numbers — what these mean for real n

nlog nnn log nn²2^n
10310331001,024

Key takeaways from this table:

  • O(log n) barely grows. n = 1M means log n = 20.
  • O(n²) explodes fast: n = 10K is already 100M operations.
  • O(2^n) is intractable past n ≈ 30-40.
  • O(n!) is intractable past n ≈ 12.

Logarithmic growth — why so slow?

LOGARITHMS, INTUITIVELY
log₂(n) = "how many times can you halve n before reaching 1?"

log₂(8) = 3 (8 → 4 → 2 → 1)
log₂(1024) = 10
log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20
log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30

Doubling n only adds ONE step. That's why O(log n) is so powerful.

Why we drop the log base

Big-O ignores the log's base because log₂(n) and log₁₀(n) differ only by a constant factor — and Big-O ignores constants.

LOGARITHM BASE CONVERSION
log_b(n) = log_a(n) / log_a(b)
So log₁₀(n) = log₂(n) / log₂(10) ≈ log₂(n) / 3.32
Constant factor (1/3.32) drops out in Big-O.

Linear vs n log n

O(n log n) is just slightly worse than O(n). For n = 1,000,000: linear is 1M ops, n log n is ~20M ops. About 20× slower — significant but not catastrophic. This is why merge sort (O(n log n)) is acceptable for huge inputs.

Polynomial vs exponential — the chasm

THE TRACTABILITY LINE
Polynomial (n, n², n³...) is generally TRACTABLE — runs in reasonable time for moderate n.
Exponential (2^n, n!) is generally INTRACTABLE — even small n becomes hopeless.

This boundary defines the famous P vs NP question in CS theory.

Outer loop runs n times. Inner loop runs n times for each outer.
2

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing O(1) with "fast." O(1) means "doesn't grow with n," not "instantaneous."

Saying "log of what base?" — Big-O hides the base. log₂, log₁₀, ln all collapse to the same Big-O.

Treating O(n log n) as "much slower" than O(n). It's barely slower — usually the right trade-off for sorting.

Forgetting that O(2^n) is hopeless. Don't write naive recursive Fibonacci.

Confusing N (input value) with n (input SIZE). For an integer N, the input size is log(N) bits; an algorithm "polynomial in N" might be exponential in size.

  • O(log n) is incredibly slow growth — n=1B → just 30 ops
  • O(n²) explodes fast — n=10K → 100M ops
  • O(2^n), O(n!) are intractable past tiny inputs
  • Polynomial = tractable; exponential = intractable (the P vs NP line)
  • Big-O ignores log base (constants drop)

The O(1) champion: accessing arr[i] by index is constant time — the address is computed directly from base + i × size, no searching involved. That direct-address arithmetic is THE defining advantage of arrays.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Constant time O(1) = cost independent of n (array index, hash lookup, stack push). The OA asks you to identify which operations are O(1) vs O(n); indexing an array is O(1), but searching it is O(n).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
arr[5]        -> O(1)  (direct address)
arr.append(x) -> O(1) amortized
x in arr      -> O(n)  (must scan)

Result: indexing is O(1); membership scan is O(n)

O(1) means the same work regardless of size. Confusing 'access by index' (O(1)) with 'search for a value' (O(n)) is a frequent miss.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Big-O is the standard language for talking about algorithm efficiency. The OA tests both the formal definition and the mechanical "drop constants and lower-order terms" rules. Master both and you can analyze any algorithm. Big-O is also the most-used term in technical interviews — fluency here is non-negotiable.

The formal definition

BIG-O DEFINITION
f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that:
  f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

In English: f doesn't grow faster than g, ignoring constant factors and small inputs.

Big-O is an UPPER BOUND. Saying "f is O(n²)" means "f grows AT MOST as fast as n² (asymptotically)." It doesn't mean f equals n² — f could be slower.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Prove 3n + 5 = O(n)

Find c and n₀ such that 3n + 5 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀.

1
Try c = 4. Need 3n + 5 ≤ 4n → 5 ≤ n. So n₀ = 5.
2
For n ≥ 5: 3n + 5 ≤ 4n. ✓
✓
So 3n + 5 = O(n) with c = 4, n₀ = 5.

Big-O mechanical rules

You rarely do the formal proof. Instead, you simplify by applying these rules:

RULE 1 — DROP CONSTANT FACTORS
O(3n) → O(n)
O(100 · n²) → O(n²)
Constants don't affect growth rate; they're absorbed into the "c" of the formal definition.
RULE 2 — DROP LOWER-ORDER TERMS
O(n² + n) → O(n²)
O(n³ + 100n² + 1000) → O(n³)
For large n, the highest-order term dominates. Lower-order terms are noise.
RULE 3 — KEEP THE DOMINANT TERM
After dropping constants and lower-order terms, you're left with the term that "wins" as n → ∞.
O(n + log n) → O(n) (n dominates)
O(n² + n log n) → O(n²) (n² dominates)
O(2^n + n³) → O(2^n) (exponential dominates)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Simplify these
1
5n³ + 100n² + 7n + 1000 → drop constants and lower terms → O(n³).
2
2n + 3 log n + 1 → 2n dominates log n → drop constant → O(n).
3
n log n + n → n log n dominates → O(n log n).
4
1000 → constant → O(1).

Computing Big-O from code

CODE → BIG-O CHEAT SHEET
Sequential statements: SUM the complexities (drops to the highest).
Nested loops: MULTIPLY the complexities.
Conditionals: take the WORST branch.
Function calls: substitute the function's Big-O.
Recursion: derive a recurrence and solve.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sequential statements
def fn(arr):
 n = len(arr)
 # Block 1: O(n)
 for x in arr:
 print(x)
 # Block 2: O(n²)
 for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 print(arr[i], arr[j])
1
Block 1 is O(n). Block 2 is O(n²).
2
Total: O(n + n²) = O(n²) (drop lower-order term).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Nested loops with binary search inside
def fn(arr, targets):
 arr.sort() # O(n log n)
 found = []
 for t in targets: # O(m) iterations
 idx = binary_search(arr, t) # O(log n) inner
 if idx != -1:
 found.append(idx) # O(1)
 return found
1
Sort: O(n log n).
2
Loop: m iterations × log n binary search = O(m log n).
3
Total: O(n log n + m log n).
⚠
If m ≈ n, this is O(n log n). If m = 1, it's O(n log n) (sort dominates).

Big-Omega and Big-Theta

Big-O is just one of three asymptotic notations.

THE THREE NOTATIONS
Big-O (O) — UPPER BOUND. f(n) is O(g(n)) means f grows at MOST as fast as g.
Big-Omega (Ω) — LOWER BOUND. f(n) is Ω(g(n)) means f grows at LEAST as fast as g.
Big-Theta (Θ) — TIGHT BOUND. f(n) is Θ(g(n)) means f grows EXACTLY as fast as g.

Θ = both O and Ω.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Linear search complexity in all three
1
O(n): worst case is at most n comparisons.
2
Ω(1): best case is at least 1 comparison (target at index 0).
3
Θ: not applicable to one description — different cases have different bounds.
✓
For WORST case alone, Θ(n) is also valid (it's both O(n) and Ω(n) on the worst input).

2n² + 5n + 1O(n²)
n³ + 100n² + 1000O(n³)
n + log nO(n)

2^n + n³O(2^n)

What Big-O ignores (and why it matters)

BIG-O IS ASYMPTOTIC
Big-O describes behavior as n → ∞. For SMALL n, Big-O can be misleading.

Example: insertion sort is O(n²) but BEATS quicksort O(n log n) for n < ~30.
Why? Constant factors. Big-O drops them, but for small n they dominate.

This is why hybrid sorts (Timsort, Introsort) switch to insertion sort for small subarrays.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Saying "Big-O of n is just n." Always wrap in O(): O(n).

Forgetting to drop constants: not O(3n) — write O(n).

Forgetting to drop lower-order terms: not O(n² + n) — write O(n²).

Confusing Big-O with "the complexity is exactly this." Big-O is an UPPER BOUND.

Saying O(n²) is "twice as slow" as O(n²/2). Constants drop in Big-O — they're the same complexity class.

Giving Big-O for the BEST case and treating it as THE complexity. Always specify which case (best/worst/average).

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Simplify O(3n² + 5n + 100)" → O(n²).

"What does Big-O describe?" → upper bound on growth rate.

"Difference between O, Ω, Θ?" → upper / lower / tight bound.

"Big-O of nested loops?" → multiply.

"Big-O of two sequential blocks?" → take the larger.

"Why drop constants?" → they don't affect growth rate; the c in the formal definition absorbs them.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Big-O = asymptotic upper bound on growth rate
  • Formal: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for n ≥ n₀
  • Two simplification rules: drop constants, drop lower-order terms
  • Code complexity: sequential = sum (take max), nested = multiply, conditional = worst branch
  • Big-Omega (Ω) = lower bound. Big-Theta (Θ) = tight bound (both O and Ω)
  • Big-O is asymptotic — for small n, constants matter; hybrid sorts exploit this
🧠 MEMORY AID

Big-O growth, best → worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). Rules of thumb: a single loop over n = O(n); nested loops = O(n²); halving the input each step (binary search) = O(log n); good comparison sorts = O(n log n). Big-O drops constants and lower-order terms.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Big-O = upper bound on growth, keep the dominant term, drop constants and lower terms. 3n²+5n+2 → O(n²). Order to memorize: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
T(n) = 3n^2 + 5n + 2
drop constants + lower terms
-> O(n^2)

Result: dominant term wins → O(n²)

Only the fastest-growing term matters as n → ∞; constants and smaller terms are dropped. Ranking the classes is guaranteed OA content.

Time vs space complexity

Time complexity: how runtime grows with input size.

Time-space trade-offs

Often you can save time at the cost of memory, or vice versa. Memoization, caching, and lookup tables are classic examples.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fibonacci, three approaches
# Naive recursive: time O(2^n), space O(n) call stack
def fib_naive(n):
 if n < 2: return n
 return fib_naive(n-1) + fib_naive(n-2)

# Memoized: time O(n), space O(n)
def fib_memo(n, cache={}):
 if n in cache: return cache[n]
 if n < 2: return n
 cache[n] = fib_memo(n-1) + fib_memo(n-2)
 return cache[n]

# Iterative: time O(n), space O(1)
def fib_iter(n):
 a, b = 0, 1
 for _ in range(n):
 a, b = b, a + b
 return a

Naive: time disastrous (2^n) for the same problem.
2

3

1. Identify n — the input size variable.
2. Walk through the code — count operations dependent on n.

🔄 Recursive Definitions

TermDefinition
RecursionA function that solves a problem by calling ITSELF on a smaller version of the problem
Base caseThe condition where the function STOPS calling itself and returns directly
Recursive caseThe step that calls the function again with input that moves TOWARD the base case
THE ANATOMY — every recursive function has both parts
def factorial(n):
  if n <= 1: return 1    # BASE CASE — stops the chain
  return n * factorial(n − 1) # RECURSIVE CASE — smaller input
WORKED EXAMPLE — 4! defined recursively, then unwound
Going down (calls)Coming back up (returns)
4! = 4 · 3!4 · 6 = 24
3! = 3 · 2!3 · 2 = 6
2! = 2 · 1!2 · 1 = 2
1! = 1 (base case)1
Calls stack up until the base case, then answers multiply back up the chain.
⚠️ NO BASE CASE = STACK OVERFLOW
Without a base case (or with input that never reaches it), the function calls itself forever until the call stack runs out of memory — a runtime crash, not an infinite "loop" you can see.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
What happens if a recursive function has no reachable base case?
  1. Infinite recursion → stack overflow
  2. It returns 0
  3. It runs once
  4. A compile error
Show answer + steps
A. Each call adds a stack frame; with no stop condition the stack eventually overflows at runtime.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Recursion is one of the most-tested topics on the OA — about 7% of questions. You need to recognize base cases, trace recursive calls, and understand the call stack. Beyond the OA, recursion is the natural way to handle anything tree-shaped or self-similar: parsing nested structures, walking file systems, divide-and-conquer algorithms, or dynamic programming. Internalizing the "base case + recursive case" rhythm pays dividends across the entire course and beyond.

Recursive thinking

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of the problem. Two ingredients are required:

REQUIRED PARTS OF ANY RECURSION
1. Base case — terminating condition (no recursive call)
2. Recursive case — calls itself with smaller input

Without a base case → infinite recursion → stack overflow

The art of writing recursion: identify the smallest version of the problem that you can solve directly (base case), then express the larger problem in terms of a smaller version of itself (recursive case).

Classic example: factorial

FACTORIAL DEFINITION
n! = n × (n − 1)! for n > 0
0! = 1 (base case)

def factorial(n):
 if n == 0:
 return 1 # base case
 return n * factorial(n - 1) # recursive case
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Trace factorial(4)
1
factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) — push frame.
2
factorial(3) = 3 × factorial(2) — push frame.
3
factorial(2) = 2 × factorial(1) — push frame.
4
factorial(1) = 1 × factorial(0) — push frame.
5
factorial(0) = 1 — BASE CASE, return 1.
6
Pop back: factorial(1) = 1 × 1 = 1.
7
factorial(2) = 2 × 1 = 2.
8
factorial(3) = 3 × 2 = 6.
✓
factorial(4) = 4 × 6 = 24.

The call stack

Each recursive call pushes a stack frame containing local variables and the return address. When a base case is hit, frames pop and return values bubble up.

The maximum stack depth equals the recursion depth. For factorial(n), depth is n; for binary search, log n; for naive Fibonacci, also n (in the deepest branch).

CALL STACK GROWTH
Linear recursion (e.g., factorial): O(n) stack frames
Binary search recursion: O(log n) stack frames
Tree recursion (e.g., Fibonacci): up to O(n) on the longest path

Stack overflow happens when depth exceeds the system limit (typically thousands to tens of thousands of frames).

More canonical examples

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sum from 1 to n
def sum_n(n):
 if n == 0:
 return 0
 return n + sum_n(n - 1)
1
Base: sum_n(0) = 0.
2
Recursive: sum_n(n) = n + sum_n(n−1).
3
sum_n(4) = 4 + sum_n(3) = 4 + 3 + sum_n(2) = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Power: x^n
def power(x, n):
 if n == 0:
 return 1
 return x * power(x, n - 1)
1
Base: power(x, 0) = 1 (anything to the 0 is 1).
2
Recursive: power(x, n) = x × power(x, n−1).
3
power(2, 5) = 2 × power(2, 4) = 2 × 16 = 32. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fibonacci
def fib(n):
 if n <= 1:
 return n # base: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1
 return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) # two recursive calls
1
Two base cases (n = 0, n = 1) — both needed because the recurrence reaches back two steps.
2
fib(5) = fib(4) + fib(3) = (3 + 2) + (2 + 1) = 5 + 3 = 8.
⚠
This naive version is O(2ⁿ) — exponential because the same fib(k) gets recomputed many times. Memoization fixes that.

Choosing a base case

The base case must be reachable. A function that recurses on n − 1 with a base case at n = 0 works for nonneg n; calling it on a negative n leads to infinite recursion. Always think about what inputs the function may legitimately receive.

BASE CASE GUIDELINES
Choose the smallest input the problem makes sense for.
Sometimes you need multiple base cases (e.g., Fibonacci needs both n=0 and n=1).
The recursive case must REDUCE toward the base — never wander or grow.
Confirm: every legal input eventually reaches a base case.

Iteration vs recursion

IterationRecursion
Uses loopsUses self-calls
O(1) extra spaceO(depth) call stack
Often faster (no overhead)Cleaner for tree/graph problems
No stack overflow riskCan overflow on deep recursion

Most simple recursions can be converted to iteration. Use iteration when:

  • The recursion is linear (each call recurses once)
  • Performance matters and call overhead is significant
  • Stack depth could be large (e.g., n > 10,000)

Use recursion when:

  • The data structure is naturally recursive (tree, graph, nested list)
  • The problem is naturally divide-and-conquer (merge sort, quicksort)
  • Code clarity is more important than micro-optimization

Tail recursion

A recursion is tail-recursive if the recursive call is the very last operation. Tail recursion can sometimes be optimized to avoid stack growth (though Python doesn't do this by default).

TAIL VS NON-TAIL
Non-tail (factorial): return n * factorial(n - 1) — multiplication happens AFTER the call returns.
Tail-recursive: return helper(n - 1, n * acc) — the call is the last thing; nothing waits.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting the base case (or making it unreachable) causes stack overflow. Always identify the smallest input first, then build up from there.

Recursive case that doesn't shrink the input. return f(n) from inside f(n) is infinite recursion.

Wrong base case: forgetting that Fibonacci needs TWO base cases (n=0 and n=1) — using only n=0 makes fib(1) recurse to fib(0) + fib(-1), which then loops forever.

Confusing "recursion" with "loops inside a function." A recursive function calls itself; a function with a loop is iterative even if it does similar work.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What is the base case of this recursion?" — Look for the IF that returns without calling the function.

"Trace this recursive function with input n = 5" — Walk through frame by frame.

"What's the maximum stack depth?" — Equals the recursion depth: usually n, log n, or 2ⁿ depending on the pattern.

"What happens if you remove the base case?" — Stack overflow.

"Convert this recursion to iteration" — Use a loop with an accumulator variable.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Recursion = base case + recursive case
  • Each call adds a stack frame; depth = number of recursive calls in flight
  • Missing or unreachable base case = stack overflow
  • Base case must be reachable from every legal input; recursive case must REDUCE input
  • Some problems need multiple base cases (e.g., Fibonacci needs n=0 and n=1)
  • Iteration uses loops with O(1) extra space; recursion uses self-calls with O(depth) stack
  • Use recursion for tree/graph/divide-and-conquer; use iteration for simple linear cases
  • Tail recursion: the recursive call is the last operation — sometimes optimized away
🧠 MEMORY AID

Every correct recursion needs two parts: a base case that stops the recursion, and a recursive case that moves toward the base case. Miss the base case (or never approach it) and you get infinite recursion → a stack overflow.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A recursive definition needs a BASE CASE (stops recursion) and a recursive case (moves toward the base). Missing/unreachable base case → infinite recursion → stack overflow. OA asks you to identify the base case or trace the result.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
def fact(n):
    if n == 0: return 1     # BASE CASE
    return n * fact(n-1)    # recursive case
fact(3) = 3*2*1*1

Result: fact(3) = 6

The base case is what terminates recursion; every recursive call must shrink toward it or the call stack exhausts.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Classic recursive algorithms (factorial, Fibonacci, Towers of Hanoi) are OA staples. You need to recognize them, trace them, and know their complexity. They're also the building blocks for almost every algorithmic technique that comes later — divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and tree/graph traversal all extend the patterns from this section.

Factorial

FACTORIAL
factorial(n) = n × factorial(n−1); factorial(0) = 1
Time: O(n) — n recursive calls, each O(1) work
Space: O(n) call stack 
def factorial(n):
 if n == 0:
 return 1
 return n * factorial(n - 1)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Iterative vs recursive factorial
def factorial_iter(n):
 result = 1
 for i in range(1, n + 1):
 result *= i
 return result
1
Iterative version: O(n) time, O(1) space — no stack frames stack up.
2
Recursive version: O(n) time, O(n) stack space.
⚠
For factorial specifically, iteration is strictly better. Use recursion when the data structure naturally calls for it.

Fibonacci (naive recursion)

NAIVE FIBONACCI
fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2); fib(0) = 0; fib(1) = 1
Time: O(2ⁿ) exponential — recomputes same values
Space: O(n) call stack

The naive recursion is exponential because fib(5) recomputes fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, etc. The recursion tree branches into 2 at each level, so the work doubles per level.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why naive Fibonacci is exponential

Counting calls in fib(5):

fib(5)
├── fib(4)
│ ├── fib(3)
│ │ ├── fib(2)
│ │ │ ├── fib(1) = 1
│ │ │ └── fib(0) = 0
│ │ └── fib(1) = 1
│ └── fib(2)
│ ├── fib(1) = 1
│ └── fib(0) = 0
└── fib(3)
 ├── fib(2)
 │ ├── fib(1) = 1
 │ └── fib(0) = 0
 └── fib(1) = 1
1
fib(2) is called 3 times. fib(3) is called 2 times. fib(1), fib(0) leaves: 8 of them.
2
Total calls: 15 — roughly 2⁵ − 1.
⚠
For fib(50), this is over 1 trillion calls. Way too slow.

Memoized Fibonacci — turning O(2ⁿ) into O(n)

Memoization caches results so each fib(k) is computed only once.

def fib_memo(n, cache=None):
 if cache is None:
 cache = {}
 if n in cache:
 return cache[n]
 if n <= 1:
 return n
 cache[n] = fib_memo(n - 1, cache) + fib_memo(n - 2, cache)
 return cache[n]
★ MEMOIZATION INSIGHT

Without memoization: O(2ⁿ) — each call branches into two new ones, redundantly computing.

With memoization: O(n) — each fib(0), fib(1), ..., fib(n) is computed exactly once.

This dramatic speedup is the gateway to dynamic programming: any recursion with overlapping subproblems benefits from caching.

Iterative Fibonacci — O(n) time, O(1) space

def fib_iter(n):
 if n <= 1:
 return n
 a, b = 0, 1
 for _ in range(n - 1):
 a, b = b, a + b
 return b

This is the version you'd actually use in production: linear time, constant space, no recursion overhead.

Towers of Hanoi

Move n disks from peg A to peg C using peg B, never placing larger on smaller. The classic recursive puzzle.

HANOI ALGORITHM
function hanoi(n, from, to, via):
  IF n == 1 THEN move(from, to); RETURN
  hanoi(n − 1, from, via, to)   # move top n-1 to spare peg
  move(from, to)     # move bottom disk
  hanoi(n − 1, via, to, from)   # move n-1 onto bottom

Total moves: 2ⁿ − 1. Complexity: O(2ⁿ).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hanoi for n = 3 disks (A → C, via B)
1
hanoi(3, A, C, B): recurse to move 2 disks A → B.
2
hanoi(2, A, B, C): recurse to move 1 disk A → C. → Move 1: A → C.
3
Move bottom of 2 from A → B. → Move 2: A → B.
4
hanoi(1, C, B, A): → Move 3: C → B.
5
Move bottom of 3 from A → C. → Move 4: A → C.
6
hanoi(2, B, C, A): → Move 5: B → A. → Move 6: B → C. → Move 7: A → C.
✓
Total: 7 moves = 2³ − 1.

The recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n−1) + 1 unfolds to T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1. So 64 disks would take 2⁶⁴ − 1 ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁹ moves — at one move per second, billions of years.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Computing the time complexity of recursive algorithms requires recurrence relations. Every recursive function makes a "promise" — to do some work and then call itself on a smaller input. Reading off the recurrence and solving it is how you determine if the recursion is O(n), O(log n), O(n log n), or O(2ⁿ). The OA shows recursive pseudocode and asks for Big-O — knowing this section turns those questions into 30-second wins.

Recurrence relations

A recurrence relation expresses an algorithm's time T(n) in terms of T of smaller inputs. To write a recurrence, ask two questions about the recursive function:

DECOMPOSING THE RECURRENCE
1. How many recursive calls? (a — the branching factor)
2. How small does each call's input get? (n/b for division, n−c for subtraction)
3. How much non-recursive work? (f(n) — usually O(1) or O(n))

Result: T(n) = a·T(input shrink) + f(n)
FAMOUS RECURRENCES — MEMORIZE
Linear recursion: T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1) → O(n)
Halving recursion: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)
Top-heavy halving: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n)
Halving + linear merge: T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n)
Halving with no merge: T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(1) → O(n)
Doubling-branch: T(n) = 2·T(n−1) + O(1) → O(2ⁿ)
Quadratic recursion: T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) → O(n²)

The Master Theorem

For divide-and-conquer recurrences T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), the Master Theorem gives the answer directly. Compare f(n) against n^(log_b a):

MASTER THEOREM — THREE CASES
Let c = log_b(a). Compare f(n) to n^c:
Case 1: f(n) is smaller (asymptotically) than n^c → T(n) = O(n^c). Leaves dominate.
Case 2: f(n) matches n^c → T(n) = O(n^c · log n). Balanced.
Case 3: f(n) is larger than n^c → T(n) = O(f(n)). Top-level dominates.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Apply Master Theorem to merge sort
1
T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). Identify a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n.
2
c = log_b(a) = log₂(2) = 1, so n^c = n.
3
f(n) = n matches n^c = n. Case 2.
✓
T(n) = O(n · log n).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Master Theorem on T(n) = 8·T(n/2) + O(n²)
1
a = 8, b = 2, f(n) = n².
2
c = log₂(8) = 3, so n^c = n³.
3
f(n) = n² < n³. Case 1.
✓
T(n) = O(n³). Standard matrix multiplication runs in this complexity.

Tracing recursive depth

Another way to read off complexity: (number of calls) × (work per call) = total work.

DEPTH × WORK FOR FAMOUS ALGORITHMS
Factorial: n calls × O(1) = O(n)
Binary search: log n calls × O(1) = O(log n)
Merge sort: log n levels × O(n) per level = O(n log n)
Naive Fibonacci: 2ⁿ calls × O(1) = O(2ⁿ)
Towers of Hanoi: 2ⁿ moves × O(1) = O(2ⁿ)

Quick-recognition cheat sheet

★ INSTANT RECOGNITION

One recursive call on n−1, work O(1) → O(n)

One recursive call on n/2, work O(1) → O(log n)

Two recursive calls on n/2, work O(n) → O(n log n)

Two recursive calls on n−1, work O(1) → O(2ⁿ)

One recursive call on n−1, work O(n) → O(n²)

One recursive call on n/2, work O(n) → O(n) (top-heavy)

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing T(n/2) (one halving call) with 2T(n/2) (two halving calls). The first is O(log n) at best; the second adds the work of doubling branches.

Forgetting to account for non-recursive work. T(n) = T(n/2) is incomplete — what does each level do? If O(1), it's O(log n); if O(n), it's O(n).

Applying the Master Theorem to non-divide-and-conquer recurrences. T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1) is NOT a Master Theorem case — it's subtractive. Use the depth × work technique instead.

Treating fib(n−1) and fib(n−2) as O(2 · T(n−1)). They aren't quite the same, but for big-O purposes the bound 2·T(n−1) is close enough — both give O(2ⁿ).

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What is the time complexity of this recursive function?" — count branches and shrinkage; match to the famous recurrences.

Specifically watch for: factorial-style (T(n−1)+O(1)) → O(n); binary-search style (T(n/2)+O(1)) → O(log n); merge-sort style (2T(n/2)+O(n)) → O(n log n); naive Fibonacci → O(2ⁿ).

Master Theorem questions: identify a, b, f(n), then compute c = log_b(a) and compare.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Write the recurrence T(n) by counting branches, input shrinkage, and non-recursive work
  • T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1) → O(n)
  • T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)
  • T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n) (merge sort)
  • T(n) = 2T(n−1) + O(1) → O(2ⁿ) (naive Fibonacci)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Selection sort and insertion sort are basic O(n²) sorts that the OA tests heavily. You need to trace them by hand and know their key differences. Beyond the OA, both have practical roles: insertion sort is what hybrid sorts (like Timsort, Java's Dual-Pivot Quicksort) fall back to for small subarrays because it's surprisingly fast on small or nearly-sorted data. Selection sort minimizes swaps, useful when comparisons are cheap but writes are expensive (e.g., flash memory, EEPROM).

Selection sort

Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum and places it at the next sorted position.

SELECTION SORT
FOR i FROM 0 TO n-2:
  min_idx = i
  FOR j FROM i+1 TO n-1:
    IF arr[j] < arr[min_idx] THEN min_idx = j
  swap(arr[i], arr[min_idx])

The outer loop "fixes" position i. The inner loop scans the unsorted portion to find the minimum. After n − 1 outer iterations, the array is sorted.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Selection sort on [5, 2, 8, 1]
1
i = 0: scan [5, 2, 8, 1]. Min is 1 at index 3. Swap with arr[0]. → [1, 2, 8, 5].
2
i = 1: scan [2, 8, 5] (index 1+). Min is 2 at index 1. No swap (already in place). → [1, 2, 8, 5].
3
i = 2: scan [8, 5] (index 2+). Min is 5 at index 3. Swap. → [1, 2, 5, 8].
✓
Sorted in 3 outer passes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why selection sort is NOT stable

Sort [3a, 5, 3b, 1] where 3a and 3b are equal-key duplicates we want to track.

1
i=0: min is 1 at index 3. Swap with arr[0] (which is 3a). → [1, 5, 3b, 3a].
2
The original ORDER (3a came before 3b) is now reversed: 3b appears before 3a.
⚠
Selection sort can scramble the relative order of equal keys → NOT stable.
SELECTION SORT COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n²) all cases (best, average, worst)
  Why? You scan the rest of the array regardless of order.
Space: O(1) — in place
Stable: NO (long swaps can leap-frog equal elements)
Comparisons: ~n²/2. Swaps: at most n − 1 (very few).

Insertion sort

Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix, inserting each new element into its correct position.

INSERTION SORT
FOR i FROM 1 TO n-1:
  key = arr[i]; j = i - 1
  WHILE j >= 0 AND arr[j] > key:
    arr[j+1] = arr[j]; j = j - 1
  arr[j+1] = key

Think of arranging cards in your hand: pick up the next card, slide it left past any larger cards, drop it in the right spot.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insertion sort on [5, 2, 8, 1]
1
i = 1: key = 2. Compare with 5 → 5 > 2, shift 5 right. Insert 2 at index 0. → [2, 5, 8, 1].
2
i = 2: key = 8. Compare with 5 → 5 < 8, stop. Leave at index 2. → [2, 5, 8, 1].
3
i = 3: key = 1. Compare with 8 → shift. Compare with 5 → shift. Compare with 2 → shift. j = -1, insert at index 0. → [1, 2, 5, 8].
✓
Sorted in 3 outer passes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Best case: already sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4]
1
i=1: key=2. arr[0]=1 < 2, no shift. One comparison.
2
i=2: key=3. arr[1]=2 < 3, no shift. One comparison.
3
i=3: key=4. arr[2]=3 < 4, no shift. One comparison.
✓
Total: n − 1 comparisons, 0 shifts. O(n) — best case.
INSERTION SORT COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n) best (already sorted), O(n²) average/worst
Space: O(1) — in place
Stable: YES (uses > not >=, so equal keys don't cross)
Adaptive: YES — performs better on partially-sorted input

Why insertion sort is "adaptive"

Adaptive sorts run faster when the input is closer to sorted. For insertion sort, the inner WHILE only shifts as far as needed — if everything's already in place, it doesn't shift at all. For nearly-sorted arrays (a few elements out of place), the runtime approaches O(n) instead of O(n²).

Selection sort is NOT adaptive: it always scans the entire unsorted portion to find the min, even if the array is already sorted.

Side-by-side comparison

PropertySelectionInsertion
Best caseO(n²)O(n)
Average caseO(n²)O(n²)
Worst caseO(n²)O(n²)
SpaceO(1)O(1)
StableNoYes
AdaptiveNoYes
Comparisons~n²/2 (always)~n²/4 average; n−1 best
Swaps/shifts≤ n − 1 swaps~n²/4 shifts average

When to use which

USE SELECTION SORT WHEN
Writes are expensive (selection makes ≤ n−1 swaps; insertion may shift many times).
You need to know the answer is exactly n²/2 comparisons regardless of input.
Note: in modern systems, this rarely beats insertion sort in practice.
USE INSERTION SORT WHEN
Data is nearly sorted (becomes nearly O(n)).
Array is small (n < ~50) — overhead beats fancier sorts.
Stability matters.
As a fallback inside hybrid sorts (Timsort, Java's sort).

Bubble sort — quick mention

You may see bubble sort referenced. It repeatedly compares adjacent pairs and swaps them if out of order, "bubbling" the largest to the end each pass. O(n²) average and worst, O(n) best (with an early-exit optimization), stable. Generally treated as the worst of the three — use insertion sort instead.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Calling selection sort stable. It's NOT — long-distance swaps can scramble equal-key order.

Forgetting that insertion sort has O(n) best case. This is its key advantage and a frequent OA question.

Confusing the two: selection scans for the MIN of the unsorted portion; insertion scans BACKWARD through the sorted portion to find the slot.

Off-by-one in the inner loop: insertion sort's WHILE uses j ≥ 0 (not j > 0) so it can shift down to the very first element.

Using arr[j] >= key in insertion sort — that's NOT stable. Use strict > to preserve equal-key order.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What's the best-case time for insertion sort?" → O(n).

"Is selection sort stable?" → No.

"Is insertion sort stable?" → Yes.

"Which is adaptive?" → Insertion (selection is not).

"How many swaps does selection sort do, worst case?" → n − 1.

"Trace selection/insertion sort on this array" — practice; they're frequent.

"When is insertion sort preferable to merge sort?" → small or nearly-sorted arrays.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Both are O(n²) and in-place
  • Insertion sort: O(n) best case (sorted), stable, adaptive — best for small/nearly-sorted
  • Selection sort: O(n²) always, NOT stable, fewest swaps (≤ n−1)
  • Selection scans for the MIN of the rest; insertion scans BACKWARD through the sorted prefix
  • Insertion sort is the fallback in modern hybrid sorts (Timsort) for small subarrays
  • Use > not >= in insertion sort's inner loop to keep stability
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Selection sort and insertion sort are both O(n²). Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly-sorted data (best case); selection sort is always O(n²) but does the fewest swaps. Both are in-place.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
insertion sort on [3,1,2]:
[3,1,2] -> insert 1 -> [1,3,2] -> insert 2 -> [1,2,3]

Result: sorted in place, O(n²) worst

Insertion sort shines when data is almost sorted (few shifts → near O(n)); selection sort's comparison count is fixed at O(n²). Know their best/worst cases.

📊 FIGURE — bubble sort's place in the curriculum
🎯 EXAM TIP
Bubble sort is taught because it is simple to learn, not because anyone ships it. If a question asks why you would use bubble sort in production, the honest answer is that you would not — its value is pedagogical, as the easiest sort to trace by hand.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Quicksort is the most-used general-purpose sort in production. It's fast in practice, in-place, and the OA expects you to know its behavior, complexity, and worst-case pitfalls. Understanding Quicksort also unlocks several related ideas: divide-and-conquer, partitioning, and the importance of pivot choice.

The idea

Quicksort works by picking a pivot, partitioning the array so smaller elements are left and larger right, then recursively sorting each half.

QUICKSORT ALGORITHM
function quicksort(arr, lo, hi):
  IF lo < hi:
    p = partition(arr, lo, hi)
    quicksort(arr, lo, p - 1)
    quicksort(arr, p + 1, hi)

Lomuto partition (simplest)

def partition(arr, lo, hi):
 pivot = arr[hi]
 i = lo - 1
 for j in range(lo, hi):
 if arr[j] <= pivot:
 i += 1
 arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
 arr[i+1], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[i+1]
 return i + 1

The pivot is the last element. We sweep through, swapping smaller-than-pivot elements to the front, then place the pivot in its final spot.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Partition [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 6] (pivot = 6)
1
i = -1, pivot = 6.
2
j=0, arr[0]=3 ≤ 6: i=0, swap arr[0],arr[0]. → [3, 8, 2, 5, 1, 4, 7, 6].
3
j=1, arr[1]=8 > 6: skip.
4
j=2, arr[2]=2 ≤ 6: i=1, swap arr[1],arr[2]. → [3, 2, 8, 5, 1, 4, 7, 6].
5
j=3, arr[3]=5 ≤ 6: i=2, swap arr[2],arr[3]. → [3, 2, 5, 8, 1, 4, 7, 6].
6
j=4, arr[4]=1 ≤ 6: i=3, swap arr[3],arr[4]. → [3, 2, 5, 1, 8, 4, 7, 6].
7
j=5, arr[5]=4 ≤ 6: i=4, swap arr[4],arr[5]. → [3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 8, 7, 6].
8
j=6, arr[6]=7 > 6: skip.
9
Place pivot: swap arr[5],arr[7]. → [3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 6, 7, 8]. Return 5.
✓
Pivot 6 is in its final spot at index 5. Left ≤ 6, right > 6.

Complexity

QUICKSORT COMPLEXITY
Best case: O(n log n) — pivot splits array evenly each time
Average case: O(n log n) — random pivots typically split well
Worst case: O(n²) — pivot is always smallest or largest (e.g., sorted array with last-element pivot)
Space: O(log n) average call stack, O(n) worst
Stable: NO · In-place: YES

Why quicksort is fast in practice

Quicksort has the same big-O average as merge sort (n log n), but in practice it's usually faster because:

  • It's in-place — no extra memory allocation
  • Excellent cache locality — operates on contiguous memory
  • Small constant factor in the inner loop
  • Tail-recursion optimization is straightforward

Avoiding the worst case

PIVOT STRATEGIES
Last element (Lomuto default): O(n²) on already-sorted input — bad.
Random: practically eliminates worst case in expectation.
Median-of-three: pick median of first/middle/last — handles common patterns well.
Introsort: start with quicksort, switch to heapsort if depth exceeds 2·log n. Used by C++ std::sort.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Calling quicksort O(n log n) without qualification. It's O(n log n) AVERAGE but O(n²) WORST.

Saying quicksort is stable. It's NOT — equal-key elements can swap past each other during partition.

Forgetting that the worst case happens on already-sorted input with naive pivot choice. This is a frequent OA trap.

Using O(n) extra memory. Quicksort is in-place — partition swaps within the array.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Average time complexity of quicksort?" → O(n log n).

"Worst case?" → O(n²).

"What causes quicksort's worst case?" → bad pivot (always smallest/largest).

"Is quicksort stable?" → No.

"Is quicksort in-place?" → Yes.

"Why is quicksort often faster than merge sort?" → in-place, cache-friendly, lower constants.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Quicksort: divide-and-conquer via pivot + partition
  • Average O(n log n), worst O(n²)
  • In-place, NOT stable
  • Pivot choice matters — random or median-of-three avoids worst case
  • Fastest general-purpose sort in practice (cache-friendly, low constants)

Shellsort’s wildcard: its running time depends on the GAP SEQUENCE used — different sequences give different complexity bounds, which is why shellsort has no single clean big-O like the other sorts.
