Quicksort: average O(n log n), WORST O(n²) (already-sorted data with a bad pivot). It partitions around a pivot. In-place, not stable. OA asks the worst case and what causes it (poor pivot choice).

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Merge sort is the canonical guaranteed-O(n log n) sort. It's stable, predictable, and the basis for external sorts (sorting data too big for memory). The OA tests its complexity, stability, and the merge operation. It's also the gateway to understanding divide-and-conquer recurrences.

The idea

Merge sort recursively splits the array in half, sorts each half, and merges them.

MERGE SORT ALGORITHM
function mergeSort(arr):
  IF length(arr) ≤ 1: RETURN arr
  mid = length(arr) / 2
  left = mergeSort(arr[0..mid])
  right = mergeSort(arr[mid..end])
  RETURN merge(left, right)

The merge operation

def merge(left, right):
 result = []
 i = j = 0
 while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
 if left[i] <= right[j]:
 result.append(left[i])
 i += 1
 else:
 result.append(right[j])
 j += 1
 result.extend(left[i:])
 result.extend(right[j:])
 return result

Two pointers walk through the sorted halves, taking the smaller one at each step. Because both inputs are sorted, the result is sorted in O(n) time.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Merge sort [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
1
Split: [38, 27, 43] | [3, 9, 82, 10].
2
Sort left half [38, 27, 43]: split → [38] | [27, 43] → [38] | [27, 43] → merge → [27, 38, 43].
3
Sort right half [3, 9, 82, 10]: split → [3, 9] | [82, 10] → [3, 9] | [10, 82] → merge → [3, 9, 10, 82].
4
Merge [27, 38, 43] and [3, 9, 10, 82]:
5
Compare 27 vs 3 → take 3. Compare 27 vs 9 → take 9. Compare 27 vs 10 → take 10. Compare 27 vs 82 → take 27. Etc.
✓
Result: [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

Complexity analysis

MERGE SORT COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n log n) — all cases (best, average, worst)
Space: O(n) — extra arrays for merging
Stable: YES · In-place: NO

Why O(n log n)? The recurrence is T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n) — by the Master Theorem this is O(n log n).

  • Tree depth: log₂(n) levels of recursion
  • Work per level: O(n) total merging (each element touched once per level)
  • Total: depth × work = O(n log n)

Merge sort vs Quicksort

PropertyMerge sortQuicksort
AverageO(n log n)O(n log n)
WorstO(n log n)O(n²)
SpaceO(n)O(log n)
StableYesNo
In-placeNoYes
Practical speedSlower (allocations)Faster (cache)

When to choose merge sort

USE MERGE SORT WHEN
Worst-case guarantee matters (real-time systems, deadlines)
Stability matters (preserving order of equal keys)
Sorting linked lists (no random access penalty, no extra space needed)
External sorting (data too big for RAM — merging is naturally streaming)
Parallelization (independent recursive subproblems)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Calling merge sort O(n²) — it's NOT, it's O(n log n) in all cases.

Saying it's in-place. It typically uses O(n) extra space for the merge buffers.

Confusing the merge step's complexity. Merging two sorted halves of total size n is O(n), not O(n log n).

Forgetting the base case. if len ≤ 1: return arr — without it, infinite recursion on empty/single-element arrays.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Time complexity of merge sort?" → O(n log n) all cases.

"Space complexity?" → O(n).

"Is merge sort stable?" → Yes.

"Why does merge sort guarantee O(n log n) but quicksort doesn't?" → Merge sort always splits exactly in half; quicksort depends on pivot.

"What's the merge operation's complexity?" → O(n) for two halves of total size n.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Merge sort: divide-and-conquer with guaranteed O(n log n)
  • Stable, NOT in-place (needs O(n) extra space)
  • Merging two sorted halves is O(n) — that's the key operation
  • Use it when you need worst-case guarantees, stability, or external sorting
  • Standard for sorting linked lists (where merge sort beats quicksort)
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Merge sort: ALWAYS O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space (not in-place). Divide-and-conquer: split in half, sort each, merge. OA contrasts it with quicksort on stability and space.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
[3,1,2,4] -> [3,1]|[2,4] -> [1,3]|[2,4]
merge -> [1,2,3,4]

Merge sort's guaranteed n log n and stability come at the cost of O(n) auxiliary memory — the key trade-off vs. in-place quicksort.

🔢 Radix Sort & Bucket Sort — sorting WITHOUT comparisons

RADIX SORT
Sort integers digit by digit, starting from the LEAST significant digit (LSD), using 10 buckets (0–9). Each pass must be STABLE (preserve tie order) for it to work.
WORKED EXAMPLE — radix sort [21, 13, 42, 33]

Two passes (2 digits), zero value-vs-value comparisons.
BUCKET SORT
Distribute values into buckets by RANGE (e.g., 0–9, 10–19, …), sort each small bucket, then concatenate the buckets in order.
RadixBucket

Comparison-based?NO — that's how they can beat the O(n log n) comparison-sort limit
⚠️ LSD FIRST, AND STABILITY MATTERS

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK

  1. The least significant (rightmost) digit
  2. The most significant digit
  3. The middle digit
  4. Any random digit
Show answer + steps

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Radix sort and bucket sort beat the O(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound by NOT comparing elements. They exploit structure in the data — fixed-width keys, known value ranges, or near-uniform distributions — to sort in linear or near-linear time. The OA expects you to recognize them as non-comparison-based and to know when their special requirements make them appropriate.

The comparison-sort lower bound

Any sort that only compares elements (like quicksort, merge sort, heapsort) has a fundamental lower bound: Ω(n log n) in the worst case. This is provable from a decision-tree argument — sorting n elements requires distinguishing n! permutations, requiring log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n) comparisons.

Non-comparison sorts work around this by using the structure of the keys themselves (their digits or values) instead of comparing pairs.

COMPARISON vs NON-COMPARISON SORTS
Comparison sorts (any sort that asks "is a < b?"): Ω(n log n) lower bound.
  Examples: quicksort, merge sort, heapsort, insertion sort.
Non-comparison sorts (work with key structure directly): can beat O(n log n).
  Examples: counting sort, radix sort, bucket sort.

Counting sort (the building block)

Before radix sort, understand counting sort: count how many times each value occurs, then output values in order.

COUNTING SORT
1. For range 0..k, create count array of size k+1, all zero.
2. For each value v in input: count[v]++.
3. Output: for i = 0..k, write i to output count[i] times.
Time: O(n + k). Stable variant uses prefix sums.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting sort on [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2, 3]
1
Range 0..5. Count array [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0].
2
Increment for each input: count = [0, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1].
3
Output: 1 (×2), 2 (×1), 3 (×2), 4 (×1), 5 (×1) = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5]. ✓

Radix sort

Radix sort sorts by individual digits, from least significant to most significant (LSD radix). Each pass uses a stable sub-sort (typically counting sort on a single digit).

LSD RADIX SORT
For each digit position d from least significant to most:
  Stably sort the array by digit d.
After d passes, the array is fully sorted.
Time: O(d × (n + k)) where d is digit count and k is digit base (usually 10 or 256).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Radix sort [170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]
1
Sort by ones digit: 170 (0), 90 (0), 802 (2), 2 (2), 24 (4), 45 (5), 75 (5), 66 (6) → [170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66].
2
Sort by tens digit: 802 (0), 2 (0), 24 (2), 45 (4), 66 (6), 170 (7), 75 (7), 90 (9) → [802, 2, 24, 45, 66, 170, 75, 90].
3
Sort by hundreds digit: 2 (0), 24 (0), 45 (0), 66 (0), 75 (0), 90 (0), 170 (1), 802 (8) → [2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802]. ✓
CHECK
Sorted in 3 passes (max digit count = 3). Stability of each pass is essential — without it, results from earlier passes get scrambled.

Why does this work? Each pass orders by one digit; because each pass is stable, ties from the current digit preserve the order from earlier passes. After d passes, the order matches all d digits — i.e., the full numeric order.

Bucket sort

Bucket sort distributes elements into buckets (one per range of values), sorts each bucket independently, then concatenates them.

BUCKET SORT
1. Create k empty buckets covering the range.
2. Place each element in the bucket for its value range.
3. Sort each bucket (often with insertion sort).
4. Concatenate all buckets in order.
Average time: O(n + k) when distribution is uniform.
Worst time: O(n²) when all elements land in one bucket.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Bucket sort on [0.78, 0.17, 0.39, 0.26, 0.72, 0.94, 0.21, 0.12, 0.23, 0.68]
1
Use 10 buckets, each spanning 0.1: bucket i covers [i/10, (i+1)/10).
2
Place: 0.17 → b1, 0.78 → b7, 0.39 → b3, 0.26 → b2, 0.72 → b7, 0.94 → b9, 0.21 → b2, 0.12 → b1, 0.23 → b2, 0.68 → b6.
3
b1 = [0.17, 0.12]; b2 = [0.26, 0.21, 0.23]; b3 = [0.39]; b6 = [0.68]; b7 = [0.78, 0.72]; b9 = [0.94].
4
Sort each: b1 = [0.12, 0.17]; b2 = [0.21, 0.23, 0.26]; etc.
5
Concatenate: [0.12, 0.17, 0.21, 0.23, 0.26, 0.39, 0.68, 0.72, 0.78, 0.94]. ✓

Complexity comparison

SortAverageWorstSpaceStable?
CountingO(n + k)O(n + k)O(n + k)Yes
RadixO(d(n+k))O(d(n+k))O(n + k)Yes
BucketO(n + k)O(n²)O(n + k)Yes

Where: n = number of elements, k = range/bucket count, d = number of digits in the largest key.

When to use non-comparison sorts

USE NON-COMPARISON SORTS WHEN
Fixed-width keys: integers, strings of bounded length, dates → radix.
Small known range: values fit in a small set of buckets → counting.
Uniform distribution: data spreads evenly across the range → bucket.
Stability required: all three are stable.
Beating O(n log n): when the data structure permits, you get linear or near-linear time.
DON'T USE NON-COMPARISON SORTS WHEN
Keys are arbitrary objects with no numeric structure (use comparison sort).
Range k is huge compared to n (e.g., 32-bit ints, n = 100): O(n + k) becomes O(k).
Skewed distribution + bucket sort: many elements land in one bucket → O(n²).
Memory is tight: extra O(n + k) space matters.

Real-world applications

★ WHERE THESE SORTS SHINE

Radix: sorting fixed-width strings (postal codes, IPv4 addresses, ISBN numbers), large integer datasets, telephone numbers.

Counting: histogram-style problems, sorting age distributions, character frequency.

Bucket: sorting floating-point numbers in [0, 1), uniformly distributed test scores, evenly-spread coordinate data.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting that radix sort requires a STABLE sub-sort. If the sub-sort isn't stable, earlier digits' ordering gets scrambled by later passes. Counting sort is the standard stable choice.

Treating bucket sort as universally O(n). Worst case is O(n²) when all elements land in one bucket — happens with skewed distributions.

Trying to use counting sort on huge ranges. If max value is 10⁹ but n is only 1,000, you allocate a billion-element count array — totally impractical.

A linked list node stores data plus a reference (pointer) to the next node:

class Node:

📘 Deep dive: the List ADT & singly linked lists

The List ADT promises an ordered collection with operations — append, prepend, insert-after, remove, search — without dictating storage. A singly linked list implements it as nodes, each holding data plus a next pointer; the list keeps a head pointer (and often a tail).

Costs to memorize: prepend at head O(1); append O(1) WITH a tail pointer, O(n) without; search O(n) — you must walk node by node; remove-after-a-known-node O(1) — but FINDING that node was the O(n) part. Contrast with arrays: linked lists trade O(1) indexed access away in exchange for O(1) insertion/removal at known positions with no shifting.

Pointer surgery, precisely: to insert node X after node P: X.next = P.next, THEN P.next = X — that order, or you orphan the rest of the list. To remove the node after P: P.next = P.next.next.

Edge cases the OA loves: inserting into an empty list (head was null), removing the head (head moves to head.next), and the last node’s next being null — the loop guard is while (current != null).

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A singly linked list node holds data + next pointer. Insert/remove at head = O(1); access/search = O(n) (no indexing). Contrast with arrays: O(1) index but O(n) insert-in-middle.

Linked list insert and remove operations are bread-and-butter OA topics. You need to update pointers correctly and handle edge cases (empty list, head, tail). Pointer manipulation is also exactly where most production bugs originate — drop one pointer in the wrong order and you've leaked a list, freed a live node, or created a cycle. Mastering the order of operations now pays off for every linked structure later (BSTs, graphs, hash table chains).

Node structure recap

class Node:
 def __init__(self, data):
 self.data = data
 self.next = None # singly linked: only forward pointer

A singly linked list is a chain of these nodes, accessed through a head pointer. Optionally, a tail pointer is maintained for O(1) append.

Search

LINEAR SEARCH
node = head
WHILE node != None:
  IF node.data == target THEN RETURN node
  node = node.next
RETURN None

Time: O(n) worst case. There's no random access, so search must walk node by node.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Search for 7 in [3 → 5 → 7 → 9]
1
node = head (data 3). 3 ≠ 7, advance.
2
node has data 5. 5 ≠ 7, advance.
3
node has data 7. Match — return this node.
✓
3 comparisons. Worst case (target not present or at tail): n comparisons.

Insert at head (prepend)

PREPEND
new_node = Node(value)
new_node.next = head
head = new_node

Time: O(1)

Order matters! First link the new node to the old list, THEN update head. Reversing the order would orphan the entire list.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Prepend 1 to [3 → 5 → 7]
1
Create new_node with data 1. new_node.next = None initially.
2
new_node.next = head (which points to node 3). Now: new_node → 3 → 5 → 7.
3
head = new_node. List: [1 → 3 → 5 → 7]. ✓

Insert at tail (append)

Without a tail pointer: walk to the last node (where next is None), then attach.

def append(head, value):
 new_node = Node(value)
 if head is None:
 return new_node # empty list edge case
 node = head
 while node.next is not None:
 node = node.next
 node.next = new_node
 return head

Time: O(n) without tail pointer; O(1) with a tail pointer maintained.

Insert after a given node

INSERT AFTER X
new_node.next = X.next
X.next = new_node

Time: O(1) once X is found

Again, order matters. The new node must be linked to X.next BEFORE X is repointed; otherwise the rest of the list gets lost.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 4 after node with data 3 in [3 → 5 → 7]
1
X = node(3). new_node = node(4).
2
new_node.next = X.next (= node(5)). Now: new_node → 5 → 7.
3
X.next = new_node. Now: 3 → new_node → 5 → 7.
✓
Result: [3 → 4 → 5 → 7]. O(1) work.

Remove from head

REMOVE HEAD
IF head is None: nothing to remove
head = head.next

Time: O(1)

1
head currently points to node(1).
2
head = head.next = node(3).
✓
Result: [3 → 5]. node(1) is now unreachable (garbage collected).

Remove a specific value

Need the previous node's reference to update its next pointer.

def remove(head, value):
 # Handle head case first
 if head is None:
 return None
 if head.data == value:
 return head.next # remove head

 # Otherwise walk and find the node BEFORE the target
 prev = head
 while prev.next is not None and prev.next.data != value:
 prev = prev.next
 if prev.next is not None:
 prev.next = prev.next.next # bypass the target
 return head

Time: O(n) to find prev. The bypass itself is O(1).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Remove 5 from [3 → 5 → 7 → 9]
1
head.data = 3, not 5. Walk forward.
2
prev = node(3). prev.next = node(5). Match found.
3
prev.next = prev.next.next = node(7). Bypass complete.
✓
Result: [3 → 7 → 9]. node(5) is unreachable.

Edge cases — the OA's favorite traps

⚠ EDGE CASES TO ALWAYS CHECK

Empty list: head is None. Search returns None; insert at head creates a single-node list; remove does nothing.

Single-node list: head's next is None. Removing head leaves an empty list.

Removing the head: requires updating head, not just relinking. This is why dummy nodes simplify code.

Target not found: walking and never finding the node. Be sure your loop terminates and you handle the "not found" case.

Inserting/removing the only node: must handle both head and (if maintained) tail pointer.

Using a dummy header

If you add a dummy node before the real head, every insert/remove avoids the head edge case — the first real node is always dummy.next, and you never modify the dummy itself.

def remove_with_dummy(head, value):
 dummy = Node(0)
 dummy.next = head
 prev = dummy
 while prev.next is not None:
 if prev.next.data == value:
 prev.next = prev.next.next
 break
 prev = prev.next
 return dummy.next # the new head (could be None)

One uniform path through the code instead of branching on whether the target is the head.

"What is the time complexity of removing the tail of a singly linked list?" → O(n) because you need the previous node.

"What edge cases must you handle when removing a node?" → Empty list, removing the head, target not found.

"Why is a dummy header useful?" → It eliminates the head edge case for insert/remove operations.

"How do you remove a node given only a pointer to it (not the head)?" → For non-tail nodes, copy next's data into current and bypass next. Trick question because it's O(1) but doesn't actually remove the original node — it overwrites its data.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Wrong order of pointer updates. Always link the new node to its successor BEFORE breaking old links.

Forgetting that singly linked lists have no back-pointer. To remove a node, you need to find its predecessor first.

Not handling the empty-list case. head.next on an empty list throws a NoneType error.

Mixing up node = node.next (advance traversal) with node.next = something (modify list).

Returning None when the result should be the head, especially after removing the head — make sure to track the new head.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Search: O(n). Insert/remove at head: O(1). Insert/remove specific node: O(n) to find.

  • Tail pointer makes append O(1)

You must reach the node before the target to relink around it; that traversal is why arbitrary removal is O(n) in a singly linked list.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Doubly linked lists add a prev pointer to each node. They enable O(1) deletion when you have a node reference, and bidirectional traversal — critical for many real-world apps. Browser history, music players, LRU caches, deques, and even text editors' line buffers all need the back-and-forth motion that doubly linked lists give you for free. The OA tests "given a node, remove it" which is O(n) singly but O(1) doubly — the difference is the entire point.

Doubly linked node

class DNode:
 def __init__(self, data):
 self.data = data
 self.prev = None # reference to previous node
 self.next = None # reference to next node

Both head and tail are typically maintained for O(1) access at either end. The first node has prev = None; the last has next = None.

DOUBLY LINKED LIST INVARIANTS
head.prev = None (head has no predecessor)
tail.next = None (tail has no successor)
For any node X: X.next.prev = X (if X.next exists)
For any node X: X.prev.next = X (if X.prev exists)

Every operation must preserve these invariants. Forgetting one direction is the most common doubly-linked-list bug.

Insert at head

PREPEND
new = DNode(value)
new.next = head
IF head THEN head.prev = new
head = new
IF tail is None THEN tail = new (empty-list case)

Time: O(1)

Insert at tail

APPEND
new = DNode(value)
new.prev = tail
IF tail THEN tail.next = new
tail = new
IF head is None THEN head = new (empty-list case)

Time: O(1) — head AND tail pointers make this trivial

Insert before a given node X

INSERT BEFORE X
new.prev = X.prev
new.next = X
IF X.prev THEN X.prev.next = new
ELSE head = new (X was the head)
X.prev = new

1
X = node(5). X.prev = node(3), X.next = node(7).
2

3
X.prev exists (node 3), so node(3).next = new.
4
X.prev = new.
✓

Remove node X — the killer feature

REMOVE NODE X (GIVEN)
IF X.prev THEN X.prev.next = X.next
ELSE head = X.next (X was the head)
IF X.next THEN X.next.prev = X.prev
ELSE tail = X.prev (X was the tail)

Time: O(1) when X is given (no need to find prev — it's stored)

This is the headline operation: in a singly linked list, removing a given node requires O(n) to walk and find the predecessor. With a back-pointer, it's O(1).

X = node(5). X.prev = node(3), X.next = node(7).
2
X.prev exists → node(3).next = X.next = node(7).
3
X.next exists → node(7).prev = X.prev = node(3).

X = node(1). X.prev = None, X.next = node(3).
2
X.prev is None → head = X.next = node(3).
3
X.next exists → node(3).prev = None (X.prev).

Bidirectional traversal

Walking forward and backward are both O(n) — but you can do either, which singly linked lists can't.

def traverse_forward(head):
 node = head
 while node is not None:
 process(node.data)
 node = node.next

def traverse_backward(tail):
 node = tail
 while node is not None:
 process(node.data)
 node = node.prev

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Traversal is the foundation for any operation on a linked list. Once you can walk a linked list cleanly, you can sort it, detect cycles, reverse it, find the middle, or merge two of them — all of which appear regularly on the OA. Iterative traversal

STANDARD ITERATIVE TRAVERSAL
node = head
WHILE node != None:
  process(node.data)
  node = node.next

Time: O(n), space: O(1). The pattern is the workhorse of every linked-list operation.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sum a linked list of integers
def sum_list(head):
 total = 0
 node = head
 while node is not None:
 total += node.data
 node = node.next

1
Visit each node once: O(n).
2
Only one variable plus the running total: O(1) extra space.

Recursive traversal

function traverse(node):
  IF node == None THEN RETURN
  process(node.data)
  traverse(node.next)

Time: O(n), space: O(n) for the call stack. Iterative is usually better unless the problem naturally pairs with recursion (like reverse-in-place).

Common traversal patterns

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Find the middle (Tortoise and Hare)

Two pointers: slow advances 1 step, fast advances 2 steps. When fast hits the end, slow is at the middle.

def find_middle(head):
 slow = fast = head
 while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
 slow = slow.next
 fast = fast.next.next
 return slow
✓
O(n) time, O(1) space. The key insight: when fast covers 2x distance, slow is at half — the middle.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reverse a linked list iteratively
def reverse(head):
 prev = None
 curr = head
 while curr is not None:
 next_node = curr.next # save before overwriting
 curr.next = prev # flip the pointer
 prev = curr
 curr = next_node
 return prev # new head
1
Maintain three pointers: prev (already reversed), curr (in progress), next (still to come).
2
Each iteration: save next, flip curr's pointer, advance both prev and curr.
✓
O(n) time, O(1) space.

Sorting a linked list

Merge sort works particularly well for linked lists. Unlike arrays, no auxiliary memory is needed for the merge — pointers are just relinked.

LINKED LIST MERGE SORT
1. If list has 0 or 1 nodes, return as-is.
2. Split list into halves (using fast/slow pointers).
3. Recursively sort each half.
4. Merge the two sorted halves into one.
Time: O(n log n). Space: O(log n) for recursion stack.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Merge two sorted linked lists

Lists L1: 1 → 3 → 5, L2: 2 → 4 → 6. Merge into one sorted list.

def merge(L1, L2):
 dummy = Node(0) # placeholder head
 tail = dummy
 while L1 and L2:
 if L1.data <= L2.data:
 tail.next = L1
 L1 = L1.next
 else:
 tail.next = L2
 L2 = L2.next
 tail = tail.next
 tail.next = L1 or L2 # attach whatever's left
 return dummy.next
1
Compare heads: 1 < 2, attach 1. Tail: 1.
2
Now heads are 3 and 2: attach 2. Tail: 1 → 2.
3
3 < 4: attach 3. Tail: 1 → 2 → 3.
4
Continue: 4, 5, 6.
✓
Result: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6. O(n+m) time, O(1) space (no allocation).

Insertion sort on a linked list: walk through and insert each node into the correct position in a new sorted list. Time: O(n²) — only practical for small lists.

Quicksort on linked lists is awkward (no random access for partitioning). Generally avoid it; merge sort is the canonical choice.

Circular linked lists

In a circular linked list, the last node's next points back to head instead of None.

USES OF CIRCULAR LISTS
Round-robin scheduling (CPU process queue)
Music playlists in "repeat all" mode
Multi-player game turn order
Buffer rings (network packets, audio samples)

To traverse a circular list, you can't loop until node is None — you'd never stop. Instead, remember the starting node and stop when you return to it:

CIRCULAR LIST TRAVERSAL
start = head
node = head
DO:
  process(node.data)
  node = node.next
WHILE node != start

Cycle detection — Floyd's algorithm

To detect whether a (possibly broken) linked list contains a cycle, use Floyd's "tortoise and hare":

FLOYD'S CYCLE DETECTION
slow = fast = head
WHILE fast and fast.next:
  slow = slow.next (1 step)
  fast = fast.next.next (2 steps)
  IF slow == fast: RETURN "cycle found"
RETURN "no cycle"

Why this works: if there's a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one inside the loop. If there isn't, fast hits None first.

Dummy nodes

A dummy header (also called a sentinel) simplifies linked-list code by avoiding head-edge cases. The first real node is always dummy.next.

Without a dummy, every operation that might modify the head needs special handling: "if I'm modifying the first node, I need to update head; otherwise just relink." With a dummy, head is never modified — only its next pointer.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Remove all nodes with value v

Without a dummy, the head case is awkward. With a dummy, it's uniform.

def remove_all(head, v):
 dummy = Node(0)
 dummy.next = head
 prev = dummy
 while prev.next is not None:
 if prev.next.data == v:
 prev.next = prev.next.next # skip
 else:
 prev = prev.next
 return dummy.next
✓
The dummy ensures even removing the first node works without special-casing.
★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Find the middle of a linked list" → tortoise and hare.

"Detect a cycle" → Floyd's algorithm.

"Reverse a linked list" → three-pointer iterative method (prev, curr, next).

"Merge two sorted linked lists" → use a dummy node and walk both lists.

"Sort a linked list in O(n log n)" → merge sort (not quicksort).

Circular lists: stop with while node != start, not while node is not None.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting to save next before overwriting it during reversal. curr.next = prev destroys the old next pointer if you didn't save it.

Trying to traverse a circular list with while node is not None — infinite loop.

Using O(n) auxiliary space (e.g., copying to an array, sorting, copying back) when O(log n) merge sort works in-place.

Forgetting that recursive traversal uses O(n) stack space — for a list of a million nodes, this can blow the stack.

Treating Floyd's two pointers as if they always meet at the start of the cycle. They meet inside the cycle; finding the cycle's start requires a second pointer reset (a separate trick).

  • Iterative traversal: O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Recursive: O(n) time, but O(n) stack space
  • Merge sort is the canonical linked-list sort: O(n log n) time, O(log n) stack
  • Circular list: tail.next points to head; traverse with a start-marker
  • Floyd's tortoise-and-hare detects cycles in O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Dummy nodes eliminate head-edge cases — use them for insert/delete operations
  • Tortoise-and-hare also finds the middle of a linked list in one pass

Naive queue on a dynamic array: enqueue at the back is O(1) amortized, but dequeue from the front is O(n) — every remaining element shifts left. (Circular buffers fix this.) Space reality of dynamic arrays: capacity grows by doubling, so an array that is half-full occupies up to 2× the space its elements need — size and capacity are different numbers.

Traversal is O(n); you cannot index a linked list in O(1). Sorting a linked list favors merge sort (no random access needed). OA asks why quicksort/heapsort fit arrays better than lists.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
node = head
while node:        # O(n)
    visit(node)
    node = node.next

Result: full traversal is O(n)

Merge sort works well on lists because it only needs sequential access; array-oriented sorts that rely on indexing (heap/quick) are awkward on lists.

The Stack ADT

A stack is a linear collection where all operations happen at the same end — the top. The result: last in, first out (LIFO).

Implementation 1 — linked list (head as top)

Push and pop at the head. Always O(1) — the head pointer is updated, no walking required.

class Stack:
 def __init__(self):
 self.head = None
 self.count = 0

 def push(self, value):
 node = Node(value)
 node.next = self.head
 self.head = node
 self.count += 1

 def pop(self):
 if self.head is None:
 raise IndexError("stack empty")
 value = self.head.data
 self.head = self.head.next
 self.count -= 1
 return value

 def peek(self):
 if self.head is None:
 raise IndexError("stack empty")
 return self.head.data

The head IS the top. Every operation is O(1) because we never walk the list.

Implementation 2 — dynamic array (top at end)

Push at the end (append); pop from the end. O(1) amortized — occasional resizes happen but average out to constant.

class ArrayStack:
 def __init__(self):
 self.items = []

 def push(self, x):
 self.items.append(x) # O(1) amortized

 def pop(self):
 if not self.items:
 raise IndexError("stack empty")
 return self.items.pop() # O(1) — pop from END is fast

 def peek(self):
 return self.items[-1]

Why pop at the end, not the beginning? list.pop(0) is O(n) — every other element shifts. list.pop() (no argument, pops last) is O(1). The end of an array is the natural top for an array-backed stack.

Implementation 3 — Python list directly

In idiomatic Python, you don't even need a class. Use a regular list with append as push and pop as pop:

stack = []
stack.append(1) # push
stack.append(2)
top = stack[-1] # peek
x = stack.pop() # pop returns x

The call stack — why recursion needs a stack

Every function call pushes a stack frame containing local variables, parameters, and the return address. When the function returns, its frame pops. The "call stack" you see in any debugger IS a stack data structure.

Implementation 1 — linked list with head and tail

Enqueue at tail, dequeue at head. Both O(1) when both pointers are maintained.

class Queue:
 def __init__(self):
 self.head = None
 self.tail = None
 self.count = 0

 def enqueue(self, value):
 node = Node(value)
 if self.tail is None: # empty queue
 self.head = self.tail = node
 else:
 self.tail.next = node
 self.tail = node
 self.count += 1

 def dequeue(self):
 if self.head is None:
 raise IndexError("queue empty")
 value = self.head.data
 self.head = self.head.next
 if self.head is None: # became empty
 self.tail = None
 self.count -= 1
 return value

Why this works: enqueue uses tail only; dequeue uses head only. They never collide.

Implementation 2 — naive array (DON'T do this)

class BadQueue:
 def __init__(self):
 self.items = []

 def enqueue(self, x):
 self.items.append(x) # O(1) amortized

 def dequeue(self):
 return self.items.pop(0) # O(n)! shifts everything left

pop(0) is O(n) because every other element shifts down by one. For n operations, this becomes O(n²) total — quadratic blowup.

Implementation 3 — circular array (the right way)

A circular array uses front and rear indices that wrap around. Dequeue just advances front; no shifting.

CIRCULAR ARRAY MECHANICS
capacity = fixed array size
enqueue: arr[rear] = x; rear = (rear + 1) mod capacity; size++
dequeue: x = arr[front]; front = (front + 1) mod capacity; size--; return x
isFull: size == capacity (or use empty slot trick: rear+1 == front)
isEmpty: size == 0 (or front == rear with separate flag)

Operations: enqueue 10, 20, 30, dequeue, dequeue, enqueue 40, 50, 60.

2

3

4
enq 30: [10, 20, 30, _, _], rear=3, size=3.
5
dequeue → 10. front=1, size=2. Slot 0 is "free" now.
6
dequeue → 20. front=2, size=1.
7

8
enq 50: write at slot 4, rear=(4+1) mod 5 = 0, size=3.
9
enq 60: write at slot 0 (now reused), rear=1, size=4.
✓
Final: [60, _, 30, 40, 50], front=2, rear=1, size=4. Notice rear wrapped past front — that's circularity in action.

In practice, Python provides collections.deque with O(1) operations on both ends. It's the standard queue in idiomatic Python.

q = deque()
q.append(x) # enqueue (O(1))
q.popleft() # dequeue (O(1))

Implementation 1 — doubly linked list

The natural fit. Maintain head and tail pointers; both ends are O(1).

class Deque:
 def __init__(self):
 self.head = None
 self.tail = None
 self.count = 0

 def addFirst(self, value):
 node = DNode(value)
 node.next = self.head
 if self.head:
 self.head.prev = node
 self.head = node
 if self.tail is None:
 self.tail = node
 self.count += 1

 def addLast(self, value):
 node = DNode(value)
 node.prev = self.tail
 if self.tail:
 self.tail.next = node
 self.tail = node
 if self.head is None:
 self.head = node
 self.count += 1

 def removeFirst(self):
 if self.head is None:
 raise IndexError("deque empty")
 value = self.head.data
 self.head = self.head.next
 if self.head:
 self.head.prev = None
 else:
 self.tail = None
 self.count -= 1
 return value

 def removeLast(self):
 if self.tail is None:
 raise IndexError("deque empty")
 value = self.tail.data
 self.tail = self.tail.prev
 if self.tail:
 self.tail.next = None
 else:
 self.head = None
 self.count -= 1
 return value

Why doubly linked: removing from the back requires the previous node's reference. Without back-pointers, removeLast would be O(n).

Implementation 2 — circular array

Use indices that wrap around modulo capacity. Front and rear can grow in either direction.

CIRCULAR ARRAY DEQUE
addFirst: front = (front − 1 + capacity) mod capacity; arr[front] = x; size++
addLast: arr[rear] = x; rear = (rear + 1) mod capacity; size++
removeFirst: x = arr[front]; front = (front + 1) mod capacity; size--
removeLast: rear = (rear − 1 + capacity) mod capacity; x = arr[rear]; size--

Note the "+ capacity" before mod when subtracting — Python's mod handles negatives, but many languages need this guard.

Implementation 3 — Python's collections.deque

Python provides a deque in the standard library. It's implemented as a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (a hybrid for efficiency).

from collections import deque

d = deque()
d.append(x) # addLast
d.appendleft(x) # addFirst
d.pop() # removeLast
d.popleft() # removeFirst
d[0] # peekFirst
d[-1] # peekLast

This is what you'd use in any practical Python code.

You can implement a stack OR a queue using a deque (just restrict yourself to one end pair). The reverse isn't true.

The sliding window maximum problem

The deque's headline algorithmic application: finding the maximum (or minimum) of every k-element window in an array, in O(n) total time.

SLIDING WINDOW MAXIMUM ALGORITHM
Maintain a deque of INDICES, where the values at those indices are in decreasing order.
For each new index i:
  1. Remove from the BACK any index whose value ≤ arr[i] (those can never be max).
  2. Add i at the back.
  3. Remove from the FRONT if it's outside the window (i − front ≥ k).
  4. After window forms, the front index is the current max's position.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sliding window max for [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k=3
1
i=0 (val=1): deque = [0]. Window not yet size 3.
2
i=1 (val=3): remove back (1 < 3). deque = [1]. Window not full.
3
i=2 (val=-1): -1 < 3. deque = [1, 2]. Front index 1, value 3 → max for window [0..2] = 3.
4
i=3 (val=-3): deque = [1, 2, 3]. Window [1..3]: front index 1 still in window. Max = 3.
5
i=4 (val=5): pop -3, -1, 3 (all ≤ 5). deque = [4]. Max for [2..4] = 5.
6
i=5 (val=3): deque = [4, 5]. Front 4 in window. Max for [3..5] = 5.
7
i=6 (val=6): pop 5 (3 < 6), pop 4 (5 < 6). deque = [6]. Max for [4..6] = 6.
8
i=7 (val=7): pop 6 (6 < 7). deque = [7]. Max for [5..7] = 7.
✓
Window maxes: [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]. Total time: O(n). Each element added and removed at most once from the deque.

When to use a deque

REAL-WORLD DEQUE USES
Sliding window algorithms — maximum/minimum in window, anagram detection
Browser history — back AND forward navigation
Implementing both stack and queue with one structure
Work-stealing schedulers — workers steal from the back of others' queues
Palindrome checking — compare front and back, advance both inward
Undo/redo with limited history — bounded deque, evict oldest
Buffer with both producers and consumers on either side

 d = deque(s)
 while len(d) > 1:
 if d.popleft() != d.pop():
 return False

2
'a' == 'a' ✓. d = ['d'].
3

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Implementing a deque with a singly linked list. removeLast becomes O(n) — you need the back-pointer for O(1).

Confusing deque (both ends) with double-linked-list (one direction only matters at a time). A deque is an ADT; doubly linked list is one possible implementation.

In circular array: forgetting to add capacity before mod when decrementing front. (front − 1) mod capacity can give negative results in some languages.

Using Python's list as a deque. list.insert(0, x) and list.pop(0) are O(n). Use collections.deque instead.

#️⃣ Hash Tables & Hash Functions

THE MAP ADT
A Map (Dictionary / Associative Array) stores key-value pairs — you look up by KEY, not index. put/get/remove/contains are all O(1) average, O(n) worst; size() is O(1). The engine that makes O(1) possible is the hash function: hash(key) → integer in [0, capacity), usually raw hashCode then mod capacity.
THE 4 PROPERTIES OF A GOOD HASH
PropertyMeaningIf it fails…
1. DeterministicSame key → same hash, every timeLookups fail
2. UniformKeys spread evenly across bucketsClustering, slow lookups
3. FastTypically O(length of key)Defeats the O(1) point
4. AvalancheSmall key change → large hash changePatterns collide
WORKED: HASH BY MOD (capacity 10)
hash(42) = 42 % 10 = 2 · hash(123) = 3 · hash(307) = 7 — but keys 10, 20, 30… ALL land in bucket 0. Patterned keys break plain mod, which is why prime capacities (13, 31, 53, 97) help. Java's HashMap uses powers of 2 + a "spread" step instead.
WORKED: POLYNOMIAL STRING HASH
h = (h × 31 + ord(c)) % capacity per character. For "ab", capacity 100: 'a'(97) → h = 97; 'b'(98) → (97×31 + 98) % 100 = 3105 % 100 = 5. Why 31? Prime, good spread, and ×31 = (×32) − 1 — fast on hardware.
⚠️ BAD HASHES & THE IMMUTABILITY RULE
hash = 0 (everything collides, O(n)) · len(s) ("cat"/"dog"/"rat" → 3) · char-sum (anagrams "abc"/"cba" collide) · no modulo (index out of range). And keys must be IMMUTABLE — mutate a key after insertion and its bucket no longer matches: lookup breaks. Load factor preview: α = n / capacity.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
With hash(n) = n % 10, where does key 307 land?
  1. Bucket 7
  2. Bucket 3
  3. Bucket 0
  4. Bucket 30
Show answer + steps
A. 307 ÷ 10 = 30 remainder 7.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Hash tables are the most-used data structure in modern software — Python dicts, Java HashMaps, JavaScript objects, database indexes, caches, and countless more. The OA tests definitions, hash function properties, and basic computation. Understanding what a hash function actually does — and why "good" matters — is the foundation for everything in this chapter.

The Map ADT

A Map (also called Dictionary or Associative Array) stores key-value pairs. You look up values by their key, not by index.

OperationDescriptionHash table time
put(key, value)Insert or updateO(1) avg, O(n) worst
get(key)Look up value by keyO(1) avg, O(n) worst
remove(key)Delete entry by keyO(1) avg, O(n) worst
contains(key)Test if key existsO(1) avg, O(n) worst
size()Number of entriesO(1)

The hash function — the heart of it all

A hash function converts a key into a non-negative integer index in the range [0, table_size).

HASH FUNCTION SIGNATURE
hash(key) → integer in [0, capacity)

Common composition:
raw = hashCode(key) # arbitrary integer (could be negative or huge)
index = raw mod capacity # constrain to [0, capacity)

Properties of a GOOD hash function

FOUR PROPERTIES OF A GOOD HASH
1. Deterministic — same key → same hash, every time
2. Uniform distribution — keys spread evenly across buckets (minimizes collisions)
3. Fast to compute — typically O(length of key)
4. Avalanche effect — small change in key → large change in hash

If even one property fails, you get problems. A non-deterministic hash means lookups can fail. A non-uniform hash means clustering and slow lookups. A slow hash defeats the whole O(1) point.

Simple hash functions for common types

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hash an integer
def hash_int(n, capacity):
 return n % capacity
1
For capacity = 10: hash(42) = 42 % 10 = 2.
2
hash(123) = 123 % 10 = 3.
3
hash(307) = 307 % 10 = 7.
⚠
If keys are all multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30, ...), they ALL hash to bucket 0 — terrible distribution.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hash a string (polynomial)
def hash_string(s, capacity):
 h = 0
 for c in s:
 h = (h * 31 + ord(c)) % capacity
 return h
1
For "ab", capacity = 100:
2
h = 0. Process 'a' (97): h = (0*31 + 97) % 100 = 97.
3
Process 'b' (98): h = (97*31 + 98) % 100 = (3007 + 98) % 100 = 3105 % 100 = 5.
4
Result: hash("ab") = 5.
✓
Why 31? It's prime, gives good distribution, and × 31 = (× 32) − 1 = (left-shift 5) − 1 — fast on hardware.

Why prime capacities help

PRIME TABLE SIZES
Using a prime number for capacity (e.g., 13, 31, 53, 97) reduces clustering when keys have hidden patterns.

Why? If capacity = 100 and many keys are multiples of 10, they all collide. If capacity = 97 (prime), the modulo operation distributes them across many buckets.

Java's HashMap uses powers of 2 (faster modulo via bitmask) but adds a "spread" function to break up patterns. Python's dict uses a similar trick.

Bad hash functions — what NOT to do

⚠ BAD HASH EXAMPLES

hash(s) = 0 — always returns 0. All keys collide. Lookups become O(n).

hash(s) = len(s) — only as many buckets as string lengths. "cat", "dog", "rat" all hash to 3.

hash(n) = n for integers without modulo — the result might exceed table size or be negative.

Sum of characters — "abc" and "cba" hash identically. Anagrams collide.

Load factor preview

LOAD FACTOR
α = n / capacity
where n = number of entries, capacity = number of buckets

α < 0.5: lots of empty buckets, some wasted memory
α ≈ 0.7-0.75: typical resize threshold (Java HashMap default 0.75)
α > 1: with chaining, average chain length grows
α near 1: with open addressing, performance degrades catastrophically

We'll see in the next sections how chaining and open addressing each handle collisions, and how the load factor governs their performance.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting that hash tables are O(1) AVERAGE, not always. Worst case is O(n) — when all keys collide.

Treating "hash function" as a black box. The OA tests basic computation: hash(42) % 10 = 2.

Using a non-deterministic hash (e.g., one that uses random or time). Lookups will fail.

Hash tables don't preserve insertion order (in older Python and Java). Modern Python 3.7+ does, but it's an implementation detail.

Hash table keys must be IMMUTABLE. If you mutate a key after insertion, you can't find it again — its hash will be different.

"What's the worst case?" → O(n).

"What does a hash function do?" → maps a key to an integer index in [0, capacity).

"What property prevents two equal keys from hashing to different values?" → determinism.

"Compute hash(42) % 10" → 2. Practice this on common values.

"Why use a prime capacity?" → reduces clustering on patterned keys.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Map ADT: key-value pairs with put/get/remove/contains
  • Hash function maps any key → integer in [0, capacity)
  • Good hash: deterministic, uniform, fast, avalanche
  • Hash table operations: O(1) average, O(n) worst
  • Prime capacities reduce clustering on patterned keys
  • String hash typically polynomial: h = h*31 + char
  • Keys must be IMMUTABLE — mutating after insertion breaks lookup
🧠 MEMORY AID

Hash tables: a good hash function is deterministic, uniform, and fast. Load factor α = items ÷ buckets; resize (rehash) when α climbs past ~0.7 to keep operations near O(1). Average lookup/insert/delete = O(1); worst case (everything collides) = O(n).

h(53) = 3  -> store in bucket 3

Result: key 53 lands in bucket 3

🔗 Collisions & Separate Chaining

COLLISIONS ARE INEVITABLE
Two keys hashing to the same bucket = a collision. The pigeonhole principle guarantees them once keys outnumber buckets — and the birthday paradox says just 23 random insertions into 365 buckets already give a 50% collision chance. So every hash table needs a resolution strategy.
THE STRATEGY: EACH BUCKET IS A LINKED LIST
put: hash → walk that bucket's chain → UPDATE if the key exists, else append (and resize if α > 0.75). get / remove: hash → walk the chain.
WORKED: CAPACITY 5, hash = ASCII sum % 5
OpHashResult
put("ab", 1)97+98=195 % 5 = 0Bucket 0: [("ab",1)]
put("ba", 2)98+97=195 % 5 = 0Collision! Bucket 0: [("ab",1), ("ba",2)]
put("c", 3)99 % 5 = 4Bucket 4: [("c",3)]
put("ab", 99)0Key exists → UPDATE: [("ab",99), ("ba",2)]
Note "ab"/"ba" colliding is exactly the char-sum anagram weakness from last lesson.
LOAD FACTOR = AVERAGE CHAIN LENGTH
α = n / capacity, and average lookup is O(1 + α). Keep α bounded (resize past ~0.75) and operations stay O(1). Chaining even tolerates α > 1 gracefully.
⚠️ WORST CASE & HASH FLOODING
Adversarial or pathological keys can pile into ONE bucket → the table becomes a linked list, O(n) lookups. Real attack: hash flooding — crafted colliding data degrades servers; Python and Java defend with a randomized hash seed. Cons of chaining: pointer overhead, cache-unfriendly. Java's HashMap uses chaining.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Collisions are inevitable — the pigeonhole principle guarantees them when you map many keys to fewer buckets. Separate chaining is the most common collision resolution strategy and is what Java's HashMap and most language implementations use under the hood. The OA tests how chaining works, its complexity, and how load factor affects it.

The collision problem

When two different keys hash to the same bucket, that's a collision. By the pigeonhole principle, if you have more keys than buckets, collisions are inevitable. Even with fewer keys than buckets, collisions are LIKELY: the birthday paradox says with just 23 random insertions into 365 buckets, there's a 50% chance of collision.

Separate chaining — the strategy

Separate chaining: each bucket is a linked list (or other small collection) of entries that hash there.

CHAINING STRUCTURE
buckets = array of capacity slots, each holding a linked list

Bucket 0: → [ ("apple", 1) → ("banana", 7) ]
Bucket 1: → []
Bucket 2: → [ ("cherry", 3) ]
Bucket 3: → [ ("date", 9) → ("egg", 2) → ("fig", 4) ]
...

Insert

def put(key, value):
 idx = hash(key) % capacity
 chain = buckets[idx]
 for entry in chain:
 if entry.key == key:
 entry.value = value # update existing
 return
 chain.append((key, value)) # insert new
 n += 1
 if n / capacity > 0.75: resize()
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert into chained hash table (capacity 5)

Hash function: hash(s) = sum of ASCII values % 5.

1
put("ab", 1): hash = 97+98 = 195, 195 % 5 = 0. Bucket 0: [("ab", 1)].
2
put("ba", 2): hash = 98+97 = 195, 195 % 5 = 0. Collision! Append. Bucket 0: [("ab", 1), ("ba", 2)].
3
put("c", 3): hash = 99 % 5 = 4. Bucket 4: [("c", 3)].
4
put("ab", 99): hash = 0. Walk chain, find existing ("ab", 1), UPDATE to ("ab", 99). Bucket 0: [("ab", 99), ("ba", 2)].
✓
Final: bucket 0 has 2 entries, bucket 4 has 1, others empty.

Search (get)

def get(key):
 idx = hash(key) % capacity
 chain = buckets[idx]
 for entry in chain:
 if entry.key == key:
 return entry.value
 return None # not found

Walk the chain at the bucket — return the value if found, None otherwise.

Remove

def remove(key):
 idx = hash(key) % capacity
 chain = buckets[idx]
 for i, entry in enumerate(chain):
 if entry.key == key:
 chain.pop(i)
 n -= 1
 return True
 return False # not found

Load factor and performance

LOAD FACTOR α = n / capacity
Average chain length = α (entries divided across buckets).
Lookup time: O(1 + α) on average — constant + chain walk.

α = 0.5: chains average 0.5 entries (mostly empty or one element). Fast.
α = 1.0: chains average 1 entry. Still fast.
α = 5: chains average 5 entries. Lookups are slower but still constant in n.
α = n/1: all in one bucket. Linear lookup.

Why O(1) is "amortized average"? If keys hash uniformly, chains have similar lengths near α. The average lookup walks ~α entries. As long as α stays bounded (resize when α > 0.75), lookups stay O(1).

Worst case — when chaining degrades

⚠ WORST CASE: O(n)

If the hash function is adversarial OR the keys are pathological, all keys could hash to one bucket. Then the table is essentially a linked list, and lookup is O(n).

Real-world example: hash flooding attacks. An attacker sends data deliberately crafted to collide, degrading the server to O(n²) processing time. Defenses: use a randomized hash seed (Python and Java both do).

Chaining complexity summary

OperationAverageWorst
InsertO(1)O(n)
SearchO(1)O(n)
RemoveO(1)O(n)

ProsCons
Simple to implement and reason about
Handles α > 1 gracefully
Easy to delete entries
No need to resize until α gets large		Extra memory for linked-list pointers
Cache-unfriendly (chains scattered in memory)
Worst case still O(n)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing chaining with open addressing. In chaining, multiple entries live IN one bucket via a list. In open addressing, the table itself probes for the next free slot.

Forgetting to walk the chain. After hashing, you must search the chain to find the EXACT key (since multiple keys can hash to same bucket).

Treating load factor as a hard limit. With chaining, α > 1 still works — just slows down. With open addressing, α near 1 is catastrophic.

Counting bucket count as table size. If 100 buckets each have 5 entries, the table size is 500, not 100.

"What is the load factor?" → α = n / capacity (entries divided by buckets).

"How does chaining handle collisions?" → appends to the list at that bucket.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Separate chaining: each bucket holds a linked list of entries
  • Average operations O(1), worst O(n)

  • Resize when α > ~0.75 to keep operations fast

  • Cons: pointer overhead, cache-unfriendly

🎯 Open Addressing: Linear, Quadratic, Double

THE IDEA
No linked lists — every entry lives IN the array itself. On collision, probe for the next empty slot. Cache-friendly, less memory; Python's dict and Ruby's Hash use it. All three examples below: capacity 7, hash(n) = n % 7, inserting 18, 32, 25, 4 (ALL hash to slot 4).
① LINEAR PROBING — (hash + i) % 7
18→4 · 32→5 · 25→6 · 4 tries 4,5,6 then wraps: (4+3)%7=0. Final: [4, _, _, _, 18, 32, 25]. (Machine-checked — the walkthrough in the full lesson below has a small arithmetic slip at this step; trust this table.)
⚠️ Primary clustering: the 4-5-6 run means ANY hash landing in it walks the whole cluster — clusters grow themselves.
② QUADRATIC PROBING — (hash + i²) % 7
18→4 · 32→(4+1)=5 · 25→(4+4)%7=1 · 4 tries 4, 5, 1, then (4+9)%7=6. Final: [_, 25, _, _, 18, 32, 4].
Jumps break up primary clustering — but creates secondary clustering: same starting bucket = IDENTICAL probe sequence.
③ DOUBLE HASHING — (hash1 + i × hash2) % 7
hash2(n) = 5 − (n % 5) sets a per-key STEP SIZE. Insert 25 after 18: hash1 = 4 taken, hash2(25) = 5 − 0 = 5, so (4+5)%7 = 2. Different keys, different step — kills BOTH clustering types.
⚠️ TOMBSTONES & THE α CEILING
You can't just blank a deleted slot — that BREAKS the probe chain for keys that probed past it. Use tombstones (deleted markers). And load factor must stay below ~0.7–0.75; open addressing degrades fast as α → 1.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Open addressing is the alternative to chaining — every entry lives directly in the table array (no linked lists). Python's dict, Ruby's Hash, and many cache implementations use open addressing because it's cache-friendly and uses less memory. The OA expects you to know all three probing strategies (linear, quadratic, double) and how clustering affects each.

The open addressing strategy

In open addressing, every entry lives in the array itself. When the natural bucket is taken, we PROBE for the next empty slot using a sequence determined by the probing strategy.

OPEN ADDRESSING SHAPE
buckets = array of capacity slots, each holding ONE entry or EMPTY

Slot 0: ("apple", 1)
Slot 1: EMPTY
Slot 2: ("banana", 7)
Slot 3: ("cherry", 3) ← may have collided with slot 2 first
Slot 4: EMPTY
...

1. Linear probing

LINEAR PROBING
Probe sequence: (hash(key) + i) mod capacity for i = 0, 1, 2, ...

Try natural bucket. If taken, try +1, then +2, etc., wrapping around at the end.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Linear probing (capacity 7)

Hash function: hash(n) = n % 7. Insert 18, 32, 25, 4.

1
Insert 18: 18 % 7 = 4. Slot 4 empty → place. Table: [_, _, _, _, 18, _, _].
2
Insert 32: 32 % 7 = 4. Slot 4 taken (18). Try 5: empty → place. Table: [_, _, _, _, 18, 32, _].
3
Insert 25: 25 % 7 = 4. Slot 4 taken (18). Try 5 (32). Try 6: empty → place. Table: [_, _, _, _, 18, 32, 25].
4
Insert 4: 4 % 7 = 4. Slot 4 taken. 5 taken. 6 taken. Try (4+4) % 7 = 1: empty → place. Table: [_, 4, _, _, 18, 32, 25].
⚠
Notice the CLUSTER at slots 4-5-6. Each subsequent collision walks farther past the cluster — primary clustering.

The clustering problem

Primary clustering: long contiguous runs of occupied slots form because every collision adds to the same cluster. Once a cluster forms, it grows faster (any hash landing in its range collides), which makes it grow even faster.

2. Quadratic probing

QUADRATIC PROBING
Probe sequence: (hash(key) + i²) mod capacity for i = 0, 1, 2, ...

Try natural bucket. If taken, try +1, then +4, +9, +16, ...
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Quadratic probing (capacity 7)

Same inserts as before: 18, 32, 25, 4 (all hash to slot 4).

1
Insert 18 at slot 4. Table: [_, _, _, _, 18, _, _].
2
Insert 32: slot 4 taken. Try (4+1) % 7 = 5: empty → place. Table: [_, _, _, _, 18, 32, _].
3
Insert 25: slot 4 taken. (4+1)=5 taken. Try (4+4) % 7 = 1: empty → place. Table: [_, 25, _, _, 18, 32, _].
4
Insert 4: slot 4 taken. (4+1)=5 taken. (4+4)=1 taken. Try (4+9) % 7 = 6: empty → place. Table: [_, 25, _, _, 18, 32, 4].
✓
Notice: probes JUMP further away each time, breaking up clusters.

Secondary clustering

Quadratic probing eliminates primary clustering, but creates secondary clustering: any two keys that hash to the same initial bucket follow IDENTICAL probe sequences. So they collide repeatedly. Less catastrophic than primary clustering, but still noticeable.

3. Double hashing

DOUBLE HASHING
Probe sequence: (hash1(key) + i × hash2(key)) mod capacity

Two hash functions: hash1 picks the starting bucket, hash2 picks the step size.
Different keys hashing to the same start will have DIFFERENT step sizes — eliminates secondary clustering.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Double hashing (capacity 7)

hash1(n) = n % 7, hash2(n) = 5 - (n % 5).

1
Insert 18: hash1 = 4, slot 4 empty → place.
2
Insert 25: hash1 = 4 (taken). hash2(25) = 5 - 0 = 5. Try (4 + 5) % 7 = 2: empty → place. Table: [_, _, 25, _, 18, _, _].
3
Insert 32: hash1 = 4 (taken). hash2(32) = 5 - 2 = 3. Try (4 + 3) % 7 = 0: empty → place. Table: [32, _, 25, _, 18, _, _].
✓
32 and 25 both started at slot 4 but used different step sizes. No clustering.

Search with open addressing

def get(key):
 for i in range(capacity):
 idx = probe(key, i) % capacity
 if buckets[idx] is EMPTY:
 return None # not found
 if buckets[idx].key == key:
 return buckets[idx].value
 return None # walked the whole table

Walk the same probe sequence used for insert. Stop on EMPTY (means key was never here) or match.

The deletion problem

⚠ WHY YOU CAN'T JUST EMPTY A SLOT

If you delete by setting a slot to EMPTY, search breaks. Example: insert A → slot 4. Insert B → collides, lands in slot 5. Delete A (set slot 4 to EMPTY). Now searching for B: starts at slot 4, sees EMPTY, returns "not found" — but B is at slot 5!

Fix: use a TOMBSTONE marker. Deleted slots are marked "deleted" but still allow probing past them. They're treated as empty for INSERT but as occupied for SEARCH continuation.

Open addressing vs chaining

PropertyChainingOpen addressing
Memory layoutArray + linked listsSingle array
Cache friendlinessPoor (chains scattered)Excellent
Memory overheadPointers per entryEmpty slots
Load factor > 1Works (slower)Impossible (table full)
Performance near α=1Gradually slowsCatastrophic
DeletionEasy (remove from list)Hard (need tombstones)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing primary and secondary clustering. Linear → primary (any collision joins the same cluster). Quadratic → secondary (only same initial bucket collides repeatedly).

Forgetting tombstones in open addressing. Naive delete breaks search.

Letting load factor approach 1 with open addressing — performance degrades exponentially. Resize at ~0.7.

Confusing probe step (in linear probing) with hash. The hash gives the START; probing finds the actual slot.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What is linear probing?" → check (hash + i), i = 0, 1, 2, ...

"Quadratic probing?" → (hash + i²).

"Double hashing?" → (hash1 + i × hash2) — uses TWO hash functions.

"Which probing has primary clustering?" → linear.

"Which has secondary?" → quadratic (and linear, but linear's primary is worse).

"Which avoids both?" → double hashing.

"Why can't you just delete a slot in open addressing?" → breaks the probe chain. Use tombstones.

"What load factor is too high for open addressing?" → above ~0.7-0.75.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Open addressing: every entry IN the array; probe for empty slot on collision
  • Linear probing: +i — primary clustering
  • Quadratic probing: +i² — secondary clustering
  • Double hashing: +i × hash2 — neither type of clustering
  • Deletion needs tombstones to preserve probe chains
  • Cache-friendly, lower memory overhead than chaining
  • Load factor MUST stay below ~0.75 — otherwise lookup degrades
  • Python dict, Ruby Hash use open addressing variants
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Open addressing stores collisions in the table itself by probing. Linear probing (i+1, i+2, …) suffers clustering; quadratic probing and double hashing spread better. Table must have empty slots (α < 1). OA: trace the probe sequence.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
h(k)=k%7 linear probe; insert 8 -> 1, insert 15 -> 1 taken
-> probe 2 (empty) -> store 15 at index 2

Result: 15 probes to the next open slot

Open addressing keeps everything inside the array; linear probing fills the next free slot but creates clusters that slow later lookups.

WHEN & HOW TO RESIZE
After each insert, check α = n/capacity against the threshold — Java HashMap 0.75 (chaining) · Python dict 0.66 · Go map 0.65 (open addressing needs lower). Then DOUBLE the capacity and REHASH EVERYTHING — the bucket index depends on capacity, so every key's home changes.

Resizes fire at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, …, n. Total resize cost = 1+2+4+…+n = 2n − 1 ≈ O(n), spread over n inserts → O(1) amortized per insert — the same doubling trick behind Python's list append.
Growth policyTotal cost of n inserts
Doubling (geometric)O(n) → O(1) amortized ✓
Fixed increment +KO(n²) ✗ — never do this

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Hash tables aren't fixed-size — they grow as load factor rises. Resizing is what keeps O(1) operations from degrading. The OA tests the amortized cost analysis (one of the most-cited examples of amortized analysis) and the distinction between hash tables for storage vs cryptographic hashes for security. Confusing them is a common interview trap.

When to resize

As more entries get added, load factor α grows. Past a threshold (typically 0.7-0.75), operations slow down. The fix: double the capacity and rehash everything.

RESIZE TRIGGER
After every insert, check: if n / capacity > threshold: resize()

Common thresholds:
Java HashMap: 0.75 (chaining)
Python dict: 0.66 (open addressing)
Go map: 0.65 (open addressing)

Open addressing needs lower thresholds — performance degrades fast as α nears 1.

The resize operation

def resize():
 old_buckets = buckets
 capacity = capacity * 2
 buckets = [empty] * capacity
 n = 0
 for entry in old_buckets:
 if entry is not empty:
 put(entry.key, entry.value) # rehash into new table

Why "rehash everything"? Because the bucket index depends on capacity. If capacity changes, every key's bucket changes too.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Resizing from 4 to 8 (hash = key % capacity)

Old table (capacity 4): keys 1, 5, 9 all hashed to bucket 1.

1
Old: bucket 1 has [1, 5, 9].
2
Resize to capacity 8. Rehash each:
3
1 % 8 = 1 → bucket 1 in new table.
4
5 % 8 = 5 → bucket 5 in new table.
5
9 % 8 = 1 → bucket 1 in new table.
✓
The cluster has been broken up. Now bucket 1 has [1, 9] and bucket 5 has [5].

Amortized cost analysis

Resize is expensive — O(n) to rehash everything. But it happens RARELY (only when α exceeds threshold). The amortized cost per insert is still O(1).

AMORTIZED INSERT ANALYSIS
Inserts 1..n into a table that doubles when α exceeds 0.75:

Most inserts: O(1) — just place and update count.
Resize inserts: O(n) — rehash everything.

Resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ..., n.
Total resize cost: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n - 1 ≈ O(n).
Total cheap inserts: n × O(1) = O(n).
Total cost for n inserts: O(n).

Amortized cost per insert: O(n) / n = O(1).

This is the same trick that makes Python list append O(1) amortized — doubling growth amortizes the rare expensive operation.

Why doubling (not adding fixed amount)?

⚠ DON'T grow by a fixed increment

If you add a fixed K slots each resize, total cost across n inserts is O(n²/K) = O(n²). Bad.

Doubling (geometric growth) gives O(n) total = O(1) amortized. The key insight: each entry is "moved" only O(log n) times in total, divided across n inserts.

Hash table use cases

REAL-WORLD HASH TABLE USES
Programming language types: Python dict, JS object, Java HashMap
Database indexes: hash index for equality lookups
Caches: LRU cache (key → value), CDN edge caches
Symbol tables: compilers map identifiers → metadata
Set membership: HashSet uses keys-only hash table
Counting: word frequencies, histogram building
Memoization: function input → cached output
Joining: hash join in databases (build hash table from one side, probe with other)

Cryptographic hashes — a TOTALLY different beast

Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3) ALSO map inputs to fixed-size outputs, but their requirements are completely different.

CRYPTOGRAPHIC HASH PROPERTIES
1. Collision resistance — finding two inputs with same hash is computationally infeasible
2. Pre-image resistance — given a hash, finding an input that produces it is infeasible
3. Avalanche — flipping one input bit flips ~half the output bits
4. Deterministic — same input → same hash
5. Fast to compute, slow to reverse

Hash table hashes vs cryptographic hashes

PropertyHash table hashCryptographic hash
Output size[0, capacity)Fixed (256/512 bits)
GoalEven distributionSecurity
SpeedVery fast (~few cycles)Slower (hundreds of cycles)
Collision toleranceAcceptable (handled)Catastrophic — must be resistant
ReversibilityOften easyComputationally infeasible
ExamplesFNV, MurmurHash, CityHashSHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3

REAL-WORLD CRYPTOGRAPHIC HASH USES
Password storage: never store plaintext, hash with salt + slow function (bcrypt, Argon2)
Digital signatures: hash the message, then sign the hash
File integrity: SHA-256 checksums to verify downloads
Git commits: SHA-1 (transitioning to SHA-256) identifies every object
Blockchain: each block contains hash of the previous (tamper detection)
Merkle trees: hash of children's hashes — efficient verification of large datasets
Deduplication: identical files have identical hashes

Confusing the two hash types. NEVER use SHA-256 for hash tables (too slow). NEVER use FNV/MurmurHash for passwords (collision and pre-image attacks trivial).

Forgetting that resizing is amortized O(1), NOT O(n) per insert. The doubling pattern is what enables this.

Resizing too aggressively (e.g., on every insert) — incurs O(n) per insert.

Not resizing at all — load factor grows unboundedly, performance degrades.

Storing passwords with MD5 or SHA-1 alone — both broken; use bcrypt/Argon2/scrypt with salt.

Special types of binary trees

FULL BINARY TREE
Every node has either 0 OR 2 children — never just one. (Sometimes called "proper" or "strict.")
COMPLETE BINARY TREE
All levels are filled EXCEPT possibly the last; the last level is filled left-to-right.
Used for heaps. Can be efficiently stored in an array.
PERFECT BINARY TREE
All internal nodes have 2 children AND all leaves are at the same depth.
Has exactly 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes for height h.
BALANCED BINARY TREE
Heights of left and right subtrees of EVERY node differ by at most 1.
Guarantees O(log n) operations. Examples: AVL trees, red-black trees.

Why height matters

HEIGHT GOVERNS PERFORMANCE
Most tree operations (search, insert, delete) take time proportional to HEIGHT.

Balanced binary tree of n nodes: height = log₂(n) → O(log n) operations.
Degenerate (skewed) tree: height = n−1 → O(n) operations (no better than a list).

This is WHY balancing matters — see AVL and red-black trees later.

Properties of perfect/complete trees

PropertyFormula
Max nodes at depth d2^d
Max nodes in tree of height h2^(h+1) − 1
Min height for n nodes⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ − 1
Number of leaves in perfect tree height h2^h

Real-world applications of binary trees

WHERE BINARY TREES SHOW UP
Binary search trees: ordered storage with fast lookup
Heaps: priority queues, heapsort
Expression trees: parsing arithmetic expressions, compilers
Decision trees: machine learning, branching logic
Huffman coding trees: lossless compression
Tries: prefix-based string lookup (autocomplete)
Syntax trees (AST): every programming language compiler
Game trees: chess engines, game AI minimax

General trees vs binary trees

Some trees allow each node any number of children — these are general trees. File systems, organization charts, and DOM trees are examples. Binary trees are a SUBSET, restricted to ≤ 2 children per node. Many algorithms (BST, heap, AVL) only make sense for binary trees.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing depth and height. Depth measures DOWN from root; height measures UP from a leaf (or down to deepest leaf).

Mixing up "complete" and "perfect" and "full." Full = 0 or 2 children. Complete = filled left-to-right. Perfect = all leaves at same depth.

Forgetting that a degenerate (skewed) tree has height n−1 — operations become O(n).

Calling any tree O(log n). Only BALANCED trees guarantee that. Unbalanced trees can be O(n).

Using "size" interchangeably with "height." Size = number of nodes. Height = longest downward path.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What's the depth of the root?" → 0.

"Height of a leaf?" → 0.

"Maximum nodes in binary tree of height h?" → 2^(h+1) − 1.

"Difference between full and complete?" → full = each node has 0 or 2 children; complete = filled left-to-right.

"Why is balance important?" → keeps height O(log n), not O(n).

"What is a leaf?" → a node with no children.

"Real-world examples of binary trees?" → BST, heap, syntax tree, decision tree.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Binary tree: each node has at most 2 children (left, right)
  • Depth from root, height to deepest leaf
  • Full: 0 or 2 children. Complete: filled left-to-right. Perfect: all leaves at same depth.
  • Balanced: heights differ by ≤ 1 — guarantees O(log n)
  • Most tree operations take time proportional to HEIGHT
  • Height-h binary tree has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes
  • Used everywhere: BSTs, heaps, syntax trees, decision trees, tries, Huffman coding
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Binary tree: each node ≤ 2 children. Full/complete/perfect/balanced are distinct terms — know them. A balanced tree of n nodes has height ~log₂n; a degenerate (list-like) tree has height n. Height drives operation cost.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
balanced n=7 -> height 2 (log2 7)
degenerate 7 nodes in a line -> height 6

Result: balance keeps height ~log n

Operation costs (search/insert) are O(height); a balanced tree is O(log n) but a skewed one degrades to O(n). Term definitions are tested directly.

THE BST PROPERTY — FOR EVERY NODE
Everything in the LEFT subtree < node < everything in the RIGHT subtree — and it must hold for EVERY node, not just the root. Classic trap: a 12 tucked under 8's LEFT subtree looks fine locally but violates the property (12 > 8). Keys must be comparable.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Binary Search Trees give you ordered storage with fast operations. The OA tests the BST property, recursive vs iterative search/insert, and complexity analysis. Mastering BST search and insert is the prerequisite for understanding self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) used in databases, language standard libraries, and OS kernels.

The BST property

A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree where, for every node:

BST PROPERTY
All values in the LEFT subtree < node value
All values in the RIGHT subtree > node value

(Or for "left ≤", duplicates allowed; depends on the variant.)

This property must hold for EVERY node, not just the root. A common mistake: a tree where root.left < root and root.right > root looks like a BST but might violate the property deeper down.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Valid vs invalid BST

VALID BST:

 8
 /  3 10
 /   1 6 14
 /  /
 4 7 13

INVALID BST (12 in left subtree of 8):

 8
 /  3 10
 /  1 12 ← VIOLATES: 12 > 8 but is in left subtree

Search — recursive

def search(node, target):
 if node is None:
 return None
 if target == node.value:
 return node
 if target < node.value:
 return search(node.left, target)
 else:
 return search(node.right, target)

Search — iterative (better for production)

def search(root, target):
 node = root
 while node is not None:
 if target == node.value:
 return node
 if target < node.value:
 node = node.left
 else:
 node = node.right
 return None

Iterative is preferred — O(1) extra space (no call stack).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Search for 6 in BST above
1
Start at root (8). 6 < 8 → go left to 3.
2
At node 3. 6 > 3 → go right to 6.
3
At node 6. 6 == 6 → found, return.
✓
3 comparisons, depth-of-target steps. Worst case is height of tree.

Insert

def insert(node, value):
 if node is None:
 return TreeNode(value)
 if value < node.value:
 node.left = insert(node.left, value)
 elif value > node.value:
 node.right = insert(node.right, value)
 # else: value already exists, ignore (or handle dup)
 return node

The new node always becomes a LEAF — we descend until we find an empty spot, then create the node there.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 5 into BST above
1
At root 8. 5 < 8 → recurse on left (3).
2
At 3. 5 > 3 → recurse on right (6).
3
At 6. 5 < 6 → recurse on left (4).
4
At 4. 5 > 4 → recurse on right (None).
5
None → create new node TreeNode(5), return.
✓
4.right = node(5). Insertion complete.

Building a BST from sequential inserts

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build BST from [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80]
1
Insert 50 → root.
2
Insert 30: 30 < 50 → left of 50.
3
Insert 70: 70 > 50 → right of 50.
4
Insert 20: 20 < 50 → 20 < 30 → left of 30.
5
Insert 40: 40 < 50 → 40 > 30 → right of 30.
6
Insert 60: 60 > 50 → 60 < 70 → left of 70.
7
Insert 80: 80 > 50 → 80 > 70 → right of 70.
 50
 /  30 70

The shape depends on insertion order

⚠ INSERTION ORDER MATTERS

Inserting [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80] gives a balanced tree.

Inserting [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70] (sorted) gives a degenerate right-only tree (essentially a linked list). Height = n−1, search = O(n).

This is why self-balancing BSTs (AVL, red-black) exist — they automatically rebalance to keep height O(log n).

Complexity analysis

BST OPERATIONS
Search: O(h) where h = height of tree
Insert: O(h)
Remove: O(h) (covered next section)

Balanced BST: h = O(log n) → all operations O(log n)
Worst case (degenerate tree): h = O(n) → all operations O(n)
Average case (random insertion order): h ≈ O(log n)

BST vs hash table

OperationBST (balanced)Hash table
SearchO(log n)O(1) avg
Insert/removeO(log n)O(1) avg
Min/maxO(log n)O(n)
Range queriesO(log n + k)O(n)
Sorted iterationO(n) — naturalO(n log n) — must sort
Worst caseO(log n) (if balanced)O(n)

Key insight: Hash tables are faster for pure key-value lookup. BSTs win when you need ORDER (min/max, sorted iteration, range queries).

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing the BST property. It's RECURSIVE — every subtree must satisfy it, not just the root.

Saying BST is always O(log n). It's O(h) — only balanced BSTs guarantee O(log n).

Inserting sorted data into a plain BST and expecting fast operations. You'll get a degenerate tree.

Recursive search uses O(h) call stack space. Iterative is O(1).

Forgetting that insert always creates a LEAF — never inserted in the middle of the tree.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Time complexity of search in a balanced BST?" → O(log n).

"Worst case?" → O(n) — degenerate tree.

"What's the BST property?" → for every node, left subtree < node, right subtree > node.

"Where does insert place a new node?" → as a leaf.

"Why might a BST degrade?" → unbalanced (e.g., sorted insertion order).

"What gives BST an advantage over hash tables?" → ordered traversal, range queries, min/max in O(log n).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • BST property: left < node < right for every node, recursively
  • Search/insert: O(h) — log n if balanced, n if degenerate
  • Insert always creates a leaf
  • Insertion ORDER determines tree shape — sorted input creates degenerate tree
  • Iterative search uses O(1) space; recursive uses O(h) call stack
  • BST beats hash table for: min/max, ordered traversal, range queries
  • Self-balancing BSTs (AVL, red-black) guarantee O(log n) regardless of insertion order

BST requirements and search: keys must be comparable (orderable) — the whole structure depends on less-than/greater-than. Searching compares the target at each node and descends left if smaller, right if larger, until found or a null child ends the hunt — O(h) where h is the tree height, which is why balance matters.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

BST invariant: left subtree < node < right subtree. Search/insert follow one path → O(h) = O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst. Inserting sorted data builds a degenerate tree. OA: place a value or identify a broken BST.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
insert 5,3,8,1 into empty BST:
      5
     / \
    3   8
   /
  1

Result: each value follows the </> rule down one path

At each node go left if smaller, right if larger; the single root-to-leaf path makes ops O(height). Sorted inserts create a worst-case chain.

THE CASE TABLE (the OA loves case 3)
CaseNode hasAction
10 children (leaf)Just detach it
21 childSPLICE the child up into its place
32 childrenReplace value with the in-order successor, then delete the successor
Reference BST: 8(3(1, 6(4, 7)), 10(_, 14(13, _))). All removal is O(h).
CASES 1 & 2 WORKED
Remove leaf 4 → set 6.left = None, done. Remove 6 (one child after 4 is gone — child 7): 3's right pointer moves from 6 to 7 — the child takes its place, and the BST property survives because the child was already inside 6's subtree.

Successor = smallest in the RIGHT subtree = leftmost of the right subtree. Walk left from 10 — 10 has NO left child, so 10 itself is the successor. ① Copy 10 into the root. ② Delete the original 10 node — it has one child (14), so case 2: 14 splices up. Root is now 10, its right child 14(13).

Remove 3 (children 1 and 6): leftmost of subtree at 6 is 4 → copy 4 over 3, delete the original 4 (a leaf, case 1).
WHY THE SUCCESSOR WORKS
It's the SMALLEST value larger than the removed node — so it's greater than the whole left subtree, smaller than the rest of the right subtree, and (being leftmost) it has no left child, so deleting it is always case 1 or 2. ◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Removal is the trickiest BST operation. Search and insert each have a single straightforward case; removal has THREE distinct cases depending on how many children the node has. The OA almost always tests the two-children case because it's the only one that requires the in-order successor (or predecessor). Master the three cases and you've got every BST removal question covered.

The three cases

BST REMOVAL CASES
Case 1: Node is a leaf (0 children) — just delete it.
Case 2: Node has 1 child — replace the node with its single child.
Case 3: Node has 2 children — replace value with in-order successor (smallest in right subtree), then delete the successor.

Case 3 — Two children (the tricky one)

You can't just promote one child — that would orphan the other. Instead:

TWO-CHILDREN ALGORITHM
1. Find the in-order successor — the smallest value in the right subtree (leftmost of right subtree).
2. Replace the node's value with the successor's value.
3. Delete the successor (which has 0 or 1 children — Case 1 or Case 2).

The in-order successor is the next value in sorted order. Replacing with it preserves the BST property because the successor is greater than everything in the left subtree but smaller than everything else in the right subtree.
