Why successor (and not just any value)?

The in-order successor is the SMALLEST value larger than the node being removed. It satisfies:

  • It's larger than EVERY value in the left subtree → safe to put as new root
  • It's smaller than every OTHER value in the right subtree → safe to leave the rest of the right subtree where it is
  • It has at most one child (right child only) — so deleting it is Case 1 or Case 2

The in-order PREDECESSOR (largest in left subtree) works equally well — pick whichever convention you prefer. Most implementations pick successor.

Implementation

def remove(node, value):
 if node is None:
 return None
 if value < node.value:
 node.left = remove(node.left, value)
 elif value > node.value:
 node.right = remove(node.right, value)
 else:
 # Found the node to remove
 # Case 1 & 2: 0 or 1 child
 if node.left is None:
 return node.right
 if node.right is None:
 return node.left
 # Case 3: 2 children
 successor = find_min(node.right)
 node.value = successor.value
 node.right = remove(node.right, successor.value)
 return node

def find_min(node):
 while node.left is not None:
 node = node.left
 return node

Complexity

BST REMOVAL COMPLEXITY
Find the node: O(h)
Find successor: O(h) (walk down right subtree's left chain)
Total: O(h) — log n if balanced, n if degenerate
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting Case 3 — the two-children case. Just trying to "promote" one child orphans the other.

Using the in-order successor's POSITION instead of its VALUE. The trick is to copy the value into the node being removed, then delete the successor's original position.

Looking for the successor in the wrong subtree. It's the smallest in the RIGHT subtree (leftmost there).

Forgetting the successor is guaranteed to have at most ONE child (right child or no child). It's the leftmost node, so it has no left child by definition.

Saying removal is O(log n). It's O(h) — log n only if balanced.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"How do you remove a node with two children from a BST?" → replace value with in-order successor, then delete the successor.

"What is the in-order successor?" → smallest value in the right subtree (leftmost of right subtree).

"Time complexity of BST removal?" → O(h).

"How many cases are there for BST removal?" → 3 (leaf, one child, two children).

"Why is the successor at most one child?" → it's the leftmost node — no left child by definition.

"Could you use the predecessor instead of successor?" → yes, equally valid.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • BST removal has three cases: leaf, one child, two children
  • Leaf: just delete
  • One child: replace with the child
  • Two children: replace with in-order successor, then delete the successor (which has at most one child)
  • The successor is the smallest value in the right subtree (leftmost of right subtree)
  • Predecessor works too (largest in left subtree); pick a convention
  • Time: O(h) — O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if degenerate

THE MNEMONIC
The name says where the NODE goes: pre = before children, in = between, post = after. Those three are DFS (recursion / a stack). Level-order is BFS — a QUEUE, level by level. All four are O(n). Reference tree: 4(2(1, 3), 6(5, 7)).

TraversalRecipeOutputSuperpower
In-orderL → N → R1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7SORTED! on a BST — the headline fact
Pre-orderN → L → R4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7Serialization / copying, prefix expressions

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tree traversals are a frequent OA topic and a foundational interview skill. The four traversals — in-order, pre-order, post-order, level-order — each have characteristic patterns and applications. In-order on a BST gives sorted output. Pre-order serializes a tree for storage. Post-order safely deletes nodes. Level-order (BFS) finds shortest paths in unweighted trees.

The four traversal orders

FOUR TRAVERSAL TYPES
In-order (DFS): Left → Node → Right
Pre-order (DFS): Node → Left → Right
Post-order (DFS): Left → Right → Node
Level-order (BFS): All depth-0, then all depth-1, then all depth-2, ...

The first three are depth-first (DFS) — they recurse into subtrees. The fourth is breadth-first (BFS) — it visits level by level using a queue.

from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
 if root is None: return
 q = deque([root])
 while q:
 node = q.popleft()
 visit(node.value)

 if node.right: q.append(node.right)

✓

Level-order applications: shortest path in unweighted tree/graph, level-by-level processing (printing tree by levels), finding the closest match at minimal depth.

All four traversals on the same tree

TraversalOutputImplementation
In-order1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7Recursion
Pre-order4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7Recursion or stack
Post-order1, 3, 2, 5, 7, 6, 4Recursion
Level-order4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7Queue (BFS)

How to remember which is which

MNEMONIC
Look at the position of the NODE visit:
Pre-order: visit BEFORE recursing (Node first).
In-order: visit BETWEEN left and right (Node in middle).
Post-order: visit AFTER recursing (Node last).
Level-order: BFS using a queue (top-down, breadth-wise).

Complexity

TRAVERSAL COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n) for all four — each node visited exactly once
Space:
  DFS recursive: O(h) call stack (worst O(n))
  BFS: O(w) queue, where w = max width of tree (worst ~n/2)

Real-world applications

Use caseBest traversal
Print BST in sorted orderIn-order
Serialize tree for storagePre-order
Delete a tree (free memory)Post-order
Compute subtree property (height, size)Post-order
Evaluate prefix expressionPre-order
Evaluate postfix expressionPost-order
Print tree by levelsLevel-order
Shortest path in unweighted treeLevel-order (BFS)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing in-order and pre-order. In-order has node BETWEEN left and right; pre-order has node BEFORE.

Forgetting that in-order on a BST is sorted. This is THE most-tested in-order property.

Using BFS for sorted output. BFS gives level-order, NOT sorted.

DFS without explicit recursion or stack — you can't traverse a tree without one.

Computing subtree height with pre-order. You need POST-order — you can only compute parent's height after both children's heights are known.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What does in-order traversal of a BST produce?" → values in sorted order.

"Given this tree, what's the pre-order/in-order/post-order traversal?" → trace it. Practice on at least 5 trees.

"Which traversal uses a queue?" → level-order (BFS).

"Which traversal uses a stack?" → DFS (any of pre/in/post — recursion uses the call stack).

"Which traversal is used to delete a tree?" → post-order (children before parent).

"Time complexity of any traversal?" → O(n).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Four traversals: in-order, pre-order, post-order, level-order
  • In-order on a BST = sorted output
  • Pre-order: serialization, prefix-expression eval
  • Post-order: deletion, computing subtree properties (height, size, sum)
  • Level-order: BFS using a queue, top-down breadth-wise
  • All traversals are O(n) time
  • Mnemonic: position of NODE in the recipe (pre = before, in = middle, post = after)
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

In-order traversal of a BST yields SORTED order. Pre-order (root first) copies a tree; post-order (root last) deletes/evaluates. OA gives a tree and asks the traversal output — memorize L-Root-R = sorted.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
tree: 5(3(1),8)
in-order (L,Root,R): 1, 3, 5, 8

Result: in-order = ascending sorted

In-order visits left, node, right → ascending values for a BST. Knowing which traversal produces sorted output (and which copies/deletes) is guaranteed content.

⛰️ Heaps: The Property, The Array, The Operations

THE TWO RULES OF A HEAP
Min-heap: every parent ≤ its children (smallest at root). Max-heap: every parent ≥ its children. AND a heap is always a complete binary tree — filled left-to-right — which is exactly what lets it live in a plain array with no pointers.
THE INDEX FORMULAS (0-indexed — memorize these)
RelationshipFormula
Parent of i(i − 1) / 2 (integer division)
Left child2i + 1
Right child2i + 2
1-indexed variant: parent i/2, children 2i and 2i+1. Check which convention the question uses!
WORKED: INSERT 5 into [10, 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 100] (sift UP)
Append 5 at index 7 → parent (7−1)/2 = 3 holds 30: swap → parent 1 holds 20: swap → parent 0 holds 10: swap → at root, stop. Final: [5, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100, 30]. One swap per level max → O(log n).
WORKED: EXTRACT-MIN from [5, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100] (sift DOWN)
Save 5 · move last (100) to root · swap with SMALLER child 10 · swap with smaller child 20 · no children, stop. Returns 5; heap: [10, 20, 15, 100, 40, 50]. O(log n). Peek is O(1). Build-heap from an array: bottom-up heapify is O(n) — faster than n inserts.
⚠️ A HEAP IS NOT SORTED
Only the ROOT is guaranteed min (or max). Siblings and levels can be in any order that respects the property — arbitrary search is O(n). Sift down swaps with the smaller child in a min-heap; picking the wrong child breaks the property. Heaps power priority queues: Dijkstra, Huffman, OS schedulers, event simulation.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
In a 0-indexed heap array, the children of index 2 are at:
  1. 5 and 6
  2. 3 and 4
  3. 4 and 5
  4. 1 and 3
Show answer + steps
A. 2i+1 = 5 and 2i+2 = 6.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Heaps are the backbone of priority queues — the data structure behind Dijkstra's shortest path, Huffman coding for compression, OS process scheduling, event simulation, and the standard library's sort-by-priority. They give you O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min/max with O(1) peek, and they fit cleanly in an array with no pointers. The OA tests heap properties, array indexing, and the operations themselves.

Heap property

MIN-HEAP vs MAX-HEAP
Min-heap: every node's value ≤ its children's values. Smallest at root.
Max-heap: every node's value ≥ its children's values. Largest at root.

A heap is also a complete binary tree — all levels filled left to right except possibly the last. This shape requirement is what lets you store it efficiently in an array.

Array representation

For a node at index i (0-indexed), the relationships in the binary tree are pure arithmetic:

INDEX FORMULAS (0-INDEXED)
Parent: (i − 1) / 2 (integer division)
Left child: 2i + 1
Right child: 2i + 2
INDEX FORMULAS (1-INDEXED)
Parent: i / 2
Left child: 2i
Right child: 2i + 1

Both conventions are common. 's coursework typically uses 0-indexed. When solving an OA problem, double-check which convention the question uses.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading a heap from its array

Min-heap stored as [10, 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 100].

1
Index 0 (root): 10. Children at 1, 2: 20, 15.
2
Index 1: 20. Children at 3, 4: 30, 40.
3
Index 2: 15. Children at 5, 6: 50, 100.
4
Indices 3-6 are leaves.
CHECK
Min-heap? 10 ≤ 20, 15 ✓; 20 ≤ 30, 40 ✓; 15 ≤ 50, 100 ✓. Valid.

Insert (sift up / bubble up / percolate up)

INSERT (MIN-HEAP)
1. Add new value at the end of the array (next free slot).
2. Compare with parent. If smaller, swap.
3. Repeat with the new position until heap property holds or at root.

Time: O(log n) — at most one swap per level, height log n.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 5 into [10, 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 100]
1
Append 5 at index 7. Array: [10, 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 100, 5].
2
Parent of 7 is (7−1)/2 = 3, value 30. Compare 5 vs 30: 5 < 30, swap. Array: [10, 20, 15, 5, 40, 50, 100, 30].
3
Now at index 3. Parent is (3−1)/2 = 1, value 20. Compare 5 vs 20: 5 < 20, swap. Array: [10, 5, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100, 30].
4
Now at index 1. Parent is 0, value 10. Compare 5 vs 10: 5 < 10, swap. Array: [5, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100, 30].
5
Now at root. Stop.
✓
Final heap: [5, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100, 30]. Min is now 5. ✓

Extract-min (sift down / percolate down)

EXTRACT-MIN (MIN-HEAP)
1. Save root (the minimum) — this is what we'll return.
2. Move last element to root position.
3. Compare with smaller child. If larger, swap with that child.
4. Repeat until heap property holds or no children.

Time: O(log n).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Extract min from [5, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50, 100]
1
Save min: 5.
2
Move last (100) to root. Array: [100, 10, 15, 20, 40, 50].
3
At index 0, value 100. Children at 1, 2: 10, 15. Smaller child: 10 (index 1). 100 > 10, swap. Array: [10, 100, 15, 20, 40, 50].
4
At index 1, value 100. Children at 3, 4: 20, 40. Smaller: 20 (index 3). 100 > 20, swap. Array: [10, 20, 15, 100, 40, 50].
5
At index 3, value 100. Children at 7, 8 — none exist. Stop.
✓
Returns 5. Heap: [10, 20, 15, 100, 40, 50].

Build heap from array

You could insert n elements one at a time: O(n log n). But there's a faster way — heapify from the bottom up. Starting at the last non-leaf node and going backwards, sift each node down.

BUILD-HEAP COMPLEXITY
Naive (n inserts): O(n log n)
Bottom-up heapify: O(n)

Why is bottom-up O(n)? Most nodes are near the bottom and have very short sift-down paths (heights 0, 1, 2, ...). Adding up the work over all heights gives a geometric sum that's bounded by O(n).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build min-heap from [40, 10, 30, 5, 20, 50]
1
n = 6. Last non-leaf: index (6/2) − 1 = 2. Start there.
2
Index 2 (value 30): children at 5 only (50). 30 < 50, no swap.
3
Index 1 (value 10): children at 3, 4 (5, 20). Smaller: 5. 10 > 5, swap. Array: [40, 5, 30, 10, 20, 50]. Now at index 3 (value 10): no children. Stop.
4
Index 0 (value 40): children at 1, 2 (5, 30). Smaller: 5. Swap. Array: [5, 40, 30, 10, 20, 50]. Now at index 1 (value 40): children at 3, 4 (10, 20). Smaller: 10. Swap. Array: [5, 10, 30, 40, 20, 50]. Now at index 3 (value 40): no children.
✓
Final heap: [5, 10, 30, 40, 20, 50]. Verify: 5 ≤ 10, 30 ✓; 10 ≤ 40, 20 ✓; 30 ≤ 50 ✓.

Operation summary

HEAP OPERATIONS — TIME COMPLEXITY
Peek (find min/max): O(1) — it's the root
Insert: O(log n) — sift up
Extract-min/max: O(log n) — sift down
Build heap from array: O(n) — bottom-up heapify
Search for arbitrary value: O(n) — heap is unsorted within levels
Delete arbitrary element: O(log n) if position known, else O(n)

Searching is slow because the heap property only constrains parent-child relationships — it says nothing about siblings or cross-tree comparisons. Heaps are NOT search trees.

Heap vs BST — when to use which

HEAP vs BST
Use a heap when you need: fast access to min/max only, priority queue behavior.
Use a BST when you need: ordered traversal, range queries, search for arbitrary values.
Heap: O(1) peek, O(log n) extract. BST: O(log n) for everything (balanced).
★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What is the structure of a binary heap?" — Complete binary tree with the heap property. Stored as an array.

"Find the parent / child of index i" — apply the index formulas. Be careful which convention is used.

"What's the time complexity of insert / extract / build-heap?" — log n, log n, n.

"Trace insert/extract on this array" — practice the swap-walk until automatic.

"Why is heap better than BST for priority queue?" — O(1) peek, simpler, no rebalancing, cache-friendly array layout.

Confusing heap order with BST order. A heap only constrains parent-child; siblings can be in any order. A BST has a strict left < root < right ordering.

Off-by-one in index formulas. 0-indexed: children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. 1-indexed: children at 2i and 2i+1. Use whichever the problem uses, consistently.

Forgetting that build-heap is O(n), not O(n log n). Bottom-up heapify saves a factor of log n.

Comparing with the wrong child during sift-down. Always swap with the SMALLER child (in min-heap) to maintain order.

Treating heap as sorted. The leaves and middle nodes can be in any order that respects the heap property — heap-sort exploits this property to extract min repeatedly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Min-heap: parent ≤ children; max-heap: parent ≥ children
  • Always a complete binary tree, stored as an array
  • 0-indexed: parent (i−1)/2; left child 2i+1; right child 2i+2
  • Insert: append, sift up. O(log n)
  • Extract: replace root with last, sift down. O(log n)
  • Build heap from array: bottom-up heapify, O(n)
  • Peek is O(1); arbitrary search is O(n) (heap isn't sorted)
  • Use heap for priority queue; use BST for ordered/searchable data
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A heap is a complete binary tree with the heap property: max-heap parent ≥ children (min-heap ≤). Stored in an array: children of i are 2i+1, 2i+2. Insert/remove are O(log n); peek-max is O(1).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
array [9,7,8,1,3]  (max-heap)
node i=0 (9); children at 1 (7), 2 (8)

Result: root is the max; ops O(log n)

The complete-tree shape lets a heap live in an array with index arithmetic; sift-up/sift-down keep the heap property in O(log n).

HEAPSORT IN TWO PHASES
① Build a MAX-heap from the array — O(n). ② Repeat n−1 times: swap the root (max) with the last unsorted slot, shrink the heap by 1, sift the new root down — O(log n) each. Total O(n log n), and the sorted tail grows from the right.

THE O(n log n) SHOWDOWN (a favorite OA table)
HeapsortQuicksortMergesort
Worst caseO(n log n)O(n²)O(n log n)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Heapsort is the third major O(n log n) sort (alongside merge and quick) and the only one that's BOTH O(n log n) worst-case AND in-place. Priority queues are used everywhere — task schedulers, Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, event simulation, top-k problems. Heapsort algorithm

Heapsort works in two phases: build a max-heap from the array, then repeatedly extract the max to the end.

HEAPSORT
1. Build max-heap from the array → O(n)
2. Repeat n−1 times:
  a. Swap arr[0] (max) with arr[end]
  b. Reduce heap size by 1 (the swapped max is now in its sorted position)
  c. Sift down the new root → O(log n)

Total: O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n)

Why it works

The max-heap always has the largest unsorted element at the root. We swap it to the end (its sorted position), then re-heapify the remaining (n−1) elements. After n−1 iterations, everything is sorted in ascending order.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Heapsort [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
1
Build max-heap: [9, 6, 4, 3, 5, 1, 2, 1]. (Heapify in O(n).)
2
Swap arr[0]=9 with arr[7]=1: [1, 6, 4, 3, 5, 1, 2, | 9]. Heap size now 7.
3
Sift down 1: → [6, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1, 2, | 9].
4
Swap arr[0]=6 with arr[6]=2: [2, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1, | 6, 9]. Sift down: [5, 3, 4, 2, 1, 1, | 6, 9].
5
Swap arr[0]=5 with arr[5]=1: [1, 3, 4, 2, 1, | 5, 6, 9]. Sift down: [4, 3, 1, 2, 1, | 5, 6, 9].
6
Continue... swap 4↔1, sift; swap 3↔1, sift; swap 2↔1, sift.
✓
Final sorted: [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9].

Heapsort properties

HEAPSORT COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n log n) — best, average, worst (always)
Space: O(1) — in-place (uses array indices, no recursion)
Stable: NO — long swaps can reorder equal keys
In-place: YES

Heapsort vs other O(n log n) sorts

PropertyHeapsortQuicksortMergesort
Worst caseO(n log n)O(n²)O(n log n)
SpaceO(1)O(log n)O(n)
StableNoNoYes
In-placeYesYesNo
Cache-friendlyNo (random jumps)YesYes

Heapsort's niche: guaranteed O(n log n) AND in-place. Used as the fallback in Introsort (C++ std::sort) when quicksort's recursion gets too deep.

Priority Queue ADT

A priority queue is like a queue, but elements come out in PRIORITY order, not insertion order.

OperationDescriptionTime (heap impl)
insert(x)Add element with priorityO(log n)
extract-max (or min)Remove and return highest priorityO(log n)
peekView highest priority without removingO(1)
isEmpty / sizeStandard utility opsO(1)

Why heaps are the standard PQ implementation

PQ ImplementationInsertExtract
Unsorted arrayO(1)O(n)
Sorted arrayO(n)O(1)
Sorted linked listO(n)O(1)
BST (balanced)O(log n)O(log n)
HeapO(log n)O(log n)

Heap matches BST's complexity but uses an array (no pointers, cache-friendly) and has minimal constant factors. That's why heapq in Python and PriorityQueue in Java are heap-based.

Real-world priority queue applications

WHERE PRIORITY QUEUES APPEAR
Dijkstra's shortest path: extract closest unvisited vertex
A* search: extract node with lowest estimated cost
Huffman coding: repeatedly merge two least-frequent nodes
Task scheduler: run highest-priority task first
Event simulation: process next event by time
Top-k elements: maintain a heap of k largest seen so far
Median maintenance: two heaps (max-heap for lower, min-heap for upper)
Bandwidth allocation: serve requests by priority
OS process scheduling: run highest-priority ready process
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Top-3 largest from [9, 4, 7, 1, 6, 3, 8]
def top_k(arr, k):
 import heapq
 heap = [] # min-heap of size k
 for x in arr:
 if len(heap) < k:
 heapq.heappush(heap, x)
 elif x > heap[0]:
 heapq.heapreplace(heap, x)
 return sorted(heap, reverse=True)
1
Process 9, 4, 7: heap = [4, 9, 7]. Min = 4.
2
Process 1: 1 < 4, skip. Heap unchanged.
3
Process 6: 6 > 4, replace 4 with 6. Heap = [6, 9, 7].
4
Process 3: 3 < 6, skip.
5
Process 8: 8 > 6, replace 6 with 8. Heap = [7, 9, 8].
✓
Result: top 3 = [9, 8, 7]. Time: O(n log k), space: O(k).
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Mixing up max-heap and min-heap. For sorting ASCENDING with heapsort, use a MAX-heap (largest goes to end first).

Saying heapsort is stable. It's NOT — long swaps can reorder equal keys.

Implementing PQ as a sorted array — insert becomes O(n). Use a heap instead.

Forgetting that build-heap is O(n), not O(n log n). The trick is sifting from the bottom up.

Using a regular queue for Dijkstra — you'll process vertices in wrong order. Need priority queue.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"Time complexity of heapsort?" → O(n log n) all cases.

"Is heapsort stable?" → No.

"Is heapsort in-place?" → Yes.

"What ADT is naturally implemented with a heap?" → priority queue.

"Insert/extract complexity in a heap-based PQ?" → O(log n).

"Real applications of priority queues?" → Dijkstra, A*, Huffman, task scheduling, top-k.

"Why use a min-heap of size k for top-k largest?" → only need to keep k elements; replace if larger than min.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Heapsort: build heap (O(n)) + extract n times (O(n log n)) = O(n log n) total
  • Heapsort is in-place AND O(n log n) worst-case — unique combination
  • Heapsort is NOT stable
  • Priority queue: insert O(log n), extract O(log n), peek O(1) when heap-based
  • PQ powers Dijkstra, A*, Huffman, task scheduling, event simulation, top-k
  • Top-k pattern: maintain min-heap of size k; replace if new value beats current min

Why heaps back priority queues: a heap balances BOTH operations at O(log n) — insert and remove-min alike. Array or list implementations make one operation O(1) but the other O(n); the heap’s balance is what wins at scale.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Heapsort = build heap O(n) + n removals O(log n) = O(n log n), in-place, NOT stable. A priority queue is the heap's ADT (always remove highest priority). OA: heapsort's complexity/stability and PQ use cases.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
build max-heap, repeatedly swap root to end + sift-down
-> array sorted ascending

Result: O(n log n), in-place, not stable

Heapsort matches merge sort's time bound and is in-place, but loses stability — the exact combination the OA asks you to compare.

A 2D V × V array where matrix[i][j] = 1 if edge i → j exists, 0 otherwise. For weighted graphs, store the weight instead of 1.

For undirected graphs, the matrix is SYMMETRIC across the diagonal. Self-loops put a 1 on the diagonal.

THE ALGORITHM
Mark the start visited, enqueue it. Loop: dequeue v, then for each UNVISITED neighbor — mark visited and enqueue. FIFO order guarantees distance-0, then all distance-1, then distance-2… Swap the queue for a stack and you'd have DFS.

★ THE KEY PROPERTY
The FIRST time BFS reaches a vertex is via the shortest path in EDGES (unweighted). Track parent pointers to reconstruct the route. Weighted graphs need Dijkstra (or Bellman-Ford for negatives). ◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

BFS is the standard algorithm for "shortest path in an unweighted graph" and dozens of related problems — finding connected components, level-by-level processing, web crawling, social network friend-suggestion, puzzle solving (Rubik's cube, sliding tiles). The OA tests BFS implementation, the queue-based pattern, and complexity. The pattern is identical across hundreds of real-world problems, so master it once and reuse forever.

The BFS idea

Breadth-First Search visits vertices in order of their distance from the start: distance 0 first (the start), then all distance-1 neighbors, then distance-2, and so on.

BFS ALGORITHM
1. Mark start as visited. Enqueue start.
2. While queue is not empty:
  a. Dequeue a vertex v.
  b. For each unvisited neighbor of v:
    - mark visited, enqueue
3. Done when queue is empty (all reachable vertices visited). 
from collections import deque

def bfs(graph, start):
 visited = {start}
 queue = deque([start])
 order = []
 while queue:
 v = queue.popleft()
 order.append(v)
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 visited.add(neighbor)
 queue.append(neighbor)
 return order

Why a queue?

FIFO order ensures level-by-level visiting. Earlier-discovered vertices (closer to start) are processed first. If you used a STACK instead, you'd get DFS (depth-first).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — BFS from A
 A
 /| B C D
 | |
 E F
1
Visit A. Queue = [A]. Mark visited.
2
Dequeue A. Neighbors B, C, D not visited → enqueue. Queue = [B, C, D].
3
Dequeue B. Neighbor A visited. Neighbor E not visited → enqueue. Queue = [C, D, E].
4
Dequeue C. Neighbor A visited. Queue = [D, E].
5
Dequeue D. Neighbor A visited. Neighbor F → enqueue. Queue = [E, F].
6
Dequeue E. All neighbors visited. Queue = [F].
7
Dequeue F. All neighbors visited. Queue = []. Done.
✓
Visit order: A, B, C, D, E, F. Notice: all distance-1 (B, C, D) before any distance-2 (E, F).

Shortest path (unweighted graph)

Because BFS visits in order of distance, the first time it reaches a vertex is via the shortest path (in number of edges). Track parent pointers to reconstruct the path.

def bfs_shortest_path(graph, start, target):
 if start == target:
 return [start]
 visited = {start}
 queue = deque([start])
 parent = {start: None}
 while queue:
 v = queue.popleft()
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 visited.add(neighbor)
 parent[neighbor] = v
 if neighbor == target:
 # Reconstruct path
 path = []
 node = target
 while node is not None:
 path.append(node)
 node = parent[node]
 return list(reversed(path))
 queue.append(neighbor)
 return None # not reachable
★ KEY PROPERTY

BFS finds the shortest path in number of EDGES (unweighted graph). For weighted graphs, you need Dijkstra's (or Bellman-Ford for negative weights).

Connected components

To find all connected components, run BFS from each unvisited vertex. Each BFS run discovers one component.

def connected_components(graph):
 visited = set()
 components = []
 for v in graph:
 if v not in visited:
 comp = []
 queue = deque([v])
 visited.add(v)
 while queue:
 u = queue.popleft()
 comp.append(u)
 for w in graph[u]:
 if w not in visited:
 visited.add(w)
 queue.append(w)
 components.append(comp)
 return components

BFS complexity

BFS COMPLEXITY
Time: O(V + E) — each vertex enqueued once, each edge examined once
Space: O(V) — visited set + queue

Same complexity for adjacency list. With matrix it's O(V²) (must scan a row to find neighbors).

BFS applications

REAL-WORLD BFS USES
Shortest path in unweighted graphs (social distance, fewest steps)
Web crawler at controlled depth from a seed URL
Friend suggestions (people 2 hops away in social graph)
Network broadcast simulation
Connected components in undirected graphs
Bipartite check (try to 2-color via BFS)
Puzzle solvers: Rubik's cube, sliding-tile puzzle, word ladders
Garbage collection (mark phase): BFS from roots
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting to mark visited at ENQUEUE time, not dequeue. If you mark at dequeue, the same vertex can be enqueued multiple times before processing — wastes work and breaks complexity.

Using BFS for weighted shortest path. BFS counts EDGES, not weights — use Dijkstra's for weights.

Confusing BFS visit order with sorted order. BFS gives level-by-level, which is NOT alphabetical or numeric.

Implementing the "queue" with list.pop(0) in Python — O(n) per dequeue. Use collections.deque.

Forgetting to handle disconnected graphs — wrap BFS in a loop over all unvisited vertices.

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"BFS time complexity (with adjacency list)?" → O(V + E).

"What's BFS good for?" → shortest path in UNWEIGHTED graphs, level-by-level processing.

"Why mark at enqueue, not dequeue?" → prevents same vertex being enqueued multiple times.

🕳️ DFS: Deep First, Then Backtrack

THE ALGORITHM
Go deep along one path until stuck, then backtrack and try the next branch. Recursion IS DFS — the call stack is the stack. Iterative version: an explicit stack (LIFO pop) — the ONLY data-structure difference from BFS.
WORKED: same graph A—B, A—C, A—D, B—E, D—F (recursive)
Visit A → recurse into B → recurse into E (dead end, backtrack) → back through B to A → C (dead end) → D → F. Visit order: A, B, E, C, D, F — compare BFS's A, B, C, D, E, F: DFS finished B's whole branch (including E) before touching C.

OrderLevel by levelDeep, then backtrack

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

DFS is the workhorse for cycle detection, topological sorting, strongly connected components, maze solving, and backtracking. It's natural to write recursively (which is why it shows up everywhere — recursion IS DFS in disguise). The OA tests both recursive and iterative DFS, plus the cycle detection and topological sort applications.

The DFS idea

Depth-First Search goes deep first: pick a neighbor, follow that path until stuck, then backtrack and try the next one.

DFS RECURSIVE
1. Mark current vertex as visited.
2. For each unvisited neighbor:
  a. Recursively DFS from that neighbor. 
def dfs(graph, v, visited=None):
 if visited is None:
 visited = set()
 visited.add(v)
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 dfs(graph, neighbor, visited)
 return visited

DFS iterative (using explicit stack)

def dfs_iter(graph, start):
 visited = set()
 stack = [start]
 order = []
 while stack:
 v = stack.pop() # LIFO — last in, first out
 if v in visited:
 continue
 visited.add(v)
 order.append(v)
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 stack.append(neighbor)
 return order

The recursive version uses the call stack implicitly. The iterative version uses an explicit stack — the only data-structure difference from BFS (which uses a queue).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — DFS from A (recursive)
 A
 /| B C D
 | |
 E F
1
Visit A. Mark visited. Output: A.
2
Recurse on B. Mark. Output: A, B.
3
Recurse on E. Mark. Output: A, B, E. E has only A as neighbor (visited). Return.
4
Back in B, no more unvisited neighbors. Return.
5
Back in A, recurse on C. Output: A, B, E, C. C only connects to A (visited). Return.
6
Back in A, recurse on D. Output: A, B, E, C, D.
7
Recurse on F. Output: A, B, E, C, D, F. Done.
✓
Visit order: A, B, E, C, D, F. Notice we went DEEP into B's branch before returning to C.

Cycle detection

CYCLE DETECTION (UNDIRECTED)
During DFS, track each vertex's parent.
If you encounter a visited neighbor that ISN'T your parent → cycle exists. 
def has_cycle_undirected(graph, v, parent, visited):
 visited.add(v)
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 if has_cycle_undirected(graph, neighbor, v, visited):
 return True
 elif neighbor != parent:
 return True # back edge → cycle
 return False
CYCLE DETECTION (DIRECTED)
Use 3 colors: WHITE (unvisited), GRAY (in current DFS path), BLACK (done).
If you encounter a GRAY vertex → cycle (back edge to ancestor in current path). 
def has_cycle_directed(graph):
 WHITE, GRAY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2
 color = {v: WHITE for v in graph}

 def dfs(v):
 color[v] = GRAY
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if color[neighbor] == GRAY:
 return True # back edge — cycle!
 if color[neighbor] == WHITE and dfs(neighbor):
 return True
 color[v] = BLACK
 return False

 for v in graph:
 if color[v] == WHITE and dfs(v):
 return True
 return False

Topological sort (DAGs only)

Topological sort orders DAG vertices so every directed edge points "forward" in the order. Use case: build dependencies, course prerequisites, task scheduling.

TOPOLOGICAL SORT (DFS-based)
1. Run DFS from each unvisited vertex.
2. After DFS finishes for a vertex (all descendants done), prepend it to the result list.
3. The reverse-finish-order is a valid topological order. 
def topological_sort(graph):
 visited = set()
 order = []

 def dfs(v):
 visited.add(v)
 for neighbor in graph[v]:
 if neighbor not in visited:
 dfs(neighbor)
 order.append(v) # appended after all descendants

 for v in graph:
 if v not in visited:
 dfs(v)
 return list(reversed(order))

2
Order appended: Capstone, CS200, CS101, Stats, Math.
3
Reverse: Math, Stats, CS101, CS200, Capstone.
✓
Valid! Math comes before CS101, CS101 before CS200, etc.

Using BFS for cycle detection in directed graphs — DFS is the natural fit because the call stack tracks the current path.

A Set stores unique elements with no implied order. Two defining properties:

SET PROPERTIES
1. No duplicates — adding an element that's already present does nothing.

Compare to a list: lists allow duplicates and have order. Sets are about MEMBERSHIP, not arrangement.

Time: O(min(|A|, |B|)) for hash sets.

Frozen sets (immutable)

Python's frozenset is an immutable set. Useful as dict keys (mutable sets can't be hashed) or as elements of another set.

groups = {
 frozenset({'alice', 'bob'}): 'project_x',
 frozenset({'carol', 'dave'}): 'project_y'
}

Sets vs lists vs dicts — the three Python collections

Use casePick
Order matters, duplicates allowedList
Unique elements, fast membershipSet
Key → value lookupDict
Immutable, orderedTuple
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Using a list and x in list for membership — that's O(n). Use a set for O(1).

Expecting set iteration to be in sorted order. Hash sets are unordered. For sorted iteration, sort it: sorted(my_set).

Trying to use a list or dict as a set element — they're mutable, can't be hashed. Use tuple or frozenset.

Confusing union/intersection. Union (∪) is OR — bigger result. Intersection (∩) is AND — smaller result.

set.remove(x) raises if x not present. Use set.discard(x) for safe deletion.

Creating an empty set with {} — that's an empty DICT, not set. Use set().

★ ON THE OA, WATCH FOR

"What's the membership test complexity for a set?" → O(1) for hash, O(log n) for tree.

"What does A ∩ B mean?" → intersection: elements in both A and B.

"What's the difference between a set and a list?" → set has no duplicates and no order.

"How do you remove duplicates from a list in Python?" → list(set(items)).

"Tree set vs hash set?" → tree is sorted, supports range queries; hash is faster for plain operations.

"Compute A ∪ B given A and B" → list every distinct element from both.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Set: unique, unordered collection
  • Hash set: O(1) ops, no order. Tree set: O(log n) ops, sorted
  • Operations: union ∪, intersection ∩, difference −, symmetric diff △
  • Python: {1,2,3} for set; {} is empty DICT (use set() for empty set)
  • Use sets for: deduplication, membership testing, visited tracking, common-element queries
  • Frozen sets are immutable — usable as dict keys or set elements

Bit vector sets: a bit vector represents a set with one bit per possible element — blazing fast membership, but only practical for SMALL INTEGER RANGES (bit i ⇔ element i). For sparse or huge domains, hash sets win.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Set = unordered, no duplicates. Core ops: union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (−). Backed by a hash table → O(1) average membership. OA: compute a set operation result or identify membership cost.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
A={1,2,3} B={2,3,4}
A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4};  A ∩ B = {2,3};  A - B = {1}

Result: union/intersection/difference results

Sets discard duplicates and order; hash-backed membership is O(1) average. Computing ∪/∩/− and knowing the lookup cost are the tested skills.

Python is the language used throughout the C949 OA, the Parcel Service PA in C950, and most introductory CS courses at . 🏗️ Python Classes & OOP

THE ANATOMY
class Dog: with def __init__(self, name, breed): — the CONSTRUCTOR runs automatically at d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador"), initializing instance attributes via self.name = name. Classes are how you build every custom structure in this course — nodes, queues, graph vertices.
SELF — the rule the OA tests
self = the instance the method was called on. Define it as the FIRST parameter; never pass it yourself — d1.add_trick("sit") is translated by Python into Dog.add_trick(d1, "sit"). Each instance owns its attributes: d1.tricks and d2.tricks are separate lists.
CLASS vs INSTANCE ATTRIBUTES
Class attributeInstance attribute
DefinedIn the class body (species = "Canis familiaris")In __init__ via self.name = …
Shared?ONE copy for all instances — change it and every dog sees itPer-object
INHERITANCE & OVERRIDING
class Dog(Animal): — Dog inherits Animal's methods and attributes, can ADD new ones, and can OVERRIDE (Dog redefines speak() → "Rex barks" while Cat's meows — that's polymorphism). super().__init__(name) reuses the parent's constructor instead of duplicating it — the standard first line of a subclass __init__ that extends it.
⚠️ TWO EXAM TRAPS
__init__ returns NOTHING explicitly (the new instance is returned implicitly). And forgetting self as the first parameter of a method is the classic Python class bug. Parent = superclass/base; child = subclass/derived. The four pillars — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction — apply here just as in Java.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
When you call d1.add_trick("sit"), what is self inside the method?
  1. d1
  2. The Dog class
  3. "sit"
  4. Nothing — you must pass it
Show answer + steps

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Object-oriented programming organizes code around DATA + the operations on that data. Classes are how you build custom data structures (linked list nodes, BST nodes, graph vertices, your own queue) — exactly what C949 expects you to be comfortable with. The OA tests class definition, the role of self and __init__, method calls, and basic inheritance.

Defining a class

class Dog:
 def __init__(self, name, breed): # constructor
 self.name = name # instance attribute
 self.breed = breed
 self.tricks = []

 def add_trick(self, trick): # method
 self.tricks.append(trick)

 def describe(self):
 return f"{self.name} is a {self.breed} who knows {len(self.tricks)} tricks"

d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
d.add_trick("sit")
d.add_trick("roll")
print(d.describe()) # Rex is a Labrador who knows 2 tricks

The role of self

SELF
self refers to the INSTANCE the method was called on.
Python passes it AUTOMATICALLY as the first argument when you call obj.method().

When defining methods, self must be the first parameter.
When calling, you DON'T pass it explicitly — Python does that for you.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Self in action
d1 = Dog("Rex", "Lab")
d2 = Dog("Buddy", "Poodle")
d1.add_trick("sit")
d2.add_trick("speak")
print(d1.tricks) # ['sit'] — d1's tricks
print(d2.tricks) # ['speak'] — d2's tricks (separate)
1
Each instance has its OWN attributes — self.tricks is per-instance.
2
When you call d1.add_trick("sit"), Python translates to Dog.add_trick(d1, "sit"). self = d1.

The __init__ method (constructor)

__init__
Runs automatically when you create an instance: obj = MyClass(args).
Job: initialize all instance attributes.
Returns nothing (returns the new instance implicitly).
Other dunder methods exist (__str__, __eq__, __lt__) for special behavior.

Class vs instance attributes

class Dog:
 species = "Canis familiaris" # CLASS attribute (shared by all)

 def __init__(self, name):
 self.name = name # INSTANCE attribute (per-dog)

d1 = Dog("Rex")
d2 = Dog("Buddy")
print(d1.species) # Canis familiaris
print(d2.species) # Canis familiaris
print(d1.name) # Rex
print(d2.name) # Buddy
Dog.species = "Genus Canis"
print(d1.species) # Genus Canis (changed for ALL instances)

Inheritance basics

class Animal:
 def __init__(self, name):
 self.name = name

 def speak(self):
 return f"{self.name} makes a sound"

class Dog(Animal): # Dog inherits from Animal
 def speak(self): # OVERRIDE
 return f"{self.name} barks"

class Cat(Animal):
 def speak(self):
 return f"{self.name} meows"

a = Animal("Generic")
d = Dog("Rex")
c = Cat("Whiskers")
print(a.speak()) # Generic makes a sound
print(d.speak()) # Rex barks
print(c.speak()) # Whiskers meows
INHERITANCE TERMINOLOGY
Parent / superclass / base class: the class being inherited FROM (Animal).
Child / subclass / derived class: the class doing the inheriting (Dog, Cat).
Subclasses INHERIT all parent's methods and attributes.
Subclasses can OVERRIDE inherited methods (Dog redefines speak).
Subclasses can ADD new methods that the parent doesn't have.

Calling the parent's method with super()

class Dog(Animal):
 def __init__(self, name, breed):
 super().__init__(name) # call Animal.__init__(name)
 self.breed = breed

super() lets you reuse the parent's logic instead of duplicating it. Common in __init__ when the child needs to extend (not replace) parent initialization.

Building a linked list — OOP in practice

class Node:
 def __init__(self, value):
 self.value = value
 self.next = None

class LinkedList:
 def __init__(self):
 self.head = None

 def prepend(self, value):
 node = Node(value)
 node.next = self.head
 self.head = node

 def __str__(self):
 parts = []
 node = self.head
 while node is not None:
 parts.append(str(node.value))
 node = node.next
 return " -> ".join(parts)

ll = LinkedList()
ll.prepend(3)
ll.prepend(2)
ll.prepend(1)
print(ll) # 1 -> 2 -> 3

This is exactly the kind of structure C949 asks you to build: a class for the node, another for the container, methods for operations.

The four pillars of OOP

PillarMeaning
EncapsulationBundle data + methods together; control access
InheritanceA subclass reuses + extends a parent
PolymorphismSame method name, different behavior per type (Dog.speak vs Cat.speak)
AbstractionHide implementation; expose interface

Common dunder methods

DunderTriggered by
__init__Object creation: MyClass(...)
__str__print(obj) / str(obj)
__repr__Debugger / interactive prompt
__eq__obj1 == obj2
__lt__obj1 < obj2
__len__len(obj)
__hash__hash(obj) — needed for set/dict keys
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting self in method definitions — Python won't auto-add it. def my_method(): ... won't work as a method.

Calling self when invoking: d.add_trick(d, "sit") — wrong. Just d.add_trick("sit"); Python passes self.

Confusing class attributes with instance attributes. Class attributes are SHARED across all instances; mutating a class-level mutable (like a list) affects all.

Forgetting super().__init__() when extending a parent class — the parent's setup never runs.

Using __init__ as if it returns something. It returns None — the instance is returned implicitly.

Capitalizing instance method names. By convention: ClassName is CapitalCase, method_name and attribute_name are snake_case.

"What is __init__?" → constructor; runs at object creation.

"What does self refer to?" → the current instance.

"What is inheritance?" → subclass reuses + extends parent's methods/attributes.

"What's polymorphism?" → same method name behaves differently in different classes.

"How do you call the parent's method from the subclass?" → super().method_name().

"Class vs instance attribute?" → class attribute is shared across all instances; instance attribute is per-instance.

"Trace this OOP code" — practice tracking attribute changes across method calls.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Class = blueprint; instance = object created from blueprint

  • self: refers to the current instance; first parameter of every method

  • Inheritance: class Sub(Parent): — subclass inherits all parent methods/attributes

  • Four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction

📖 Worked example — a hard complexity problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — Big-O of a tricky nested loop
for (i = 1; i <= n; i = i * 2)      # i: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... → log₂n passes
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++)          # n passes each time
        work()
Outer loop doubles i, so it runs ~log₂n times; the inner runs n times per pass. Total work = n · log n → O(n log n).

The method: count each loop’s passes SEPARATELY (doubling → log; linear step → n), then multiply nested counts. Doubling/halving anywhere = a log term — the single most useful pattern for hard Big-O questions.
⚠️ RECURSION COUNTS THE SAME WAY
A recursive function that halves its input and does O(1) work per call is O(log n) (binary search); halving with O(n) merge work per level is O(n log n) (mergesort). Match the recurrence to a known shape before deriving from scratch.

Complexity of Loops & Recursion

To bound a loop nest, sum the inner work over every outer iteration instead of multiplying blindly. A loop whose counter multiplies (j*=2) runs log₂n times; one that halves the remaining range does too. When the inner bound depends on the outer index, you get a triangular sum.

⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Triangular: Σ(n-i) = n(n+1)/2 = Θ(n²)
  • Geometric decay: n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = Θ(n)
  • Master-style recurrences: 2T(n/2)+O(n)→Θ(n log n); T(n/2)+O(1)→Θ(log n); 2T(n-1)+O(1)→Θ(2ⁿ).
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Comparison sorts cannot beat Ω(n log n).
  • Insertion sort is adaptive: O(n) on nearly-sorted input.
  • Quicksort worst case O(n²) when the pivot is always the min/max (already-sorted input with naive first-element pivot).
📝 TECHNIQUE

Binary-search variants (leftmost/rightmost/insertion point) keep the invariant and change only the tie-break: on equality, move hi=mid to find the first occurrence, or lo=mid+1 for the last.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Merge sort is stable and always O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space; heapsort is in-place but not stable. Selection sort does the fewest swaps yet stays Θ(n²) comparisons even if sorted.

📖 Worked example — a hard data-structures problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — choose the structure from the requirements
Problem: You need (a) O(1) average lookup by key, (b) iteration in insertion order is NOT required, (c) frequent inserts and deletes.

Walk the candidates: sorted array — O(log n) lookup but O(n) inserts ✗; linked list — O(n) lookup ✗; BST — O(log n) if balanced, still not O(1) ✗; hash table — O(1) average lookup/insert/delete ✓.

Then the follow-up trap: “what degrades a hash table to O(n)?” — many collisions (bad hash function or high load factor) chaining everything into one bucket. Requirements → eliminate candidates one property at a time; never pattern-match on a single word.
⚠️ “BALANCED” IS DOING THE WORK
Every O(log n) claim about a BST silently assumes balance (AVL/red-black). A plain BST fed sorted input degenerates to a linked list — O(n). Hard questions hinge on exactly that assumption.

Structure Operations at a Glance

Master each structure by its pointer or index mechanics, not just its Big-O. A singly linked reversal walks three pointers (prev, cur, next); deleting a node splices prev.next = cur.next.

⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Load factor α = n / table_size; open addressing degrades sharply as α→1.
  • Heap of n nodes has height ⌊log₂n⌋; child indices 2i+1, 2i+2.
  • BFS/DFS visit every vertex/edge: O(V+E).
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • BST inorder yields sorted order; preorder is root-first (good for copying).
  • Deleting a BST node with two children replaces it with its inorder successor (leftmost of the right subtree).
  • Push into a min-heap sifts up; pop swaps last into root and sifts down.
📝 TECHNIQUE

Linear probing on a collision tries (h+1) mod m, then +2, wrapping around; the first empty slot wins. Trace the wrap carefully near the end of the array.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

BFS uses a queue (FIFO) and finds shortest unweighted paths; DFS uses a stack/recursion and does not. Their visit orders differ, and both depend on the neighbor-iteration order you assume.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Intro to Data Structures & Algorithms

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Algorithms, Data Structures & ADTs

▸ THE KEY DISTINCTION An ADT is a contract ("what"): a Stack promises push/pop/peek with LIFO order. The underlying data structure is the "how": that Stack could be built on an array OR a linked list — callers never need to know which.

⚠ ADT ≠ DATA STRUCTURE "Stack" is an ADT (a set of rules); "array" is a data structure (a memory layout). Don't call an array an ADT, and don't call the Stack ADT a "data structure" on the OA.

Introduction to Algorithms

▸ PSEUDOCODE A structured, language-independent way to describe an algorithm's steps — precise enough to implement, without real syntax to get bogged down in.

⚠ CORRECTNESS BEFORE EFFICIENCY An algorithm that's fast but WRONG is worthless. Always verify correctness first (does it work on edge cases: empty array, one element, duplicates?), then worry about speed.

Data Structures vs Algorithms

▸ THE RELATIONSHIP An algorithm's efficiency often depends ENTIRELY on which data structure it operates over. The same task can be fast or slow purely based on that choice.

⚠ NO SINGLE "BEST" STRUCTURE Every data structure trades one operation's speed for another's. Choosing one always means choosing what you're willing to make slower.

Applications of ADTs

⚠ THE OA TESTS SCENARIO-MATCHING Expect questions phrased as a real scenario ("customers wait in line," "the most recent undo") — translate the ORDERING RULE (LIFO vs FIFO vs priority vs key-lookup) to find the right ADT: stack for undo/back, queue for waiting lines, priority queue for "most urgent next," dictionary/map for lookup by key.

"},"C949/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 Searching & Algorithm Analysis

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Linear Search

▸ THE ALGORITHM Check each element ONE BY ONE, in order, until you find the target or run out of elements. Works on ANY list — sorted or not.

⚠ NOT FOUND STILL COSTS O(n) Searching for a value that ISN'T in the list still requires checking every element before concluding "not found" — that's the worst case, not a shortcut.

Binary Search

▸ THE REQUIREMENT The array MUST be SORTED first. Binary search compares against the MIDDLE element and eliminates half the remaining search space each step.

▸ TIME COMPLEXITY O(log n) — each comparison halves the remaining elements: 1,000,000 elements takes at most ~20 comparisons.

⚠ UNSORTED DATA = BROKEN ALGORITHM Run binary search on an unsorted array and it can miss the target entirely — the halving logic only works because sorted order guarantees which half to discard.

Constant Time & Growth of Functions

▸ GROWTH ORDER, SLOWEST TO FASTEST-GROWING O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)

⚠ CONSTANT-TIME EXAMPLES array[i] access, push/pop on a stack's top, hash-table lookup (average case) — all O(1): the SAME cost whether the collection has 10 or 10 million items.

Big-O Notation

▸ DEFINITION Big-O describes an algorithm's worst-case UPPER BOUND on running time, as a function of input size n. It answers: "how does this SCALE?" — not "how many milliseconds?"

⚠ DROP CONSTANTS AND LOWER-ORDER TERMS O(2n + 5) simplifies to O(n). O(n² + n) simplifies to O(n²) — the fastest-growing term dominates as n gets large; the rest becomes irrelevant.

Algorithm Analysis

▸ TIME vs SPACE COMPLEXITY Time complexity: how many steps as n grows. Space complexity: how much EXTRA memory as n grows (beyond the input itself).

⚠ BIG-O USUALLY MEANS WORST CASE Unless a question explicitly says "best case" or "average case," assume Big-O refers to the WORST case — that's the standard convention.

"},"C949/cheat/c3":{"body":"

📋 Recursion

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Recursive Definitions

▸ THE ANATOMY — every recursive function has both parts def factorial(n): if n <= 1: return 1 # BASE CASE — stops the chain return n * factorial(n − 1) # RECURSIVE CASE — smaller input

⚠ NO BASE CASE = STACK OVERFLOW Without a base case (or with input that never reaches it), the function calls itself forever until the call stack runs out of memory — a runtime crash, not an infinite "loop" you can see.

Recursive Algorithms

⚠ EACH CALL GETS ITS OWN VARIABLES factorial(3) and factorial(2) each have their OWN n. Recursion works because every stack frame is independent — values don't overwrite each other.

Analyzing Recursive Time Complexity

▸ THE METHOD: COUNT THE CALLS × WORK PER CALL Total time = (number of recursive calls) × (work done inside each call, ignoring the recursive call itself).

▸ SPACE COMPLEXITY = MAXIMUM STACK DEPTH Recursion's memory cost is the DEEPEST the stack gets, not total calls: factorial(n) → O(n) space · recursive binary search → O(log n) space.

⚠ DON'T CONFUSE CALLS WITH DEPTH fib(5) makes 15 CALLS but its stack only gets 5 DEEP (one branch at a time). Time counts all calls; space counts only the deepest chain.

"},"C949/cheat/c4":{"body":"

📋 Sorting Algorithms

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Selection & Insertion Sort

▸ SELECTION SORT Repeatedly SELECT the smallest value from the unsorted part and SWAP it into the next sorted position.

▸ INSERTION SORT Take the NEXT element and INSERT it into its correct spot among the already-sorted elements to its left (shifting larger ones right).

⚠ THE OA'S FAVORITE DISTINCTION "Which sort performs best on NEARLY-SORTED data?" → INSERTION sort, O(n) best case. Selection sort never speeds up — it scans the whole unsorted part every pass no matter what.

Quicksort

▸ THE STRATEGY: PARTITION AROUND A PIVOT 1) Pick a PIVOT · 2) PARTITION: everything smaller goes left of it, everything larger goes right · 3) The pivot is now in its FINAL position · 4) Recursively quicksort the left and right parts.

⚠ THE WORST-CASE TRAP Quicksort's O(n²) worst case happens on sorted (or reverse-sorted) data with a naive pivot — each partition strips off just ONE element instead of halving. That "already sorted input can be the…

Merge Sort

▸ THE STRATEGY: DIVIDE, SORT, MERGE 1) Split the array in HALF recursively until pieces have 1 element (trivially sorted) · 2) MERGE pairs of sorted pieces back together in order.

⚠ THE TRADE Merge sort's superpower is its GUARANTEED O(n log n) worst case (no bad-pivot disasters like quicksort). Its cost: O(n) extra memory — it's not in-place.

Radix & Bucket Sort

▸ RADIX SORT Sort integers digit by digit, starting from the LEAST significant digit (LSD), using 10 buckets (0–9). Each pass must be STABLE (preserve tie order) for it to work.

▸ BUCKET SORT Distribute values into buckets by RANGE (e.g., 0–9, 10–19, …), sort each small bucket, then concatenate the buckets in order.

⚠ LSD FIRST, AND STABILITY MATTERS Radix processes the LEAST significant digit first, and each pass must keep equal-digit items in their existing order (stable) — otherwise earlier passes get scrambled and the result…

Sorting Algorithms Compared

▸ THE DECISION GUIDE Nearly-sorted data → Insertion (O(n) best) · Guaranteed worst case → Merge · Fast in practice, in-place-ish → Quicksort · Fixed-width integers → Radix · Tiny arrays / minimal swaps → Selection

⚠ THE COMPARISON-SORT FLOOR No COMPARISON-based sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case — that's a proven lower bound. Radix/bucket only "beat" it by not comparing values at all.

"},"C949/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Linked Lists

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

List ADT & Singly Linked Lists

⚠ NULL MARKS THE END The last node's next pointer is null — every traversal loop uses that as its stop condition. Forgetting it = walking off the end.

Singly Linked: Search, Insert, Remove

▸ SEARCH — walk from the head cur = head while cur ≠ null: if cur.data == target: return cur cur = cur.next — O(n): no shortcuts, no jumping to the middle.

⚠ POINTER ORDER IS EVERYTHING In insert-after, if you set B.next = X BEFORE saving B's old next into X.next, the reference to C is GONE — the rest of the list is lost forever. New node's next gets set FIRST, always.

Doubly Linked Lists

▸ THE UPGRADE Each node now has TWO pointers: next AND prev . You can walk the list in BOTH directions, and remove a node without hunting for its predecessor.

⚠ MORE POINTERS = MORE WAYS TO BREAK Every insert/remove must update BOTH directions. Miss one (forgetting C.prev = X) and forward traversal works while backward traversal is silently corrupted.

Linked List Traversal & Sorting

▸ THE UNIVERSAL TRAVERSAL PATTERN cur = head while cur ≠ null: visit(cur.data) cur = cur.next — the skeleton of printing, counting, summing, searching: everything.

▸ SORTING A LINKED LIST Insertion sort adapts beautifully: no shifting — just unlink a node and relink it into place. Merge sort is the classic choice: it only needs sequential access (split by walking, merge by relinking) → O(n log n) with no random access required.

⚠ BINARY SEARCH IS A TRAP ON LINKED LISTS Binary search needs O(1) jumps to the middle — a linked list takes O(n) just to REACH the middle. So binary search on a linked list is O(n) per step, worse than plain linear search. Binary search's O(log n) only holds on structures with O(1) indexing — arrays, not linked lists.

"},"C949/cheat/c6":{"body":"

📋 Stacks, Queues & Deques

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Stack ADT

▸ IMPLEMENTATIONS & USES Array (top index) or linked list (push/pop at head) — both O(1). Uses: undo/redo, browser back, the function CALL STACK, checking balanced parentheses "( [ ] )" — push openers, pop and match on closers.

⚠ PEEK ≠ POP peek() reads the top and leaves it; pop() removes it. Trace questions love mixing them to catch you.

Queue ADT

▸ IMPLEMENTATIONS & USES Linked list with head=front and tail=back gives O(1) at both ends. Arrays use a CIRCULAR buffer (wrap the indices) to avoid shifting. Uses: printer queues, task scheduling, BFS graph traversal, streaming buffers.

⚠ OPPOSITE ENDS Enqueue at the BACK, dequeue from the FRONT. Adding and removing at the same end would make it a stack — that's the whole distinction.

Deque ADT

▸ DEFINITION A deque ("deck") allows insertion AND removal at BOTH ends — front and back. It's the most flexible of the three linear ADTs.

▸ A DEQUE CAN IMPERSONATE BOTH Use only ONE end (add + remove at back) → it behaves as a stack . Add at back, remove at front → it behaves as a queue . Implementations: doubly linked list or circular array — O(1) at both ends.

⚠ DEQUE ≠ DEQUEUE "Deque" is the DATA STRUCTURE (double-ended queue). "Dequeue" is the queue OPERATION (remove from front). The OA loves this near-homonym.

"},"C949/cheat/c7":{"body":"

📋 Hash Tables

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Map ADT & Hash Functions

▸ THE MAP ADT A Map (Dictionary / Associative Array) stores key-value pairs — you look up by KEY, not index. put/get/remove/contains are all O(1) average, O(n) worst ; size() is O(1). The engine that makes O(1) possible is the hash function: hash(key) → integer in [0, capacity) , usually raw hashCode…

⚠ BAD HASHES & THE IMMUTABILITY RULE hash = 0 (everything collides, O(n)) · len(s) ("cat"/"dog"/"rat" → 3) · char-sum (anagrams "abc"/"cba" collide) · no modulo (index out of range). And keys must be IMMUTABLE — mutate…

Collision Resolution: Chaining

▸ COLLISIONS ARE INEVITABLE Two keys hashing to the same bucket = a collision . The pigeonhole principle guarantees them once keys outnumber buckets — and the birthday paradox says just 23 random insertions into 365 buckets already give a 50% collision chance. So every hash table needs a resolution…

⚠ WORST CASE & HASH FLOODING Adversarial or pathological keys can pile into ONE bucket → the table becomes a linked list, O(n) lookups. Real attack: hash flooding — crafted colliding data degrades servers; Python and…

Open Addressing

▸ THE IDEA No linked lists — every entry lives IN the array itself. On collision, probe for the next empty slot. Cache-friendly, less memory; Python's dict and Ruby's Hash use it. All three examples below: capacity 7, hash(n) = n % 7, inserting 18, 32, 25, 4 (ALL hash to slot 4).

⚠ TOMBSTONES & THE α CEILING You can't just blank a deleted slot — that BREAKS the probe chain for keys that probed past it. Use tombstones (deleted markers). And load factor must stay below ~0.7–0.75; open addressing…

Resizing & Cryptographic Hashing

▸ WHEN & HOW TO RESIZE After each insert, check α = n/capacity against the threshold — Java HashMap 0.75 (chaining) · Python dict 0.66 · Go map 0.65 (open addressing needs lower). Then DOUBLE the capacity and REHASH EVERYTHING — the bucket index depends on capacity, so every key's home changes.

⚠ CRYPTOGRAPHIC HASHES ARE A DIFFERENT BEAST SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3 need collision resistance and pre-image resistance and are SLOW by design. Table hashes (FNV, MurmurHash) need speed + uniformity. NEVER use one for the other's job: a hash table built on SHA-256 wastes time; a password system built on MurmurHash is a security hole.

"},"C949/cheat/c8":{"body":"

📋 Trees & Binary Search Trees

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Binary Trees & Applications

⚠ HEIGHT GOVERNS EVERYTHING Tree operations cost O(height). Balanced → height log₂(n) → O(log n). Degenerate (every node one child) → a linked list in disguise, height n − 1 → O(n). That's the entire reason balancing…

BST: Search & Insert

▸ THE BST PROPERTY — FOR EVERY NODE Everything in the LEFT subtree < node < everything in the RIGHT subtree — and it must hold for EVERY node, not just the root . Classic trap: a 12 tucked under 8's LEFT subtree looks fine locally but violates the property (12 > 8). Keys must be comparable.

⚠ INSERTION ORDER DECIDES THE SHAPE Feed the SAME values in sorted order [10, 20, …, 70] and every insert goes right → a degenerate right chain, height n − 1, O(n) search. This is precisely why self-balancing BSTs…

BST: Removal

▸ WHY THE SUCCESSOR WORKS It's the SMALLEST value larger than the removed node — so it's greater than the whole left subtree, smaller than the rest of the right subtree, and (being leftmost) it has no left child , so deleting it is always case 1 or 2. The predecessor (largest in the left subtree) is…

BST: Traversals

▸ THE MNEMONIC The name says where the NODE goes: pre = before children, in = between, post = after. Those three are DFS (recursion / a stack). Level-order is BFS — a QUEUE, level by level. All four are O(n). Reference tree: 4(2(1, 3), 6(5, 7)).

⚠ THE THREE EXAM HOOKS In-order on a BST = sorted output (the main reason BSTs exist — sorted iteration in O(n) with no sort). Queue ↔ level-order; stack/recursion ↔ the DFS three. Post-order deletes safely because children are visited before their parent — you never free a node while its subtree is still needed.

"},"C949/cheat/c9":{"body":"

📋 Heaps & Priority Queues

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Heaps & Heap Operations

▸ THE TWO RULES OF A HEAP Min-heap: every parent ≤ its children (smallest at root). Max-heap: every parent ≥ its children. AND a heap is always a complete binary tree — filled left-to-right — which is exactly what lets it live in a plain array with no pointers.

⚠ A HEAP IS NOT SORTED Only the ROOT is guaranteed min (or max). Siblings and levels can be in any order that respects the property — arbitrary search is O(n). Sift down swaps with the smaller child in a min-heap;…

Heapsort & Priority Queues

▸ HEAPSORT IN TWO PHASES ① Build a MAX-heap from the array — O(n). ② Repeat n−1 times: swap the root (max) with the last unsorted slot, shrink the heap by 1, sift the new root down — O(log n) each. Total O(n log n) , and the sorted tail grows from the right.

⚠ TWO EXAM TRAPS Heapsort is NOT stable — long-distance swaps reorder equal keys. And building the heap is O(n), not O(n log n) — the extract phase is what costs O(n log n).

"},"C949/cheat/c10":{"body":"

📋 Graphs

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Graph Terminology & Representations

⚠ THE DEFAULT IS THE LIST Social networks, the web, road maps — real graphs are sparse, so the adjacency list is the default. Choose the matrix only for dense graphs or constant-time edge checks.

Breadth-First Search (BFS)

▸ THE ALGORITHM Mark the start visited, enqueue it. Loop: dequeue v, then for each UNVISITED neighbor — mark visited and enqueue. FIFO order guarantees distance-0, then all distance-1, then distance-2… Swap the queue for a stack and you'd have DFS.

▸ ★ THE KEY PROPERTY The FIRST time BFS reaches a vertex is via the shortest path in EDGES (unweighted). Track parent pointers to reconstruct the route. Weighted graphs need Dijkstra (or Bellman-Ford for negatives). Connected components: run BFS from every unvisited vertex — each run finds one…

⚠ MARK VISITED AT ENQUEUE Mark when you ADD to the queue, not when you remove — otherwise a vertex can be enqueued twice. Complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V) space. Uses: shortest unweighted path, friend suggestions, web…

Depth-First Search (DFS)

▸ THE ALGORITHM Go deep along one path until stuck, then backtrack and try the next branch. Recursion IS DFS — the call stack is the stack. Iterative version: an explicit stack (LIFO pop) — the ONLY data-structure difference from BFS.

⚠ DFS ≠ SHORTEST PATH DFS can reach a vertex the long way first. For unweighted shortest path, it's BFS — a distinction the OA loves.

"},"C949/cheat/c11":{"body":"

📋 Sets

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Set Operations

▸ THE TWO DEFINING PROPERTIES ① No duplicates — adding an existing element does nothing. ② Unordered — no index, no first/last. A set answers one question brilliantly: "is x in here?" Lists are for arrangement; sets are for MEMBERSHIP.

⚠ TWO PYTHON TRAPS {} is an empty DICT — an empty set is set() . And frozenset is the immutable variant — usable as a dict key or inside another set. Bit-vector sets: blazing membership but only for small integer universes — one bit per possible element, so they shine for dense ranges like 0–1023, not arbitrary strings.

"},"C949/cheat/c12":{"body":"

📋 Python Fundamentals

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Python Control Flow

▸ THE PYTHON RULES INDENTATION defines blocks (no braces) · colon after if/elif/else/for/while/def · boolean operators are and, or, not (never && || !) · comparison chaining works: 0 <= x < 100 · falsy values: empty containers, 0, None, False · no ++ — use count += 1 .

⚠ FUNCTION SIGNATURES Default args def greet(name, greeting='Hello') · *args (positional varargs) · **kwargs (keyword varargs). break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration.

Object-Oriented Programming

▸ THE ANATOMY class Dog: with def __init__(self, name, breed): — the CONSTRUCTOR runs automatically at d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador") , initializing instance attributes via self.name = name . Classes are how you build every custom structure in this course — nodes, queues, graph vertices.

⚠ TWO EXAM TRAPS __init__ returns NOTHING explicitly (the new instance is returned implicitly). And forgetting self as the first parameter of a method is the classic Python class bug. Parent = superclass/base; child = subclass/derived — the child inherits and can override, and super() reaches the parent's version.
